Well, I was ACTUALLY tied to a desk with a 2.5ft cord 10hrs a day with only 10 minutes total of personal time to pee or get some water. Not at all allowed to leave my desk. Calls would drop into our headset one after another and if your calls were too long or if you were wrapping up and documenting in a patient's chart you were penalized. OH, and getting Covid 3 times, while working in Healthcare, it'll get you fired. But first, they force you to get vaccinated. When you're working from home. This place is absolutely the most mismanaged, disorganized, income focused, put on a good face, most unethical, group of trash I've ever met. Patient care is 100% not the focus. The goal is to keep calls (to patients, paging physicians, triaging, refill requests, suicide callers, limited English speakers, etc) under 5 minutes. You get 21 days off a year. But you have to take PTO for all mandatory off holidays. And if you get sick, you get pointed. If your family gets sick, you get pointed. I mentioned my family had Covid 3 times while I worked for Summa, for 12 months. I had to call off a lot but I was willing to pick up hours or even reduce to part time so I could care for myself and family. Further, this year was personally terrible. Close family deaths, broken rib, stage 3 pelvic prolapse, plus a chronic illness that often leaves me bedridden. Taking time off is not at all possible. Every single time I hurt myself, was sick, or my kids were sick, I got SUMMA doctor's notes or was willing to provide my grandma's obituary, for example. I felt so guilty every time I called off, I called my nurse supervisor and took a LIVE COVID TEST just so no one would write me up. You cannot take off work. Nope. Not an option. They pointed me to the point that I had to quit before termination. ......but my patient satisfaction ratings and audits were almost 5 stars or whatever point system they had. I would often take double the calls of my peers in a shift. Further, when I expressed my feelings my job was in danger no team lead, supervisor, manager, or director would help me. I contacted HR and they were also the worst (BTW I have a bachelor's in human resources). No one would help me. The leadership in the Clinical Access Center, with few exceptions, are not worth one single penny. My health was failing and I was forced to go on leave for surgery but thankfully got wind that I was going to be terminated, so I resigned. I could go on and on. When I was hired, they promised I could get on to a 7-3 shift and that was never offered even though when I was hired I was clear on my needs, instead they put on new people for desirable shifts just so they could fill seats. They also promised a $2hr raise at 90 days. That didn't come. And when I voiced that I wasn't being paid for the lunch shifts I worked through, they basically told me to shut up about it if I wanted to keep my job. I have never been so stressed out in my life than when I worked there. I am so relieved to be working for an organization who want to employ people with a good work ethic AND morals.

I have been having a great experience and am impressed with the CCT program. I am ALWAYS able to reach the CCT RN manager or my supervisor with any issue I run into, and very importantly they are both actively listening and are both easy to approach. I believe these are excellent characteristics as I believe a manager and supervisors need to be easily approachable and a good listener as this will allow the employees to be able to come forward comfortably with issues that need to be addressed or even clarifications. They both listen to everything being said and will provide input, constructive criticism, solutions, clarifications, and investigate any matter that requires attention. They are both easy to get a hold of at any time of day or night, they check in regularly, provides a lot of support, and will always follow up. They are always open to suggestions and feedback. While I was in training, the CCT manager would check in regularly and frequently with both me and my preceptor. An important point is that she would pull me aside and ask me how training is going and if there is any issues or concerns I may have. I believe this is another example of good leadership as it is building a positive relationship with your employees and allows them to bring up any issues or concerns without their preceptor present. My last job was in the ICU, and it was my first ICU job as I have most my experience in Emergency Department. As I was being oriented there were many issues, however because I did not have management check in with me regularly or even individually without my preceptor present, those issues were never addressed and had also become problems further on that were never resolved and affected training, training quality, and even when I was off training. That is why I believe it is important how she was checking in frequently with me. They are very big on the team aspect, working as a team, supporting the team, and taking care of the people under you. The CCT manager is very careful with the RN’s she selects to be part of the team, which is evident with the RN’s that are a part of the CCT team and how everyone interacts as a team. The culture of the CCT program is great and very supportive and the CCT team has a lot of diversity in the talent and skills it offers with the nurses she has selected and their background. It is exciting to see the new equipment such as the Zoll ventilators and the new Zoll monitors. Seeing the new bags that are being established at the Modesto station along with the new equipment and tools that are being implemented is also very exciting, such as the VividTrac. The new bags that are being set up are very logically organized in that supplies that would be used are grouped together and easy to find. The new changes with the supplies and tools are exciting because it is providing necessary equipment, resources, and education for us to be able do our jobs and to provide the best care possible for the patients. The CCT manager is a big advocate for her CCT team and is big on the safety of the team. This is very important to me knowing that I can rely on her as it allows me to focus on my job, knowing that my manager is doing everything she can in the best interest of the CCT team and safety of the CCT team. The other part that is important to me and I believe is important is to make the members of the team feel appreciated by their superiors and I feel appreciated every time I communicate with the manager, and other members of the CCT team. Overall I am very satisfied with the CCT program, leadership, team culture, resources and equipment being provided and implemented.

- The prospect of job growth appears uncertain, as employees often find themselves stuck in the same grade for years without any prospect of advancement. The process for promotion lacks transparency. Promotion hinges upon the achievement of targets that are unattainable and lack strategic merit. - There are redundant grades and promotion schemes put in place to stall employees' growth. A prime example is the Senior Executive Trainee (SET) grade, which falls between the Executive Trainee (ET) and Assistant Banking Officer (ABO) grades. Another example is the 'ABO designate' grade; basically, you are out of the SET bucket, but not quite an ABO yet. Again, these grades are more or less black holes intended to suck 3-6 years of your career while erroding your value and marketability in the job market, so that if you were to switch to a different bank, they would typically only be considered for the next grade, which is ABO. - UBA's remuneration package is not competitive with the market rate. This, coupled with a lack of career progression, means that employees may find themselves in stagnant positions that offer little room for growth, while also being compensated less than their counterparts in other banks. To compound the matter, the bank does not offer performance bonuses, and the targets that such bonuses are dependent upon are often unrealistic, leaving staff to feel as though they are chasing unattainable goals. This has caused many employees to feel undervalued and underappreciated. - One of the key issues at UBA is the top-heavy organizational structure, which results in senior management being compensated far more generously than the lower-level staff who are responsible for carrying out the actual work. - Additionally, the staff health plan appears to be inequitable and poor, as the bank does not provide sufficient compensation for health insurance. As a result, employees may be subjected to substandard treatment from their Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) and the hospitals registered with them. To deal with this, staff typically have to carve out part of their already insufficient income in order to access proper healthcare. - The current management at UBA appears to be disconnected from reality, as there is a noticeable absence of proper strategic management. Instead of developing a comprehensive plan, the bank's approach to strategic planning revolves around short-sighted goals such as surpassing competitors in a particular field; "This month, our goal is to 'overtake' the Orange Bank!" This myopic and juvenile approach appears to be borne out of a lack of long-term vision. In addition, management tends to be impatient with the delivery of strategic initiatives, often expecting quick results for initiatives that require a long-term approach. - There is no work/life balance. The bank requires too much from overwhelmed staff that are not appropriately compensated. - I do not also believe UBA is a great institution for learning and growth. There is no structured graduate training program that allows for a hands-on approach to learning and development; in some cases, trainees have been left out in the cold, without proper work tools or direction. - The bank is not a future-thinking one, choosing to remain uncreative in its approaches. No creativity, no innovation. Just dead strategies and old people. - A sad place to work.

Working at Interfor has been one of the best career moves I have made. Although my base role was as a recruiter for our salaried operations, I have worked with almost every department in HR on projects and initiatives related (and sometimes not) to my role. As someone who has worked with a lot of recruitment processes and systems in the past, I can say that Interfor has some of the most progressive recruitment processes I have worked with. Even when things have been seemingly perfected, the team here is not one to rest with the status quo, they are always looking at the next trend or development in recruitment that we can implement or try. The management at Interfor seems to really care about engaging employees and keeping them excited and motivated about their job. During my Career Development Plan meetings, I've been asked every year what I'd like exposure to, and within weeks I've been set up with that team or put on a project related to that. Interfor is also a very family friendly place to work, I don't feel micro-managed and I am fully trusted to do my job, even if that means working from home to take care of a sick child. You've only got to Google Evri to see all the bad press around them. Who'd of thought that paying the absolute minimum and pushing for maximum productivity would be a flawed system that results in parcels going missing and a delivery driver shortage? The maths. £1 insurance per day. Car wear and tear. Petrol was about £40-50 a week. So that's £230 before tax and NI. standard rate is 50p per parcel delivery (you can negotiate and they put mine at 75p). So at 50p, you'd have to deliver 160 parcels a day to make £80 (which isn't always possible). £1600 minus £230 and the tax and NI you'd end up with £1050. Plus, delivering 160 parcels would take at least 8 hours. I worked it out and I was getting about £5 an hour. Being self-employed there's no minimum wage which is how they get away with it. Pretty sure the warehouse isn't health and safety compliant. Takes them ages to get back when you submit a pay review (I submitted one on the 29th of December and haven't heard back). The pay needs to increase about 10% for anyone with 5+ years experience, anytime there is a new starting wage the senior tm wage needs to adjust accordingly. The stress of the job is relative to who your direct manager is - mine was great, but there is a major inconsistency between divisions, regions, and sales areas. Where to even begin… I am honestly sad at what this company has come to. I took this job for its values. It cared greatly about its people, their health, and their families. It is no longer that. We are working under a “Reynolds First” moto, and that spills into everything else. You are expected at 100% at everything you do, and that is very hard to do for a company who makes it very clear you are nothing but a number to them. We are working long days and hours to just make our coverage, and aren’t even able to utilize our vacations. The stress and toll this job has taken on so many people is unbelievable. I used to be proud to work here and how I’m honestly embarrassed I still do.

Since BAT took over the previous company value of "work, life, balance" is gone. The Last restructure was brutal. Statements made about it being a global restructure where false. Most of the cuts were "made in America" (their top earning global entity). The new parent company has no empathy. We all waited 6 months to find out our fate and no one was motivated. Instead of inspiring workers to achieve high standards they created a "swinging door" mentality. Those of us left are now cleaning up the mess from colleagues who embraced this call coverage strategy with no intention of working until they discovered their fate.
Workload is still very high, however the leadership is aware and are making efforts to improve the balance.

While I had a great career at RAI, the only thing I miss about the job are the friends I made along the way in all levels of the organization. The job I was hired to do was no longer the job that I was doing when I left which is to be expected as a career spans over the long number of years that I gave to the company. However, there was almost nothing about the job that was challenging, enjoyable or fun when I left. I no longer felt fulfilled or like I had any autonomy to use my sales experience or expertise to accomplish my goals and felt more like a robot being told what to do. It is bearable if you have a good, supportive manager (I always did, thankfully!), but miserable if not with the constant pressures to achieve more, faster. Through my time at Willamette Valley Vineyards, it's been quite a journey. For the first couple days, one of the first things I noticed was the stellar wine and delicious food (hooray for shift glasses!). Then I was here for a week, I started to meet all sorts of great people. I learned about the history of the company, and I was astonished by the passion, drive and endurance of the foundation of the company. I couldn't stop learning about the inventive ways our Founder, Jim Bernau, kept the early days afloat! It's certainly not all too often we see a company become a wild success to the point that the company is recognizable to an entire region just by the name. When I heard about the opportunity to work there, I knew it must be a good place to work. I grew up seeing the sign for the McMinnville Tasting Room, and Willamette Valley Vineyards was a common brand brought up all over my hometown. Moving on from the "story" and getting specific, this company has been and continues to be a place where we can feel welcome. New ideas are regularly welcome, the CEO is quite accessible for bringing up issues and when everyone works together as a team, nothing is unachievable here. I've seen a few friends start at "Entry Level" positions and move on to management and boy, do they deserve it. Although the structure can be a little confusing to someone without much Business Management experience (someone like me), it makes sense in the way of checks and balances. There's been a time or two where I found myself asking "Why is this my responsibility rather than such-and-such department?" Each time, I realized that it was because each department will have their own piece that fits perfectly into the 'puzzle'. The structure is intended to not only keep the company safe, but to ensure that everyone feels supported. That's not something you see in every work place. This place has been packed full of new experiences for a person, like me, who hadn't had a workplace so full of passion. Willamette Valley Vineyards is truly an inspiring place, and it has helped me get my career on track by learning through new experiences, feeling supported and being actively encouraged to be a part of such a great team.

Willamette Valley Vineyards is not for the faint of heart. The work environment across all departments is fast paced and brisk. Self-starters, motivated, and and those who can adapt to a quickly changing environment are very successful. I don't know of any other organization that offers as many opportunities for growth as Willamette Valley Vineyards. There are many examples of employees who were hired to fill entry level positions that within a few years move into leadership roles. The leadership team is good at identifying talent and quickly positioning it in areas that are a better fit for both the employee and the company. It is no surprise that more than 50% of the management team is comprised of women. If you work hard, you will find success. My experience has been overwhelmingly positive. I feel engaged, challenged, and fulfilled on a daily basis.

It is my recommendation to each employee to monitor this within yourself. We all want you to stay happy and healthy, and the best thing you can do to stay that way is to not let yourself get burnt out. The quickest way to get burnt out is by overworking yourself.

The reasons that make Willamette Valley Vineyards a great place to work are also the reasons that make it challenging for others. If you are looking for predictable work environment where you do the same thing day in and day out, then Willamette Valley Vineyards is not for you. If you cannot adapt to the changing landscape, then Willamette Valley Vineyards is not for you. If you can't work well as part of team, if you are easily offended, if you find it hard to communicate with others, or if your expectations are not aligned with the reality of working in a dynamic environment, then Willamette Valley Vineyards is not for you. We definitely sacrifice our future success for the good of the shareholders today. We seem shortsighted in our decisions (or lack thereof). In a very risk averse culture we frequently pass up on opportunities for growth and improvement, and consistently resist investments that don't pay off IMMEDIATELY. A lot of decisions that simply don't make sense. I think this comes along with a switch from management that "started at the bottom" within Eastman to external mangers who understand business, but not manufacturing or technical innovation. The qualities that get you promoted are RARELY the qualities that actually make a good manager. Probably as good as any big company, but suffers under the burdens big companies suffer under. I would love to see more drive to achieve and more focus on growth. Another topic, (and I hate to complain because I definitely consider myself an ally) but I don't like the way Eastman is pushing diversity goals right now. It's like it's the only thing that matters, and everyone's too afraid to say anything about it. As a woman in STEM, I absolutely admire the goal of getting more women and engineering in management, however, we go about it SO WRONG. We just decided to not change ANYTHING about the culture, or dig into WHY female engineers leave the company, we just unilaterally made a goal to get gender parity by 2030. Without any other changes, the only way to do this is only hire women (whether they are the most qualified or not) and/or push out men who have done nothing wrong. I wish we would instead improve support for new parents, or offer day care, or adopt flexible WFH policies. All of these would achieve our goals of RETAINING good women, instead of just hiring 90% women with the understanding that most will quit, and ignoring perfectly qualified men. People already grumble about unfair promotions and frankly I'd rather be a minority than equally represented but resented and perceived as unqualified. Finally, Eastman no longer seems to value employees and reward service the way it did in the past. Initial offers are lucrative, but raises are consistently below inflation (3% this year with inflation at 6.5%). This would be fine if the company were suffering, but it's making plenty of money. As an individual handling multi million dollar savings processes but giving up my breakroom coffee because of budget cuts, I am resentful. I truly love the people and community here, but it seems to be leftover from a golden age gone by, and good people (who wanted to spend their lives in Kingsport) are being pushed out.

Before applying to any part of this company, please look into the current owners of this company and its' current financial state, along with the ongoing lawsuits. Please also look at what happened to their previous schools/organizations as well. The nature of the job is very fickle. Your job roles and responsibilities are often changed, and you do not have a say in that. Additional expectations are added often. There are metrics you have to meet per day, per week per month, and per year. Failure to do so is penalized. Technical issues are not taken into account; you may be logged as clocked out during the time so you are not paid, which is understandable in some cases, but if not, then it is lost time in which you are failing to meet your expected numbers. All work is timestamped and evaluated closely. Most of the day is phone work, receiving calls via a queue system, making calls from assigned lists, and making calls via a dialer system. Coordinating with other departments is difficult and frequent, and there is no way to log a complaint or report someone from a other department when they are aggressive or display legitimately concerning behavior towards you or others. Raises are scarce and monetary bonuses are even more rare, and heavily taxed. Often, instead of a raise or bonus, employees receive corporate gifts (plastic cup/notebook) with the company logo. My team managers and coworkers were generally very pleasant and helpful, though I think that is uncommon in this company. And higher management consistently overrules what little your own manager can do for you. Mentioning any mental health issues or any disorders (ADHD, autism, anxiety, etc) has made a negative impact every time I've heard or seen it happen, and has placed the employee under scrutiny. I made a friend while here, but nothing else- the workload is worsening and the metric numbers are even more strict, which is why there is a high turnover rate here and most are extremely unhappy with their job. People are constantly looking for other employment.

Adventhealth used to be an organization with integrity but somewhere between their bottom line and acquisitions, they've lost their ability to follow through on their word. When the pandemic hit us instead of laying off employees they required us to spend our PDO so that they could ultimately settle their books. Everyone was okay with it because we still had work when so many didn’t . During that time period, we were allowed to work fully remote because no one was sure about the transmission of covid and they assured us that they cared for us. They continued to assess things and even instituted metrics for many departments who didn’t have any previously. Even with being at home we continued to surpass our markings and hit unbelievable goals with supporting our organization. Many of us work long hours beyond the 8 to 5 scope because volume dictated that. We were fine with doing that because we have the flexibility of working from home. We were promised that home is where we’d remain with occasional in-person meeting. Now we have executive leadership pulling the plug on something that isn't broken. They're once again meddling just to flex their muscle despite what the number say and it's disgusting. We literally sit in cubicles all day long and never speak to each other because quite frankly, our jobs don't require it. We are in cubicles that go above our head basically creating a fully partitioned space but we're going back in for “culture”. They don’t truly understand how culture is implemented and it's showing. We made life changes based on the word of Adventhealth and they've been less than honest with us. People are scrambling to find new work, vehicles or even new departments that don’t fall under the corporate scope because we were lied to. We’re responsible to carry out service standards for our organization: Love Me, Keep Me Safe, Make it Easy & Own It. But somehow we're always getting the short end of the stick. The service standards clearly don't apply to us because if they did, we wouldn’t be facing this level of transition that's threatening the entire ecosystem of our department structure. The standards mean nothing in you all pick and choose whom they apply to and not make everyone who wears a heart tag is responsible for holding them up.

We worked the extra hours being remote and didn’t have a problem with it—no commute, flexibility with work and home balance, but we still got the work done working those long hours and weekends. Productivity has increased dramatically with this flexibility. Even with all the extra work, I have never been happier in my career than with the remote lifestyle. The corporate team was told last year that we would stay remote and only need to come in once a month. Based on this promise, team members changed their lives—they moved, sold cars, made changes to their family dynamic, all while still managing to get the work done. Trust has been broken as we were lied to. We are now being told we must return to the office three days a week. If team members don’t trust their leaders what does that say about AdventHealth? I have actually talked more with coworkers through teams than I ever did in the office. With the three-day mandate back to the office team members will leave. It's a great place for several reasons: - Work-life balance is highly respected. - Really tightly-knit community. - Super-flexible in terms of work at home, flex hours, etc. - No pidgeon-holing, and no discrimination. If you are willing to take on a challenge, you get to do it. Performance talks, not politics or old boy's clubs. - Easy to move around to different roles within the company if you need a change. - Good team vibes, people generally work together and help each other out. I was hired at BAE from out of state and told I had a job. Sold my house and moved. Right as my house is closing I'm told "actually find something else as we don't know if this is your start date now but we'll let you know". Then a month later it's "You have one more interview. If you don't pass then you don't have a job." This is despite me having an offer letter and moving across states and buying and selling a house. Finally I get a start date and leave my temporary job. When I get to the job it's not at all what the listing said (the listing is still being used so ask questions if you're applying for this position) or what the interview said. And the shift isn't what I was told either. "Well I guess I'll make due. I'll work on getting my masters degree since they offer to pay for some of it" I think. Except I can never reach my boss about it. Neither can my coworkers. You ask 3 questions that are important and only get one answered a week later. You find your bosses supervisor doesn't respond at all. Eventually I turned in my notice and essentially had to offboard myself. I've never seen a more disorganized company based on my experiences.

Market rates (pay) consistently behind the rest of the market and other companies. Employees should not have to try and take an opportunity elsewhere to receive a pay rate that matches their worth. Changes to processes, procedures, software and hardware needs to happen much quicker for the IT portion of the company. Process for being cleared to various programs broken, difficult, and takes far too long.

Company is really big on bate and switch. The job you end up doing doesn't even remotely resemble the job description you apply for. Benefits are horrible. There's little incentive to want to do a good job other than to keep your job. The facilities in Nashua are very old and outdated. They car more about diversity, equity, and inclusion than anything else.

They brag about how they're one of the top employers in the state for job satisfaction, but I saw some very high turnaround. While they do a great job and onboarding and making you feel welcome, the work can be extremely boring. On top of that, software/clearance access can take months, which means you might not be able to do anything for at least 3 months after joining. I felt the work itself was meaningless. I "reviewed" documents, and put notes into a folder. I asked why, and I was told that my notes would be helpful for the next reviewer. I still feel this accomplished nothing, and was a waste of tax dollars. Non-engineers seemed to love it, but no engineers stayed around for more that a year or two.

Taxes are real high for what you get in the area. Fortunately houses are cheap compared to many places, and you can pretty easily live across the border in PA to get much lower property taxes. Salaries are lower than urban areas, in line with the lower cost of living around here. There are some pros to being part of a massive corporation - financial stability is a big one. But it also means that there can be a lot of red tape and regulations. There's a bit of a college-age scene downtown, but it's definitely not a big-city cultural experience. I should note there are also have facilities in Ft Wayne Indiana and Austin Tx which have the same work culture, same management structure, but let you live somewhere else if you want.

Pay practices are infuriating and wrought with errors. What they pay falls short of what they will promise during interview and will be divided in to arbitrary pay categories defined by pay letters that expire. Even after letters are issued, roll out of pay letters, covering everything from annual pay raises to annual bonuses and additional pay for working outside of a standard 9-5 schedule, promise date for pay to show up in checks is missed repeatedly. The need to audit paycheck vs. hours worked is constant. Delays for pay increases/bonuses/differential pay is always at least 3-6months, no doubt with the hope that people will depart before paid what they are owed. Consequently, there is unanimous frustration and disgust across the work force. When my company was purchased by Brillio, I did a bit of research and found that Bane Capital companies were known for buying companies for badges and cutting a majority of the staff. Our tale was no different, it just took about a year for it to really happen. Over the course of my last year there, when we became official 'Brillio employees', it became very clear that we were considered second-class. Not being considered for projects that we were over qualified for, being given computers that weren't capable of doing the work we required them to do, not knowing where our employees were actually located (which lead to many 2am phone calls from IT support), and just an overall disregard for the fact that they now had to manage North American employees. Larger than all of the little things was the gas-lighting by the HR department when it came to our pay. The process of moving us over to Brillio's payroll was a painful one - what was initially promised as a 10% flat pay bump in lieu of the existing bonus program, by the end of it all, landed at a 3-5% bump (still in lieu of our 10-12% bonuses), which equals a fairly large pay cut for a majority of employees. This was supposed to take effect multiple times, with multiple communications including dates that this would take effect. Each time one of these changes was announced, we wouldn't hear that it wasn't happening until a week or two after it was supposed to be implemented. Any time we would reach out for an update on what would be happening to our pay, we were met with disregard or, more commonly, silence. When we attempted to relay what had been told to us in previous meetings, we were told 'no one ever said that, so let's stop talking about it', and suddenly the recordings for said meetings were 'accidently corrupted'. You can make your own assumptions there, but I know that I am not alone in feeling as though these were deliberate actions by the company to mislead their employees. This all came to a head when they began calling over 50% of our employees, giving them two weeks' notice of their termination without even having discussions with those employee's managers (I was one of them - my job was only saved because I was making the company a bunch of money). All of this, and they do not give annual raises that outpace inflation and already pay their engineers significantly lower than the market rate. This is partially to do with the fact that they have a very small presence in NA, with most of their staff being offshore. If you have an offer to go work at Brillio, or you are an unfortunate soul like me whose company just got bought out by Brillio, run far and run fast.

Instead I had to work on other rides, and since the ride I was hired for might come back "at any moment", they refused to give me many chances at advancing. Also, if you advance to a Lead or higher in promotion, expect to get stabbed in the back eventually then fired. companies.name: Hodgson Russ LLP
allPros: The attorneys I work for are awesome! The paralegals I work with are equally amazing. This is my first job as a paralegal and everyone in my department has been so patient with me and are always so willing to answer all of my many questions. The environment here is great. Everyone cares about the well-being of each team member and it honestly feels like a family!

So far, I am happy working at Hodgson Russ. I have been quite busy at times, and it can be demanding, but I love what I do and feel it is the nature of the business. With that said, they aim to promote a healthy work-life balance, even if it does not always turn out that way. Most of the folks I work with are approachable, genuine, understanding and grateful for staffs' hardwork. The training is pretty thorough and is on-going. They are understanding that while you have experience in the field, it takes time to adjust to the firm's practices. They have also been understanding when I need to work from home and have even encouraged it on certain occasions. Therefore, you do not feel obligated to come to the office if someone in your household is not feeling well, if the weather is poor or if you need to run an errand during the day. I think they recognize it makes more sense for their employees to work from home as opposed to either calling out or taking the time to drive in to the office after an appointment (within reason of course). In fact, I will be permitted to work from home 1 day a week routinely after 1 year of service. I am not sure if legal secretaries are given the same level of understanding though. While they are permitted to work from home at times, it appears to me they are expected to be more discretionary with this practice. I bring this up because there is often some cross-over between paralegals and legal secretaries. The pay and benefits are good, but bonuses are unclear to me at this point. Albeit, I am not quite at my 1 year mark (I have been at the firm for 11 months). On the other hand, I did receive a decent annual increase. It appears that this is one of the few firms that tend to offer advancement opportunities, but it is unclear how you would go about being a candidate. The key to me is how approachable almost everyone has been thus far. I can say that while there are exceptions, I still genuinely like everyone I have worked with to this point, which speaks volumes, especially considering they are a larger firm.
allCons: There aren’t separate banks for sick and vacation time. As a working mother with small children, I feel like I’ll never be able to take a real vacation with my family because the little time off I receive is always being used for sick time and/or doctors appointments.

TCB was once a great place to work. I thought I would spend the rest of my career there until Rob Holmes showed up with plans to turn TCB into JP Morgan 2.0. Unfortunately for TCB, there is a big difference in $3.8T in assets and $28Bn in assets. Therefore the deal profiles that bankers have been tasked with targeting are unrealistic given they don’t have the balance sheet to play that space. This is evidenced by a severely underperforming corporate banking vertical which was supposed to drive deposit growth to propel the new investment bank. Strong employees have been leaving in droves as the average tenure of the current staff is 6 months - 1 year. Not to mention that all of the newer employees are getting paid materially more than those who had been there. So - all that’s left at TCB currently is a bunch of overpaid seat-fillers and management knows it (as evidenced by the layoffs that affected ~10% of the workforce). All of that to say that is is strongly discouraged to take a position at TCB at this time unless you are completely desperate.

Paycom has truly changed my life. In 7 years I have risen through the ranks from an entry level TSR position, to management, to a regional manager, to senior leadership. I have promoted several other leaders on my path up the ladder and it is amazing how many "Congratulations" speeches I have had the honor to craft over the years. Because of my success at Paycom, I am building an incredible life for my family. My children will be afforded opportunities I only dreamed of growing up. Our goals of retiring abroad are real and attainable. Along the way I have learned so much personally and professionally and I have made life-long friendships. Every day I am challenged and pushed outside my comfort zone. I am surrounded by people who are smart, hard-working, and care about me and my success. I have autonomy and I am given the opportunity to lead huge strategic initiatives with big impacts. Paycom is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity with unlimited growth potential. The culture here is the real deal. Paycom also invests so much in developing and training their employees and I love that I am always learning and growing. I am so excited about the future of Paycom and it is fulfilling to play a role in that.
Great corporate culture. Lots of opportunities for growth. Good salary. Great benefits.

The role itself doesnt provide a lot of incentive to work hard and grow unless you want to promote to a team leader. Specialists who have been here a long time will make a lot more no matter how hard they work. The financial incentive to take on more clients isn't there until years into the role, and even then it is minimal. There can be quite a bit of micromanagement when common problems are identified. You truly need to be internally motivated to stay here. The potential to make good money is there, but requires a perfect storm of hard work, the right team/opportunities, and a solid amount of luck.

Unrealistic expectations. Humans are not capable of doing things as fast as they want and still providing good quality. Even mediocre quality really. Sometimes if you make a mistake they make such a big deal out of it that they make you want to quit. I don’t know. Maybe that is their goal. But I’m not going nowhere unless they make me. I know it’s important for them to say they have work life balance, but that is not the case. At least not three months out of the year. Instead of limiting how many codes someone can take or hiring more people, they just keep loading it on. And then they get mad if you can’t meet their deadlines.
Required to work on site, Parking, buildings at capacity, commute, toxic hustle culture

The workload for this position is ridiculously high for 1 person. Managing your 80-160 assigned client’s emails, jira tickets, and several other internal emails (which can easily range on a daily between 80-150 emails). Must meet SLA of 2 hours on emails. No one can leave, until everyone in your hub is at ZERO emails, even after your shift has ended. On top of all that, you’re required to be in queue your entire shift answering incoming calls while simultaneously replying to emails. If that’s not enough, when a teammate is OOO, email coverage is needed so you’re pushed into taking on their email workload while still be required to adhere to the above items. When calling out unexpectedly, you’re responsible to cancel meetings on your calendar and find email coverage. WHILE YOU’RE OUT SICK or an EMERGENCY!!! Burnout is apparent on a daily. No work life balance. Turnover rate is always high. No time for self development. No Time to learn product updates. Management seems to think by continuing to put band-aids on these real and present issues will eventually get resolved. “Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.”

I don't fully agree with or understand some upper management decisions, although I do fully trust my immediate supervisors. Your work experience can vary a good amount depending what team you work on. The work itself may not change, but the process and environment "feel" will be different. You have a say on where you get placed, and every team works a bit differently, thankfully I love my team. Paycom traffic is definitely noticable. I work 7-4, so I don't notice it as much, if at all. But something to be aware of at 8AM and 5PM.

I've had the opportunity to work deals with exciting logos early in my career. The enablement is world-class. On both Product & the Technology Sector as a whole. I am compensated handsomely for the hard-work I put in. (Also DDOG Employee Stock hold a ton of value) The environment is fast-moving & competitive. Meaning, you perform well, and you can advance your professional roadmap quickly. (I'm on my 4th promo in 3 years)

Datadog has excellent products and has made some really strong hires in CS over the last 24 months. Great Product that works in most tech stacks.
Great pay - it’s a tech company formed in the late aughts that blossomed right before the pandemic. Salary is great. They try VERY hard to be seen as a good company to work at.

- Great pay - Good work / life balance - Product is well-designed and good at what it does and is thoughtfully expanding to new use cases - Product used by biggest (and coolest) companies on planet - Everyone on product & engineering is extremely intelligent, most are thoughtful and kind - You spend little to no time managing Jira or writing tickets, mostly focusing on vision and execution

Datadog is the premier product in the monitoring and observability space. As we are an expensive product you very rarely lose deals based on the products capabilities. The sales culture here is very lively and collaborative where it is very easy to learn from your peers who are seeing success. I came in to this role from being an SDR at another tech company and Datadog has given me the skills to really thrive in a sales career at any company. The benefits are also top notch with full health coverage and $1200 for a fitness reimbursement.
good training and fun teams
allCons: Hybrid environment & very difficult to get fully remote. This is why most people leave because there isn't much flexibility unless you want to move where there is another office location.

The Cons of being an AE/Salesperson at Datadog depends on an individuals desires & goals within their new role. For example - If someone is looking for a role with the majority of their salary coming from base pay, New Business Sales at DD (and most tech companies) is not a perfect fit. If someone is looking for a role with a heavy amount of inbound pipeline, the Account Executive seat at DD is not a perfect fit. If someone isn't driven to reach promotion in a competitive environment, and would like a more steady 9-5 role, the Account Executive seat at DD is not a perfect fit. All in all - it's an environment & role fit for people driven to make significant strides in professional development, work complex deals, and receive compensation that reflects their input.
Product usage and pricing can get confusing internally and externally. We are a 3-day in-office hybrid workforce. Salary is starting to get more competitive elsewhere.

Unless you are promoted internally, you will have an extreme challenge succeeding in your role. Favoritism is an understatement here. It is the classic "Best sellers make the best leaders" (They don't) and if you do not fit the mold of your manager, you will be shunned like an ugly duckling. Leadership is the main problem here. With a massive "selling bro" as the director, anyone who was not in a frat, didn't play lacrosse or doesn't enjoy drinking with their coworkers till 4 AM on a Wednesday will be looked at as a "loser". Middle management tries to provide an open door policy, but slip up and say anything negative and you can expect to be forced to quit via an unachievable PIP or fired on the spot. When in the interviewing process, ask the managers how many people have been on and off their team over the past calendar year. Ask how many reps an account goes through before being closed out. Ask the director how they train/empower their leaders. Ask how many reps have quit the job without any other jobs lined up (The number is staggering).

This is just my situation. But it is a doozy. I was contacted by one of their recruiters, looking to hire for the position since the person who had that position got promoted. Interview was fine, expect for one Sr level person who the recruiter warned me was an odd person. Little did I know how odd. I got the position, and took the job. The immediate team and manager were fantastic, but there was some cult-ish and strange sense that I could not shake. Almost 2 years into the position, it became very clear just how thin skinned the Sr level manager really was. If management even gets a hint of a worker who has a mind of their own, be prepared for surveillance. I was contacted by a Sr person in the HR (people ops! Naturally!) dept telling me to take my TikTok account down because it seemed like I was speaking negatively of the company. Meanwhile, the Sr person who had just become my manager recently was actively looking at ways to get rid of me. Eventually it came to a place where there was just no way to be at the company and maintain my sanity. But it is amazing the lengths at which HR will go to bat for bad leadership and make excuses. I heard from other employees during my tenure how bad things could be, and I am sad to learn that no one exaggerated just how bad things can be. The CEO and his co founder are pretty aloof for all their talk of how much they consider themselves part of the team. Which is fine, they’re both worth multiple billions. But they’re pretense that they are just like us - that’s not an honest picture. For all their talk of being a very modern company, sadly Datadog is just as “corporate” as 100+ year companies.

allCons: The appraisal process at Lenskart is quite disappointing. The fact that the company extends the appraisal process all the way until 31st July, instead of ending it by the usual deadline of 1st May, in order to prevent employees from leaving, Lenskart prioritizes retaining employees over providing fair and timely evaluations. This approach seems to be more focused on manipulating employees rather than empowering them. By extending the appraisal process, Lenskart effectively prevents employees who are dissatisfied with their current job from leaving and pursuing better opportunities elsewhere. This is not only unfair, but it also creates a negative work environment where employees may feel trapped and undervalued. Moreover, the company's retention strategy seems short-sighted as it doesn't address the root causes of attrition. Instead of addressing the reasons why employees may be considering leaving, Lenskart is merely trying to prevent them from doing so. This approach leads to a culture of mediocrity where employees are not motivated to perform their best and don't feel valued. Overall, the appraisal process at Lenskart seems to be flawed, and the company's approach to employee retention seems to prioritize short-term gains over long-term success. Employees deserve a fair and timely appraisal process that accurately reflects their performance and provides them with the opportunity to grow and succeed in their careers.

Contentsquare has established a strong reputation as the go to leader in digital experience. As the company continues to grow and expand its presence throughout the world, I am very excited about the potential for personal success and growth. The trajectory of the company is truly special and I look forward to being a part of this exciting journey and contributing to its continued success. The SDR Manager, Nick, always makes himself available for coaching and truly cares about the wellbeing of his team. One of the things I noticed right away was that Nick never asks you to do something that he wouldn't do himself and is always open to constructive feedback. Weekly 1:1's provide the opportunity to ask questions, talk strategy, refine your process, and even discuss life outside of work. Onboarding was quick and the training resources were easy to digest. Repeated layoffs of valued, loyal, hard-working employees who had been with the company for years, have happened in secret. HR then threatened anyone who posted about the layoffs on LinkedIn and denied to greater Nordic that this had even happened. Greatly respected leaders who were responsible for creating profitable divisions have been forced to leave. Management was forced to break salary bands and progression models for hard work employees by new direction from HR. companies.name: Sacramento Chinese Community Service Center
allPros: Open work flow. As a team leader, you have the opportunity to cater your plans to the kind of students you have. My group of 5th and 6th graders were an active bunch, so everyday without fail, after an hour of homework, my students would vote on what physical activity we would do together. Plenty of dodgeball, basketball, and tetherball tournaments! Like most jobs working with children, the work can be so fulfilling! It does come with the caveat that you'll have a crazy incident every now and again that you have no control over and you'll promptly be blamed for it as the low man of the totem pole, but you just have to keep on pushing. Believe that your work matters because it does! The students as well as the teachers were provided free meals (sometimes just snacks) by the school.
allCons: Few opportunities to get more hours. You're pretty much stuck at roughly 4-5 hours a day since it's an after-school program. All team leaders across the program work the same hours, so it's not as if you could pick up an extra shift. How much you will enjoy your work is highly dependent on which schools you are placed at. I worked at two extremely different locations, substituting a few times at a third. Each school (and your manager) has their own way of running the ship on a day-to-day basis. If you transfer or substitute at another location, prepare to walk into a completely different operation. You won't be prepped at all by management. Most of the time at a new location, it was the kids telling me how things were supposed to be run: "We're supposed to do this thing now! Why don't you know this? Isn't this your job?" Umm, because management didn't think to tell me. Thank you very much, kiddos Some schools are totally organized from top to bottom, whereas other schools are complete anarchy. At one particular school, I was totally left out to dry by my manager, where the kids would completely trash their classroom, swear at the Team Leaders, get into fights, literally hop the school fences and run away, and do whatever else they wanted. This happened frequently. I was a new transfer at that location, where that type of behavior had been normalized prior to my transfer. When I brought up the issue, my manager said, "Sorry, I know it's hard, but there's nothing we can do about it. We aren't teachers. A lot of the behavior is just a product of the kids' environments." I don't blame him for that--it was a rough school in a rough area. If the students weren't getting the right kind of support at home or at their school, then you're in for it, doubly so as a powerless after-school program worker. If you aren't cut out for that kind of environment, try another location. It can make a world of difference!

It is a lot of pressure to have these high balances on your own cards. - COVID-19: They waited until the last day to close the offices, and only a week before that did they stop the fingering scanning to clock in/out. Zero plan was communicated during this time from upper management. We were expected to use our personal computers, with a very outdated remote system (someone had to be in the office to turn on computers if they shut down.. which completely defeats the purpose) So our tech department was responsible for still being in office during COVID. - The company opened back up immediately during phase 1 - this was communicated on the Friday, that we were opening on Monday. - They started with a pen and paper check-in to confirm your mandatory presence in the office and then moved to a website clock, with your location enabled to make sure you’re coming into the office. - The owner frequently made random laps around the office to see who was there and ‘take attendance’ – though he probably couldn’t tell you 90% of the people’s names that were there anyway - No changes were made in the office as far as adding dividers or spacing people out. If you felt unsafe it was your responsibility to fix it. - Upper management made comments not long after that COVID was not real and there was nothing to worry about. (July 2020) You were mocked for wearing a mask. - As upper management mandated a 5 day back in office work day, they said it was because it creates a ‘more positive work environment’ as their reasoning. However, not one employee seemed to be asked how they felt about it or what the environment actually is. - They were not flexible to work from home and not helping many parents in need during this transition of entering remote schooling. Long time employees had to become freelance and lose benefits so they could manage through this time. They often refer to the team as the ‘Jordache family’ but honestly, no family should treat each other like this.

CONS: *Inside sales people are not considered to be actual sales professionals, or treated as such. *Pay is WELL BELOW market rate for the same job classification//title anywhere else in the nation. *Veterinary Software and Services is run from the top down like a tight fisted, old school, trickle-down economy that’s designed to profit only the organization. *Income caps, claw-backs and frequently gutted comp plans make it a rigged game *Constant price hikes make it hard to sell products. *No real software product development resources allocated. This leads to solutions that can't compete in the market. *Little to no opportunity for career growth. *Low morale and non-existent culture. *Favoritism is the key to advancement. To make matters convoluted, VSS, the one division that has Inside Sales positions uses this job classification as a blanket label for every non-management level employee that works under that umbrella. In reality, there are two kinds of ‘Inside Sales’ positions in this division. One is an ISR, which is what would normally be considered a Customer Service Rep. These folks work in a call center type environment that’s micromanaged down to the second. Every minute of their day is counted, measured and timed. If you fancy asking for permission to use the rest room, feel free to submit an application. The second type, which is also called ‘Inside Sales’ are your typical Inside Sales/Account Manager type roles. If you Google any large company who is well-known in their industry, you’ll find loads of Inside Sales / Account Manager positions that are remote, hybrid or in-office. Bottom line is that these folks simply don’t get into a vehicle and drive around a territory to perform their role. They have quotas, KPI’s, and need to prospect just like any sales professional, but everything is done over the phone or via web meeting. The difference between IDEXX and other companies is that at IDEXX, these people are not considered actual sales professionals. The field sales representatives are glorified by Executive leadership – these folks are flown around the country to attend trade shows and sales conferences periodically throughout the year, while being wined and dined. Those who are in Inside Sales roles get a company mug, a notepad and a jacket once a year and told they matter. What’s truly disappointing is the complete unwillingness on the part of the organization to look at endemic, long-term problems in the Software and Serices division. Specifically, anachronistic management styles and outdated ways of thinking have drained the humanity out, leaving a dull, weary culture in its wake. Executive Management continues to stand idly by, looking in the other direction. The company continues to promote annual employee surveys which consist of a handful of multiple choice questions, cleverly designed not to skirt the real issues and solicit any real or direct feedback. While everyone is pressured to participate by the top dogs, employees are left shaking their heads at how year-over-year, absolutely nothing changes. By the time I left, a record low number of employees had bothered to respond to the survey at all. All in all, if you choose to work here, you’ll get a steady paycheck and a benefits package. The PTO is decent for starting out (although not as generous as what progressive companies offer) and the benefits are average, but you’ll be repeatedly reminded that they’re outstanding and you’re fortunate to be so well compensated. Don’t bother asking for cost of living adjustments or raises unless you enjoy being condescended to. If you’ve had a real career before this, think long and hard before accepting an offer, unless you’re an activist personality type and enjoy fighting City Hall. You’ll also be forced to fight your organization’s goalkeepers for every single penny of compensation you earn, including competing against your colleagues on other teams, as the portfolio of products is a crazy mashup of competing programs. It used to be that folks living in Maine didn’t have a lot of choices, but the pandemic has tipped the scales, thankfully. This company has coasted way too long on a past reputation as a premier employer. Donating to local charities and sponsoring various community endeavors is great, but buying a good reputation only lasts so long. What I’ve found through keeping in touch with a number of people who have left is that I don’t know a single person who didn’t end up with better pay, better benefits, and isn’t much happier now that they’re gone. The saddest thing about all of this is that it doesn’t have to be this way. If only they were willing to look – the problem and the answers are all right there out in the open.

Maintaining tenure is likely the most challenging thing about this role. While you interview, you will see lots of folks who have been there for a long time and you might think that is because it's a great place to work - but once you spend some time there you'll see what is really going on. The metrics are CUTTHROAT. If you don't hit your goals, you'll quickly be placed on a PIP, and if you continue to lack performance you'll be asked to leave the same day. The goals are aggressive and require you to work long hours into the evening/weekends in order to hit and maintain them. They will lure you in with compensation (read: all-in cash; the salary is laughable) which sounds impressive until you realize what you have to do to achieve those cash goals. Through your placements, you'll have to pay back your salary (which is basically starts you in the negative) and then anything you accrue over that is considered a "bonus" -- but only after the house (Corporate) takes its cut, and your managers take theirs. So basically you're left with a small additional bonus that is nowhere near the 6-fig compensation they tout. If it's so bad, how are there so many tenured people? GREAT QUESTION! This is because they constantly hire young and driven individuals that want to succeed. These kids will break their backs to meet their aggressive goals and try to "bonus". Once they are unsuccessful, they are quickly terminated and all of the revenue from their accounts gets moved to others on the team. As you can imagine, the last one standing (read = tenured) is left with all of the revenue pouring in from little-to-no maintenance work that was all established by those that resigned or were fired. This burn-and-churn model has worked successfully for the company, and if you're considering joining go into knowing you are that low-totem pole person. Good luck and god speed!

There are a lot of immature and inexperienced 'head of' folks that simply do not know how to do the work required for their role. A typical 'head of' leader looks like 1) Elite school 2) 2 to 3 years as an IC at a famous company then 3) 1 to 2 years at Gusto then TA-DA 'head of' product, marketing, data science, etc. There is no career path through middle management. If you have a wealth of previous experience before coming to Gusto and are not a 'head of' upon arrival at Gusto, your subject matter expertise will be rejected, resisted and refused. My class was dual trained on both brands instead of one as they typically hire on for. We went through 4 weeks of training not even given the ability to access the several platforms we would need to utilize to help customers. After months of abuse from angry customers, passing every evaluation and being told how amazing I was doing, I still was told that I could not be guaranteed a hired in position as they did not know if there would be positions available. It was brought to my attention that the company was hiring a new training class to start for a full time hired in position receiving more pay and immediate benefits. When I questioned why I was still not offered the position to be hired in I was told to still be patient and they would let me know if positions were available. After being completely lied to, I decided I would not like to work for a company that would choose to keep me stringing on after working so hard for them during their peak season.

That had our class doing basically the work of 2 people for $15/hr. And threw us to the wolves around Christmas time to deal with customers who had problems we couldn't do anything about. Also didn't want us to escalate legitimately supervisor-esque questions to supervisors. Customer Service reps are just -vastly- underpaid meatshields. A lot of my training class seemed like some of the few in the company who went through the proper techniques we covered in training. Lots of passing the buck or just people not doing their jobs and others paying for it later. If you take this job I recommend doing it part time since that adds up to about full time during the peak season.

The company promises items to arrive by a specific day and then especially around the holidays completely drops the ball, leaving agents to deal with verbal abuse from customers who’s orders wont arrive in time. Supervisors claim to be there to help but in many cases could be rude and unhelpful and would brush you off when you really need help. Training is long and a joke, after 4 weeks none of my group really knew what we were doing once we got to taking calls. No one wanted credit cards, and since it was the same pool of people, they just kept saying no. Plus, the company would come out with a new term for their credit card every so often "preferred guest card" "diamond card" etc. which felt deceitful. So these goals were really set to be hard/impossible to achieve and that would be the reason I could never have a pay increase. Oh and they go through CEO's like crazy.

Wish I had a working interview or a trial period, not what I expected. It's not glamorous and you won't get rich doing it but it pays better than a lot of the menial jobs I and many others had before delivering mail. . . I've said my peace!

Very physically demanding and taxing waking up extremely early. Management structure is poor, and the employees abuse the Union making a poorer environment for the rest of the workers. They also expect you to be flexible as a PSE sometimes traveling to multiple Post Offices to help out other locations.

Everything else. Steady raises but crafts aren't paid equally. Federal holidays but in the plant you don't get the actual day off bc they're open 24/7. No discipline. Nepotism runs rampant. New employees run this show. Stopped doing background checks etc and the work force reflects that. Too easy to move up in management, ZERO criteria has to be met. I'm not kidding. There is basically a bunch of children working who hang out with management fraternizing on the weekends, all on social media. This means there's no punishment for attendance etc. And that's what slows the mail down. This is why the richmond plant specifically suffers. As I said in the pros, you can't get fired. The union protects the bad eggs while the good ones overwork in their place.

Inhumane conditions that are above and beyond the tough conditions a mail carrier would normally face. Crews disallowed to sort packages and prepare parcel loads indoors with management and the heaters, but rather outside in what I experienced as low as 9*F (NINE degrees!) The LLV vehicles are constantly in demand and rarely are there enough for all carriers. Newer RCA's are forced to use their private vehicles. Hours are ridiculously long, days off are taken away readily, and RCA's work as many as 9 and 10 days in a row without options. The postmaster couldn't care less about the RCA's and the new-hires come and go quickly, filing through the facility at a furious rate through their ever-revolving door. A toxic environment.

- The volume of both mail and parcels is ridiculously high in many regions. - Many offices are so understaffed that you will be forced to work 60-80 hours whether you want to or not. This is true throughout the state of Colorado for instance. - Pay is the same at every office throughout the continental US and quite low for many areas. - No vacation or retirement until you are promoted to a career position. Some offices will hire straight to career, but many don't. As of this writing, City Carriers convert to career after 2 years, but Rural Carriers are stuck waiting til a route opens up, which could be quick or it could literally take a decade. - Good supervisors quit for better jobs. Odds are you'll be stuck with terrible ones. - Rural Carriers may be expected to deliver mail out of their own personal vehicles. - The current fleet of mail trucks is mostly 30 years old. These trucks do not have air conditioning, radios or modern safety features like airbags. Do a quick google search and you will find that a shockingly high number of carriers have DIED in their mail trucks do to heat/cold/lack of safety features. Sometimes these vehicles even catch on fire. I'm not joking.

The worst part of working for USPS is dealing with the supervisors. Most are former carriers who decided they no longer wanted to carry mail. They will pressure you too do as much as you can as quickly as you can and belittle you if you don't. They preach safety, but don't really care about it. They just have to preach so it absolves then of any responsibility if you do something unsafely just to meet their expectations. There is also rampant favoritism shown towards some carriers who either are remotely attractive or will do whatever the supervisors ask. The vehicles provided are 30+ years old, break down a lot, and have no AC in them.

Where to begin? Basically everything else is a con but here's a quick list: - The sales team is king, all hail the sales team for they are the bringers of business. If you question the sales team, you are automatically wrong. They will overpromise to existing and new clients and set up the development teams to fail with unreasonable deadlines that they get the clients excited about. - There is no support or training for any new technologies despite the constant expectation that people master new technologies. Existing SMEs are inaccessible (read: far too busy for your trivial questions) and unhelpful when they have time for you. Lunch and learns are not training and pointing at Linkedin Learning is not teaching. - This place is just woefully understaffed. They will put you on a project in a role that you have no training for with nobody to support you and then expect you to have expert level knowledge in that area to be able to answer client questions from the get-go. Related, they really don't care about your professional interests and management is unresponsive when changes are requested. - Management is inaccessible and fluid. I can count on one hand the number of times I had a meaningful conversation with my direct report in my time here and still have fingers left over. They have also had major turnover in management in the last few years. - Speaking of turnover, this place is a revolving door when it comes to developers. There are a few mainstays and then everyone else spends a couple years here and leaves or is a contractor with an expiration date. You will rarely work with the same people from project to project and there is no opportunity to foster mentor/mentee relationships among developers. - Projects tend to be pretty boring and the clients don't understand what they bought half of the time. Bored devs and confused clients do not mix well. - You are constantly defending how you use your time. Project managers don't seem to understand that concepts may need to be learned over time or that spending time to actually solve a problem rather than write bad code is time worth spending. - "Documentation? What documentation? The client isn't paying for documentation, now get back to coding!" is what you'll hear if you say the word "documentation". - No 401k match, pretty meh benefits besides, you will most likely be underpaid in the sub-25th percentile range, and raises do not beat inflation so you will be taking effective pay cuts each year while management gets to say they are "helping". - Culture-wise, there are few opportunities to connect with colleagues. Also there is a very heavy drinking culture that is apparent in both private conversations and conversations with clients. - As far as diversity and inclusion goes, this place does not have many women in technical roles and few people of color at all. People make misogynistic comments more frequently than I'd expect, even for tech. HR might talk a big game, but nobody actually implements any changes.

allPros: Anyone 50+ years old knows IDEO

IDEO still produces amazing design solutions for clients. Like any design firm it’s struggling with the u certain economy, but has managed to maintain an excellent base of design talent and the new CEO seems highly promising and inspiring.

Innovative and Collaborative Culture: IDEO is known for its human-centered design thinking approach and fostering a highly collaborative work environment. Employees have the opportunity to work with a diverse team of designers, engineers, and strategists, allowing them to learn from each other, share ideas, and develop groundbreaking solutions together.

-Amazing, very knowledgeable, considerate people to work with who are passionate about what they do - Open to new ideas, freedom to experiment, - Growth opportunities with extra effort put into defining a clear path ahead - Focused on DEI, equality and respect in the workspace - great benefits, healthcare and flexible leave policy
Incredible people. Many people were very intelligent.
IDEOers are inspiring! The work is meaningful.
allCons: IDEO as a company is currently struggling. The brand has become outdated, and the leadership, which comprises individuals who have been at IDEO for 10-20 years, lacks fresh perspectives on overcoming creative barriers and managing the business. As a result, the company is now compelled to focus on acquiring new clients. Frequent layoffs have become the norm, first in 2020, then at the end of 2022, and most recently in May 2023. Despite claiming to value diversity and inclusion, IDEO falls short in its internal practice. It is common to find all-white teams or teams with only one person of color. IDEO maintains a strict hierarchical structure, which is surprising in this day and age. Only those at the Director level and above have decision-making power. Those below this rank are micromanaged and must seek approval from a Director for every decision. Taking on strategic projects or receiving credit for your ideas is nearly impossible if you are not a Director or above. Lastly, the compensation at IDEO is low, considering the political maneuvering and gamesmanship required to remain with the company.

This is not where people stay for a salary commensurate with tech firms, though many of our designers get snatched up by the usual suspects in search of bigger pay in the short term. The past few years have been really challenging for IDEO, forcing new conditions on the org that can feel in conflict with employees.

Highly Competitive Environment: Due to IDEO's prestigious reputation and the high demand for their design and innovation expertise, the work environment can be quite competitive. Employees may experience pressure to consistently produce exceptional work and constantly prove themselves among their talented peers.

Working at The Motley Fool has been an eye-opening experience, revealing a toxic work environment hidden beneath a facade of friendliness. The leadership's gaslighting, false narratives, and relentless micromanagement have created a detrimental atmosphere that hinders professional growth and well-being. Behind The Motley Fool's seemingly positive image lies a leadership team that excels at pretending to be nice while engaging in manipulative behavior. Gaslighting is rampant within the organization. Everyone has to pretend everything is great amazing to keep the facade going. The Motley Fool's toxic environment extends beyond false narratives and gaslighting. The leadership's obsession with micromanagement hampers productivity and employee morale. Instead of fostering collaboration and open communication, the company thrives on an atmosphere of control and constant scrutiny. Attempts to voice concerns or offer constructive feedback are met with defensiveness, dismissal, or even retaliation. The lack of accountability and empathy from the leadership further exacerbates the toxic work culture, leaving employees feeling trapped and undervalued. Choose an organization that respects and empowers its workforce, as your happiness and career prospects should not be sacrificed for the sake of a toxic workplace.

Like most remote companies, communication can be challenging, but the company does a good job of using all channels to communicate important information. We rely a lot on messaging tools like Slack which can make conversations quick and easy, but without the necessary context at times. However, video conferencing like Zoom makes it easy to immediately clarify anything that may have been misunderstood. Additionally, TMF went from in-office to fully remote over these last 3 years so it seems like our culture is adjusting to the new workplace environment. TMF doesn't have linear career journeys; it's more like a jungle gym where the more you move to different areas of the business, the better your understanding of the business and better exposure for different opportunities. If you're motivated, curious, and open to new things, then TMF might be good for you, but if you're looking for the corporate track and a clear path, then TMF might not be for you. If you're just getting started, especially remotely, it's really important to make friends -- it can make or break your experience -- but most people are friendly and willing to help new employees figure out the ropes.

A couple of years ago this company was a place with some amount of compassion (even though the extent was often exaggerated). This has utterly changed. There is inhumane treatment of employees everywhere you turn. They are pretty good at hiding it, so the real extent must be way greater than any one employee could attest to. After a year of being with the company, one begins to see the stark differences between the glossy promises and grim reality. The main issues revolve around incompetent management, excessive favoritism, lack of career growth and direction, and stringent micromanagement. The turnover rate is high - many employees leave within their first 1-2 years, feeling disillusioned and unsatisfied. Those who do choose to stay tend to be "the favorites", who get raises even in the midst of budget cuts, take advantage of the company's five-month parental leave on top of the unlimited PTO, and keep their dissatisfaction quiet. Management positions seem to be filled from this pool of favorites. Unfortunately, these individuals lack the necessary leadership training and are incapable of leading a team or inspiring their subordinates. It's a commonly held belief that people leave bosses, not companies. In the case of The Motley Fool, it holds true. The culture of the company is rife with conflicts and issues. Even though the company encourages open communication, raising your voice against the prevailing issues appears to be career suicide. Retaliation and gaslighting are all too common here. If you dare to raise concerns against "the favorites", you may find yourself denied a raise, promotion, or even worse, faced with termination. While the Motley Fool has potential to be a great workplace, it is currently a long way from living up to its promises. Unless drastic changes are made, the company is bound to lose valuable talent and foster a toxic work environment.

There will always be ample work to be done and new adversities to overcome in this very challenging post-COVID climate in healthcare, but somehow we always manage to make time to enjoy each other's company, have a laugh over lunch, attend the residents' 70s Disco, and never feel ashamed to be a little silly and make the residents smile.
