Taking time off can be difficult and confusing based on their points system and staffing needs. Higher ups don’t listen to the concerns of the people actually doing the work every day. When I started there was only a 2 chat maximum. Soon they integrated a 3 chat maximum and said that it would be less than 10% of the time. That was a lie. It was a constant thing and was often made worse because workforce was always randomly deciding that we didn’t need as many agents working certain times so would let people go home early. When everyone voiced their concerns about the new workload and stress we were all under we were constantly dismissed and never compensated for our work. Also because of the increased chats QA scores suffered which meant you didn’t get your bonus if your score was low. Also the constant pressure to upsell customers when you’re trying to juggle so many chats is ridiculous. I was docked points on a QA because I didn’t try to sell a customer a year supply when he was trying to figure out why he hadn’t received the contacts he had already ordered (they were discontinued but still on the website to be purchased).

I have never felt more dismissed when my concerns arise than I have through 1800Contacts. I wish I could rave about them like I once did, but that is simply not the case. Recently they have rolled out a change from 2 to 3 chats at the same time without consulting agents who actually do the work. Hearing “it used to be this way” from managers was nothing but salt in the wound. When the conversation about the additional stress, higher wages, or the fact we’re not being heard is brought up, the agents are to blame. Essentially, they’re paying less people (for the same wage) to do 1.5x the work with no additional training or support. They blame us for avoiding change, but this is incredibly wrong. None of us wanted this. I don’t know one single person I’ve talked to that is excited or hasn’t cried on the clock due to their negligence. It saddens me to make this review, but I was thriving prior to the unexpected changes and the ignorance cannot go without criticism. These managers don’t even take chats and will not hesitate to write you up.

For those not in the know, if you try and leave TaskUs, they will send you an email/letter saying you have X amount of days to follow their demands or they will reduce your already terrible wage to minimum wage. I’ve met people who gave into these demands and got minimum wage anyways. My advice? Don’t give them two weeks noticed, just stop showing up because their NDA doesn’t let them disclose this to other jobs, and don’t return the equipment to them. Make them come pick it up. And don’t sign anything. Overall, TaskUs will go down as the worse company I’ve ever worked for, and I think it would be impossible to match. Ignore every 4-5 star reviews because they’re either outright fake, or exaggerated by the people TaskUs deems are “worthy” enough. Similar to other higher ed institutions, decisions are often made centering the ego of deans, tenured faculty, and certain students. As staff, you will spend many, many hours writing and rewriting documents and e-mails to ensure the correct tone, according to leadership, is achieved. There are many non-mandatory (but in reality, mandatory) team-building activities that you are required to attend that will eat away at your time, as well as many standing weekly and bi-weekly check-in meetings that prevent you from getting work done during the work day and force you to work outside of 9-5pm hours. You will constantly be reminded that the department is less focused on expediency and rather prioritizes how things get done and that the “correct” processes and methods are followed. The trial period for any new employee is one year; you will frequently be reminded of this during your first few months as well as be reminded that many people want to work at Stanford. Your actions, words, and tone will be scrutinized, especially as a new hire, to ensure that you meet leadership’s expectations. Your colleagues will be encouraged to make note of and communicate to leadership any behavior that does not align with leadership’s expectations. Leadership has known and worked with each other for many, many years, have similar backgrounds, and will construe any questions raised regarding processes as pushing back on their leadership. Your success with the department is directly correlated to how well you get along with leadership. If you speak differently or have different values and make them known, you will not be successful. Stanford GSB values Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, as long as nothing changes. In the same vein if, as a person of color, you raise concerns regarding not feeling psychologically safe to Stanford Staff Help Center, HR, or Employee & Labor Relations you will be told “Stanford takes such matters seriously and appropriate action will be taken”, however, nothing changes.

companies.name: Watts Guerra
allPros: For lower entry level positions, the work is easy- mostly data entry and returning client phone calls. For a law office, you do get weekends off and a steady 8-5 job. They cover the costs of healthcare. A well stocked snack cabinet for all the stress eating you will do there. Two 15 minute breaks a day are provided and a 1 hour lunch break from 12-1. The people you work with in the departments alongside you are in the same boat as you are and often become good friends through shared trauma.
allCons: As you advance in rank/responsibility, your task list becomes too long to manage and because of the mess of procedures constantly changing, meetings being canceled, procedural changes never being communicated down the line and everyone around you is too stressed to help or answer you, you are left on your own to figure out how things “should” happen. Many of the case manager tasks are done in bulk across thousands of clients within the software, and pulling accurate data quickly is a requirement for the position. (Example, when the lawyer requests an excel sheet of everyone who has a certain paper on file or went to a certain pharmacy, trying to mass update information across the set of clients or keeping track of defense deadlines (which if one is missed out of thousands of clients you’ll be very quickly fired). However; because data is updated incorrectly or missed by the data entry employees- either because they’re rushed to complete quickly (sometimes even the yearly bonus is threatened if they don’t make the quota) or the turn over rate is so high that the employees are always new, you end up with a messy report that involves hours of clean up and follow ups as to why it’s not ready. Leadership gets frustrated when you don’t take charge of your tasks and just complete but then gets upset that you made a decision to handle in a certain way because that’s not how they would have handled- but again, they weren’t available to you when you asked for advice. It’s a place that micromanages to the point where if you make one wrong move, you get fired- but also are in trouble for asking how to handle. It creates a toxic environment where people who have made a mistake can point their fingers at someone else and play the blame game. Which happens frequently all the way from the top lead attorney down through the coords and typically ends at the case manager level- because “you should have caught whatever it was”. The phone people spend hours trying to return phone calls to angry clients without having the latest info on hand to provide and no HIPAA training on what can/should/can’t be said; the document processing center is inundated with client emails complaining about no call backs, docs from clients that the case manager needs updated immediately because of required reports; and trying to create the thousands of new clients that come in a day, so they’re always behind and in “trouble” because something important wasn’t handled (keep in mind that everything ends up being important with no way to set priorities as the department head) so no matter what department you join, expect to be overworked, stressed, always doing something incorrectly even if you were trained to do it a different way, and on the verge of making a mistake simple enough that can get you fired but you had no idea because you weren’t told the big picture. Old employees who were there for a long time started leaving in droves, but the company keeps it under wraps as best as they can- sometimes not even mentioning that someone in charge of something left over a week prior and now you’re expected to take over the task without any of the information the last employee knew about it. Torts are shuffled around like musical chairs with management so as soon as you learn the structure and rules for one thing, you’re thrown on something different or then required to manage both. The mass tort handling attorney will give you sweet promises of pay raises, nice yearly bonuses, the fact that they care about your work/life balance and that she’s there to support you: but with direct and indirect experiences; your pay will never increase by much (both because they promote in Jan-March but don’t do pay raises to match title until the end of fiscal year in Dec and because they hang the carrot of a nice bonus which will make up for lower wages); your bonus will never grow to what was promised (because this year we “hired more employees”, “didn’t settle any torts” “our overhead was high”); and you will still be called in a panic after-hours needing information in a report, clarification on something you provided and when it comes time to show her support, will just as quickly throw the case managers or coords as a whole under the bus for whatever problem comes to the attention of Mikal Watts. Sometimes those mistakes were her call to make- “let’s put all calls on hold for a week to let the team catch up on voicemails”, but then “I had no idea pausing calls would mean that we can’t reject clients for not talking to us now and it’s your fault for not bringing to my attention earlier”. There are a few people who run the office who have been there a long time, who probably are the few who are paid well to put up with it and they end up being the problem with no clue why the employees under them are unhappy or frustrated. They are stressed and busy and often just as frustrated as everyone else, but the answer is ALWAYS to micromanage more, create a new middle man role by promoting people without experience into the chaos and create a new meeting that ends up not being structured and then gets canceled each week until it just goes away for good. You will only get trauma, nightmares of incomplete reports, stress of taking on too many tasks for one person to handle and then when you ultimately decide to leave- essentially treated like garbage and used as a scapegoat for any and all issues, because someone who isn’t there anymore is an easy person to blame. Stay away from this company and save yourself the headache, the financial strain and the feeling of never doing anything right.

The company's attempts to become a global medical company are not going well for several reasons. Firstly, the organization is heavily hierarchical and top-heavy, with VPs and Directors involved in operational details. They create plans and timelines without consulting impacted regions, resulting in late projects and a culture of blame-shifting. Unfortunately, there is a lack of real leadership in the company, and many higher-ups are only doers without any innovative ideas. As a result, the company's communication is very poor, especially between regions, leading to urgent issues and frustrated employees. Furthermore, the entire workday is consumed by meetings, with additional meetings held after hours. Consequently, work-life balance suffers, causing dissatisfaction among employees. Additionally, the company's Quality Management System is inadequate, leading to multiple FDA warnings. This is because many of the VPs and Directors are incompetent, and there are significant gaps in processes. Projects are rushed, and unrealistic expectations are set due to the absence of project planning and poor management. To summarize, the company's attempts to become a global company are impeded by a hierarchical organizational structure that lacks leadership, poor communication, a lack of work-life balance, and an inadequate Quality Management System. Think twice before joining this mess.

Although a lot of effort (yes, a lot) has been put to change this, the general feel in the company is that it hasn't worked out. A lot of attention is put in cross-departmental movement, which indeed works well at SBA, but less is put on same-department movement. That recipe helps better entry-level position holders or generalists that can easily pivot. Not easy for specialized functions. The effort is appreciated but the problem remains. We are losing and will lose more talent because of that. Millennials and Gen Z are not as patient as prior generations. - Pay. The pay is OK. If career advancement remains a challenge, the company should start paying more. A mix of aggressive bonus practices and/or intralevel increases are a good start. - Flatness. Flat hierarchical structures contribute to the problems above. Create more levels. Or sublevels, for that matter. Offer a little bit more money by sublevel. It costs almost nothing for the company and it helps the employees to feel seen. The entitlement is real and it's here to stay. It's a generational thing. The company does not fix it by leveling up.

I worked as an IA Agent/Customer Service Rep for Education Dynamics LLC for two years. While there were some positive aspects to the job, overall, I cannot recommend this company. I have some serious concerns about the company's practices. Speaking up is not encouraged, and if you do, you may be punished. This alone creates a toxic work environment that is not conducive to healthy communication. In addition, there are ethical concerns with the company's business practices. Customers often fill out job applications online, but these applications are never submitted, making it feel like we were scamming people. The company continuously hires, which should raise some red flags. Communication between employees was poor, and I often felt unsure about my role within the company. Shady practices were prevalent, and upper management seemed manipulative and untrustworthy. The HR department was also two-faced, which made it difficult to raise concerns about questionable actions taking place. The company has a high rating on BBB,(A+) but this seems rigged and does not reflect the reality of the work environment. Raises were not available, and there was no review and evaluation plan that indicated any raises would be offered, which made it difficult to plan my future with the company. Promotions were not handled appropriately, and there was no stability. However, the flexible schedule and work from home option were beneficial, and the 40-hour workweek from Monday to Friday with no weekends was appreciated. Overall, I would not recommend Education Dynamics LLC as an employer due to the ethical concerns, poor communication, and manipulative upper management.

In the past year or so the culture at HubSpot has taken a complete nosedive. There has been a total exodus of highly tenured, knowledgeable people across so many departments who had been with the company for many years and held so much knowledge. It seems most everyone you now meet has been here under 2 years, which should tell you something. Leadership keeps joining from major Fortune 500 companies and along with it they have brought the toxic cultures. They continue “benchmarking to the market” which basically means doing away with the benefits and culture that made HubSpot special and different from the typical corporation that treated you as just a number. Work-life balance was terrible to begin with and was made worse after the layoffs. Constant communications via emails and Slack at all hours of the day and everything is somehow an emergency that needed to be completed yesterday. People are already on the edge of burnout, yet somehow we’re now pushing this new “high performance culture” that HR and leadership have barely been able to articule and explain what exactly it means.

Little time to sell because of back-to-back internal meetings every day. Having a family AND being successful here is not possible. You must let one of these options go because in order to meet quota, you will need to work 12 hours per day. Poor health benefits. Poor morale - is anyone happy here anymore? Working with so many people who hate their job is toxic and feels awful. Monthly quotas rather than quarterly.

One of the most concerning aspects is the prevailing culture that demands conformity. If you do not conform to the established norms and hesitate to challenge existing ideas, you are quickly labeled as a troublemaker or disruptive. Instead of fostering a learning environment where new ideas are welcomed, they tend to isolate individuals who don't conform, making it difficult for them to thrive. HubSpot's resistance to diversity and differing perspectives creates an echo chamber where innovative thinking is stifled. It is disheartening to witness the missed opportunities for growth and improvement that could arise from embracing a more inclusive culture. Moreover, the consequences of not toeing the line are severe. Those who dare to challenge anything often find themselves on the bad side of management, facing subtle retaliation and sometimes even attempts to push them out of the company. This behavior only further perpetuates a culture of fear and inhibits personal and professional growth.

Since Hubspot understaffed support via the 7% workforce reduction earlier this year , and this short staffing has been further exacerbated by massive attrition since, Hubspot's culture has shifted dramatically. Leadership doesnt care about experience, seniority, or history of loyalty in employees. All that matters now is your production numbers this month. There is no context that can explain low numbers and no compassion for employees. I personally know a mentor-type person with years of experience who was cut loose in recent months after their numbers dropped due to stress caused by their move across the country, and the general burn-out culture we work in 40 hours a week. Everyone i know is leaving as quickly as possible. This ship is sinking while on fire

This is a complete bureaucracy now. Any merit based teams are few and far between. Those teams are also probably not hiring, as they are being forced to conform or actively being managed out by being given unrealistic expectations. Culture, teamwork, and comradery are all rapidly declining as teams feel pit against each to produce.

HubSpot has very rapidly declined in how they treat their employees and the lack of accountability in upper management. Right now most support reps are staying due to their unlimited holidays but if this was removed there would be a massive exodus. There is no incentives for hard work and the salaries are mediocre. There was also a feeling that it was impossible to get out of support through internal mobility . People with experience and Master degree being stuck in this team for years. Recently, more and more highly skilled employees are moving on to other companies after trying to get promoted over 8 or 9 times.

There's been quite a few high impact people fired in recent months because they were doing "fine" for one quarter instead of exceeding expectations. They get a PIP, no clear guidance for improving, ignored by managers and then fired after a month. These are people who have been around for years, previously did well enough to get promoted, and are now suddenly not good enough. They built HubSpot and their reward is being cut off when they stop burning their candle on both ends. Performance measurement has gone from being story based to metrics based and it's hurting morale.

You will find that sometimes prioritizing the work you have to do is challenging since there are many other things outside your scope of work that you have to do, for example: owning a topic for your office, preparing and hosting meetings, attending meetings and events, office projects, training, etc. If you bring knowledge from previous companies unfortunately that expertise won't be considered too much and you will be seen according to what career level entitles you in the current role you cover. There is a back-to-the-school feel in how the processes are handled. Everything you do is evaluated and tracked and you have to show your team and managers what you did, achieved, or how you contributed every quarter. Targets and KPIs get higher and higher, the best you perform the higher targets you get. At the end of the quarter, your managers will evaluate you and you will have the feeling that what you do is never enough even though you did your best. They have career journeys for each role within the department. allCons: Upon joining GovTech (GDS), I was informed that it operates with a startup mindset. I did not expect it to be taken to the extreme of being as dysfunctional as a startup as well. Despite emphasizing "Agile" as a core value, there is a blatant disrespect for agile development practices: - Product owners who don't spend any time on the product and are clueless about the product's direction. - Delivery managers who are not even aware of what features are supposed to be delivered. - Engineering Managers and Technical Leads often urge their teams to forgo unit tests and resort to hard coding, all in an attempt to "save time." - The standard solution to challenges is to add more people and work longer hours, instead of finding innovative and efficient ways to resolve the underlying issues. In this organization, the focus leans towards meeting immediate goals rather than delivering high-quality software. Short-term gains are prioritized over the product's long-term health. Additionally, there is a concerning tendency to apply temporary fixes to issues and pass them on to successors, rather than addressing problems head-on and finding sustainable solutions.

The senior management team in GDS central may come across as kind and friendly, but they true character is far from it. They are solely concerned with impressing their superiors and showcasing the software's capabilities, without regard for the challenges faced by software developers in implementing such features. Despite the impracticality of these demands, they puts immense pressure on the team to deliver, often requiring excessive overtime. Their only concern is saving face, with little regard for anything else. Another issue is the company's salary policies. When employees have raised concerns about their salaries not being competitive, the senior management dismissed them, citing their salaries as already being too high. It is apparent that this statement only applies to the senior management, who take credit for the work of the software engineers and reap the rewards, such as good grades and high bonuses. Meanwhile, the developers themselves receive mediocre grades and low bonuses, despite their hard work. It is advised to approach joining Govtech, particularly GDS central, with caution. The senior management team put little regard for their well-being.

- Low salary (was already low a few years ago, and now with no tracking of inflation it's not even in the same ballpark as the industry standard) - Treated like a child - manager will monitor you to make sure you're coming to the office (which by the way is in the middle of nowhere and almost everyone has a massive commute) - Despite the CEO outwardly making claims about MDA's technical innovation (e.g. in regards to things like AI), the actual internal technical vision for the company is basically to lean on our past successes (Canadarm2) - the attitude of every technical leader who has been around for a while is "if it ain't broke don't fix it". While this attitude does often makes practical sense, it means it's pretty unlikely that new engineers will get to really innovate or build things that are truly novel. Furthermore this makes me pretty concerned that MDA will eventually get left behind. The robotics industry at large is advancing at an incredible pace and we're pretty much sitting here trying to sell 1998 technology.

I worked at this company for 15 years and I was very disappointed with their work from home policy. They only allow remote work twice a week on *approval* and the days you can work from home are static for the entire week for all employees (so you know those on-site days are packed with employees). Work from home policy feels like something the company had to offer to further prevent the large amount of employee turnover/attrition. Management appears to be immune to these policies and they seem to work as many days of the week as they prefer and on the days of their choosing. While regular employee on-site attendance are heavily monitored. Compensation is severely below average, you will find yourself experiencing Stockholm syndrome trying to justify the poor pay because the company does "Cool space stuff". Meetings scheduled during your lunch or off-hours is common. Management micromanages and is distrustful of remote workers, this often made me feel guilty or unprofessional for working from home.

Some of the leads and managers are stuck in the past, insisting on micromanaging you and then acting completely petty towards you when you don't let them. Processes and policies prevent real work from getting done, despite the fact that real solutions exist to MDAs (self-imposed) problems. It appears that senior management refuses to do anything about the issues that will ultimately erode MDAs ability to compete in a modern economy. They talk a lot about "One MDA" and launch new tools with much fanfare, but refuse to publicly acknowledge that employees can't actually use the tools as intended because they aren't compliant with MDAs own policies.

Typical minor negatives that all companies could have. No employee stock buying incentive program. Easy to think that grass is greener on the other side....but I have been to the other side and have happily returned to MDA.

Lack of support: Bad management can lead to a lack of support for employees, both in terms of resources and emotional support. Lack of focus: Too many meetings can lead to a lack of focus and attention on important tasks. In my division, the top guy listens only to his direct reports: almost everyone else is invisible and expendable. This is not a good place for mid-career professionals looking to work hard, make an impact and get ahead. You need to put 10+ years and strike the right coalitions before you become visible, Not worth it, IMHO. There is high turnover, and most of the new hires are entry level, who get adept in playing the system: they get the experience on their CV, they get some formal education and certifications on the house and then they get another job. Overall, pay is below par, bonuses are clipped, technology is a mess (still struggling to get on the cloud), and plenty of managers do not practice empathy, The place has a musty air: same people in the same position doing the same thing for ages. allCons: A Slow Decline: 1 on 1s eventually go away with the exception of the few simple check-ins. You'll start feeling stressed and exhausted. Many people leave as new people join the team and the new people get what you had years prior. You'll bring up these concerns of the impact of high employee turnover and they're initially shrugged off, but then you'll start to see some changes in the office such as more lunch is brought in. Once that distraction wears off, you'll realise hardly anything has changed and you're just as stressed as before. Utilization: The billable hours system is more harmful than it is beneficial. While it works well with helping you set personal, traceable goals, it lacks helping you achieve them. The supervisor(s) don't know what needs to be done to improve it. It creates this 0 - 100 scenario where you'll sometimes have virtually nothing to do, and that will eat away at your utilization percentage, or, whether you're trying to compensate for it or an assignment merely falls in your lap, you'll have too much to do. You'll hear people practically pulling their hair out who are in the same mindset and sometimes they'll even take a personal day to regroup. And while that may sound nice, it actually isn't. What you're doing is delaying the inevitable where the day you come back, you're in a deeper hole than before, and you've lost 8 hours of billable work that counts against your utilization.

The company was founded on psychological safety, don't be evil, hire smart creatives, etc.. Today, the company has grown so fast and so large that now the majority of people seem to be typical tech industry employees. That means most of the management has now come from outside the company, so that has killed the culture. Psychological safety is gone, especially after the way the layoffs were handled. I miss Laszlo Bock; he knew how to treat the workforce. I miss Larry, Sergey, and Eric. The general quality of my peers has gone down. Not as people, they're all lovely, but as practitioners. Most of them do what we'd have considered low-quality work 5 years ago. It's shockingly bad, really, by comparison. They've all been hired so fast and in such an environment where they weren't properly trained or didn't have the proper background to begin with or haven't been given the time and mentorship required to become great (investing in people).

The recent layoffs were handled very poorly. Performance played almost no factor, meaning that we are left feeling like it doesn't matter how productive we are or how good we are at collaborating and helping others. The recent news that Cloud is doing hot-desking and desk sharing seems absurd for a company as wealthy as Google and which depends so heavily on its employees. The announcement presentation of Bard was a debacle; how do we not make sure we have a backup phone for a demo like that? It was disheartening to see from the level of employees "on the ground", where we work very hard to have redundancy for important things and do our jobs as well as we can.

Google likes to think it's still a fast moving tech company, but in reality it is political and bloated. The net effect of that is that it has all of the worst of both worlds: working at a start up (custom tools, lack of process, lack of testing) and working at a huge company (bureaucracy). The worst part of Google, though, is the way that it "motivates" employees. The Perf system encourages individual contributions to the point that its hard to be efficient and collaborate. Everyone is doing things just to put it on their Perf. Work life balance is also a joke, no matter how many wellness bonuses they give us. Even though you technically don't need to kill yourself, they use promo to push you to work ridiculous hours. If you're not looking to get promoted (anytime soon), leadership doesn't know how to motivate you otherwise. People who push back on only working 100% of the time are seen as "not a team player". Don't be fooled - free lunches, remote work setups, and massages are just ways to keep you overworking.

Role-specific: - Very bureaucratic + lots of red tape when it comes to hiring. As a result, hiring process takes minimum 3 months (usually closer to 4/5 months) for a req to close and the recruiter really can't control this timing much. This makes it hard to keep candidates happy and difficult to meet quarterly goals since making each hire often takes longer than a quarter. - Some hiring managers can be tough to work or exhibit an elitist attitude; hard to convince some to follow inclusive hiring steps since they will have such a clear idea of the "type" of candidate they want. In general: - You really are just a number while working at Google. It's possible to build strong relationships and not feel this during the day to day, but leadership makes it clear. Examples: Lay off method was cold and not based on employee impact or performance. Leadership will remove benefits without warning, such as being able to work remotely. - Upward and internal mobility is extremely difficult. Promos take years and applying for internal roles is very competitive, so make sure you're prepared to stay in the role you're hired into for 3-4 years before even being looked at for mobility.

Lost its soul. Google is no different than any other big corporation out to make money. The values the company used to have would sacrifice some traditional money making objectives to benefit the employees. Over the years they have taken away more and more from the employee. It will lay thousands off while still making billions and simultaneously giving the CEO hundreds of millions of dollars of compensation. Google has largely lost it's way with poor upper leadership. It's become a bloated organization with multiple levels of Directors and VPs reporting to even more Directors and VPs.

Where to start, I'm so wildly disappointed by what Google has become and seems hell bent on preserving. Leaders: we do not have real leaders, we have people who in the earliest and least experienced parts of their career were lucky enough to land at Google and never left. Our CEO is not a business leader by training. Our CMO has had her job for over 20 years (red flag). Our CPO is MIA because we operate in such silos. Career: Join Google if you want to be severely under-leveled, have your experience minimized, be patronizingly led by people less qualified and less experienced than you, and have near zero prospects for upward mobility. Future: This company has no strategy. All you have to do is follow the news to see Google as a company woefully out of touch with the rest of the world. We have no clue how to do marketing, which is obvious from Bard to the graveyard of things we've killed off. I do not believe the future is bright given current leadership, and see a change unlikely until stuff hits the fans.

Google used to have the culture that they treated their employees well so they really wanted to work there and do amazing things. This is definitely not true anymore. In more and more spaces I’m seeing “how do we do the minimum to make people work”. It’s very disheartening and incredibly difficult to be a manager now.

Some coordinators understand that when it's 5pm, people usually go home. Some don't. Absolutely dominated by Korean hierarchy, which is a tough sell to the American workforce. Employment laws are often not followed. Complaints are met with dismissal. Any progress made with Korean Coordinators about US Employment Laws is erased every four years as they send over a new Coordinator that is not properly educated on the laws they must abide by. Viscous cycle that has lead to a culture of high turnover and quiet quitting amongst the employees that stay. This is not one facility, this is engrained. It is in West Point, GA. It is is Fountain Valley, CA. It is in Montgomery, AL. It is in Ontario, CA. It is in Brazil. It is in Mexico. It is everywhere. It bleeds like an open, unaddressed wound. If you consider yourself a scientist by nature, you should reconsider a job here as the culture seemingly goes directly against it. The fundamental question of "why" that likely drives you, is not tolerated here. Drawings and specs will likely be kept from you because "spies". You may get lucky and get a good coordinator, they do exist, and for the employees under them, they usually have a good experience during those years. However, more likely than not, that will end in under 4 years. You may think it will be different, that maybe you can help change the culture, but in will come a fresh new coordinator, eager to impose his authority over anyone younger or further down the food chain, because that is what the Korean working culture tells him he HAS to do, lest he look like a terrible manager. This is the harsh reality of working for this company.

companies.name: Omaha Steaks
allPros: Decent Pay Good Coworkers Good Culture

Omaha Steaks has been a great company to work for. They very fairly compensate in their salaries and offer a nice yearly bonus that is based on total company performance, not on individual performance. This is optimal because it encourages teamwork vs. competition between channels/areas within the company. They also do a yearly employee engagement survey and have listened to employees feedback and made changes the last few years. I have been impressed with senior management's efforts to really listen to feedback and provide a positive workplace and somewhere I enjoy working at. In the marketing, creative, and product areas within the company we have a team that plans out food days and events that make for a fun environment. We also get a decent employee discount and get to sample a lot of Omaha Steaks products throughout the year.

The people here for the most part seem to actually like their jobs, and care about the company. I can't tell you how rare that is. Company success correlating to bonus's certainly has a hand in that. Still, Omaha Steaks is a big company, that feels small. Close group, hard working, flexible. It also feels like Omaha Steaks is coming up. Let's of new innovators and ideas. A good time to be a part of this company.

Omaha Steaks is currently experiencing a infrastructure change as they focus on improving processes, systems and technologies. Much of the workforce works from home and are currently using systems and processes that are a bit out of date, which can be challenging at times. Important to note is that this company has alot of tenure with employees rising up through the ranks and often having decades of tenure in their belt. As a result, sometimes navigating the red tape when it comes to implementing change can be tricky, but overall, the company is well aware of the necessary change needed to bring the company into '23 and into the future. Great company discount, great culture of people to work with and for change managers there is opportunities abound. Ideas for improvement are encouraged and for those that want to get involved there is plenty of opportunities to work within your strengths to push through status quo. Overall Omaha Steaks is a strong place to work, especially for those who desire a great work from home or hybrid opportunity depending upon your department.

As of 2022 Colorado is 49th in the nation in funding higher ed per student. Arizona is 50th – though that is a little bit of a misnomer because ASU has tens of thousands on online students who comparatively cost less per pupil to educate. So, per in person pupil Colorado is probably dead last. MSU Denver, in turn is the lowest funded University in Colorado, thus the headline. It could be the lowest funded University in the US – I wouldn't be surprised. The problem is due to systemic State constitutional issues (google "Tabor amendment") that were passed during Colorado's small-government libertarian heyday and will likely never be fixed. Instead of being ashamed by the dismal state of higher-ed and seeking to rectify it, the current Democratic/Libertarian governor Polis's messaging and actions seek to de-emphasize the value of higher education. This situation is so intractable it has its own term "The Colorado Paradox" which seeks to answer the question of how Colorado is able to maintain a robust economy with such dismal higher ed. The answer is... Educated people from other states continue to move here in droves. What this means: • Non-competitive salaries • Understaffed administrative offices and/or staffed with junior level people. (ex. it routinely takes 4-5 months for HR and Financial Aid to approve a work-study student to begin work.) • Constant exodus of talent and turnover among competent staff • 10% faculty service expectations ballooning to unsustainable levels to make up for staffing shortages • Faculty regularly doing the job staff would do at a different institution; academic advising, tech. support, facilities management • All of this culminating in workload expectations that are not aligned with the salary or the stated goals or values of the institution

I have been part of the Placement Department for over two years now. Over those two years, we have seen tremendous growth (job security!) The work that we do is truly meaningful and so impactful, especially after what our great nation and the rest of the world experienced after the pandemic. Our work is directly impacting a depleted healthcare workforce that is in dire need of quality nursing change agents. With tremendous growth inevitably comes small bumps and challenges. The individuals successful in the Placement Department are the ones that embrace change and look to see how they can adapt to ensure the needs of the business (Keypath) and our partners continues to be met. Sadly, as in every bunch, a few “bad apples” have tried vehemently to spoil the entire batch. Instead of building their peers and rising to the challenge, they complain, are combative, and try to take away and distract from the hard and meaningful work most of us contribute to daily. The change to the consortium model undoubtedly took time to adjust. Our leaders recognized this and truly worked to put resources in place to ensure we felt comfortable in our roles and could continue to do quality work. Those who pushed back are ones who likely never worked where metrics needed to be met to ensure everyone was carrying their fair portion of the team’s workload. Metrics are in place to act as benchmarks for us – it helps us gauge our own workload and determine where we may need to spend more time and focus. I have worked in many industries before Keypath. This is the first company where I felt the VP of the department and management truly cared and invested in their people. Our VP makes herself available and works tirelessly to ensure we have what we need to be successful in our roles. The VP and management recognizes that we went through a major transition. Placement Dept pulse checks/surveys are routinely sent out and our feedback is HEARD and ADDRESSED! NOT MANY OTHER COMPANIES WOULD CARE TO DO THIS!!! Our VP and Placement Dept Leaders are transparent and make themselves available for us when needed. To be successful in the Placement Department, you must be one who thrives working autonomously while also embracing change. The work is definitely fast-paced, but that is what I LOVE about it!!! Each day is a new challenge as I work through new areas and regions to try to secure new clinical partnerships. This is the essence of what we do. You must be willing to work hard and show up with a good attitude. If you can’t do that, Placement likely is not the place for you. Placement Dept and Keypath Senior Leaders – Please continue connecting with your people just as you have been doing since day 1! I mentioned how the VP of the Placement Department is so closely in-tune with her employees – the same is with our CEO, Steve. I never worked for a company that had a CEO who could engage a room full of people with a smile and a fun, lighthearted joke. THIS is the type of environment people truly DREAM to work at!!!!! You can appreciate it if you have worked elsewhere... where you were just a voice behind a phone doing the same mundane work day to day with no positivity, care, concern, or connection from your senior leaders. Keep doing great work, Placement and Keypath Leaders. I have found my dream job because I have purpose in what I do. I am proud and eager to continue to make an impact on our future generation of healthcare workers.

The most contact you have with your manager is a 10-15 minute meeting once every two weeks. It is counted against your statistics if you consult tier 2 or any other department for assistance, however, there us no chat support after 7:00 PM EST. There is very little communication between departments, and it is very common to just be told "I don't know" by a member of management. When you ask them if they can try to find out for you, they shrug it off. Management also takes time off very frequently and does not get in trouble for doing so. The only calls that are listened to by quality are those 15 minutes or less, so the more common hour+ long calls where you really have to work hard to fix a complex issue are never listened to or acknowledged by anyone. No one can see how seriously you take the job, you are just another number taking calls. There is also a one year minimum that you have to be in customer care before moving to another position. A few months into my role, there was a major re-organization that resulted in over 70 layoffs, one of them including my team director. He was the absolute best manager I have ever worked for, putting his AC's first and genuinely caring about us as people, not just as workers. He didn't micromanage us, and instead, would celebrate every single win we made. He helped me grow professionally even in that time, and always asked what he could do to support my professional development. 2U lost amazing people during that time. I was, however, lucky to be put under another amazing manager who also treated us like people first, and encouraged us to work hard while also balancing work and our personal lives. I never felt anxious or anything while under this manager, but sadly, these types of managers are few and far between now. This manager was forced to move to another team last year, and that's when everything went downhill. Metrics got harder to achieve, managers became less understanding, and the micromanaging got so bad. This started to affect my mental health, and last year I actually took a leave of absence (something my doctor recommended). When I came back, not even a week later, I was switched to another team and that manager was even worse with the micromanaging. I felt so overwhelmed, constantly anxious and having panic attacks. My metrics were perfect, but he found something to lecture me about. It was never ending. The last straw for me was when my manager got HR involved (to micromanage me some more) and of course he picked his friend. It was the most uncomfortable meeting of my life, especially as a woman with two men interrogating you and you just sitting there trying to defend yourself. I knew in that moment that it was in my best interest for my mental health to leave 2U after 4 years. It is upsetting because even after all the organizational changes and shifts, I loved being an admissions counselor. I loved talking to my students on the phone. I truly put them first and sadly I am unable to continue supporting them because the management has gotten so toxic that I just couldn't stay there anymore. When I put in my resignation letter, my manager told me to just stop working, he didn't need me anymore. It was a very uncomfortable exit for a company I dedicated 4 years of my time and effort to. My exit interview with HR also got cancelled the day of so I wasn't able to express my thoughts and concerns at all and wasn't even given any off-boarding instructions. The way I was treated at the end is so unacceptable. To think at one point I loved 2U so much, I even referred 7 people during my time there (now only 2 remain), is just so sad because it is not the same company it once was. They also put so much emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion, but inclusion only means whatever they say it does. Example: the CEO changed his mind about the work from home policy post-pandemic that had everyone uneasy after being told they could choose to be full-time remote and now there was an in-office expectation. My friend shared a religious sermon to help others who were feeling anxious in our company-wide chat and she was bullied because she shared something religious, more specifically, of the Christian faith, however, we have clubs and groups at 2U for different religions with no issue, and other employees are free to discuss politics, and anti-religious ideologies however and whenever they please because they feel they "deserve to express their thoughts freely and the company should encourage that". My friend received awful chats from people bullying her, and some employees even contacted her manager. When she contacted HR about it to express how uncomfortable and unsafe she felt, she was completely ignored. No one ever got back to her. She left because of this. I wish the old 2U never left, but this company is not the same anymore and is only getting worse. This is my honest review of a company I used to love and would recommend all my friends to that I can't truthfully say the same about anymore.

Recently did a reorg where people got demoted but were gaslit and told it's not a demotion. In this reorg all job descriptions were updated to indicate more responsibility for the same pay and the new demoted job title - once again when brought up were gas lit to say there was no significant change. Basically if you were going above and beyond your original job description it doesn't look like it anymore because theyve re-written it into your new description. If you're unhappy with the change they'll tell you to wait and prove yourself around annual promotion time but now you have a new manager and new VP who at that time will most likely tell you they dont know enough about your work. After the reorg people with your same title could have been promoted while you were demoted without any explanation. Finally, after talking to many folks I've come to realize this has been a trend for many years at 2u and is not specific to the current layoff trends and pandemic recovery. Folks have stories and stories about feeling bullied by management or gaslit or not feeling valued enough for promotion.

Benefits have been stripped over the last year: • UPTO is now just normal PTO (anything beyond the set number of days requires skip-level management approval). • Tuition reimbursement now only covers edX courses (i.e. not a full degree) • No in-person company meeting/time to connect with the team face-to-face unless you work in one of the offices. When I first accepted this job, HR and management advertised the past company meetings in places like Disney World, Las Vegas, etc. I understand that covid and other factors have since required adjustments, but we were later promised there would be upcoming events last year/this year. Unfortunately, there wasn't a single opportunity in the four years I worked here to actually meet my team in person. Constant changes that are poorly planned/executed: • Three different managers and numerous directors over four years. • Two re-orgs, drawn-out lay-off periods • The company is currently undergoing a tumultuous re-org internally. Changes started in August and are still impacting the day-to-day in a way that is hard to navigate/balance as an individual contributor. Growing pains are natural, but it's going to be years before the dust settles and edX/2U are truly merged and functioning efficiently. • The nature of the work has changed to accommodate the re-org goals. Unfortunately, in my experience, it has been to the detriment of creativity with an over-focus on efficiency and cost-saving measures. • No training for employees new to the role/team as a result of the re-org. Completely up to the individual contributors to bring new employees up to speed in addition to massive workloads. • Workload and work/life balance is poor since the re-org, despite flagging concerns with project management and management in general. Small concessions were made, but overall heavy amounts of work with unrealistic and arbitrary deadlines. Management's hands are tied: • My direct managers were empathetic, helpful, and did their best to address my needs and concerns (on their own–management training is lacking in general). Feedback is lost further up the pipeline though–you're just a number and will need to fend for yourself. • C-Suite is completely out of touch with the reality of lower-level employees day-to-day. CEO can get defensive when pushed or questioned. Toxic positivity and gaslighting from leadership about the reality of day-to-day contributors, how the company is doing, the "success" of the re-org, etc. Sure, the numbers may be looking better depending on the day, but what about the mental health and well-being of the people making things happen? • No recognition of anniversaries, success, holidays, etc. besides a short Slack message. • Team morale is exceptionally low. If you don't buy into the new direction or voice an alternative perspective, then you're viewed as a disruption to "progress". Unacceptable: • The CEO sent a company-wide email about the restructuring last August, outlining that large-scale layoffs were imminent, then making everyone wait for weeks to find out of their role would be impacted or not. The mental toll this took on me (and literally everyone else I've talked to on my team), has been traumatizing and is something I'm still trying to recover from. • During this period, employees took to chat channels to air concerns/grievances. Soon after, the ability to post in company-wide channels was revoked. This came across as attempting to control the message rather than promoting a safe space for employees to find solidarity and support during a scary time.

While working as a peer health educator at UD can be a rewarding and fulfilling experience, there are some potential cons to consider: Limited hours and pay: Peer health educators are often employed on a part-time basis, with limited hours and lower pay than some other jobs on campus. Emotional demands: Peer health educators may have to deal with emotionally challenging situations, such as supporting students dealing with mental health issues, sexual assault, or substance abuse. This can be difficult and stressful, especially for those who are new to the role. Training requirements: Peer health educators typically have to complete extensive training, which can be time-consuming and demanding. This can be a barrier for those who are not able to commit to the required training schedule. Limited career growth: While the experience gained as a peer health educator can be valuable, there may be limited career growth opportunities in this field. Working with diverse populations: Peer health educators may need to work with students from different backgrounds and with diverse needs, which can be challenging and require a high level of cultural competency. It's important to weigh these potential cons against the benefits of the job and your personal goals and priorities before deciding whether to pursue a position as a peer health educator at UD or elsewhere.

The change in leadership and - in turn - strategy around fundraising events is dizzying. It is difficult to be successful when every few years there is a new approach to event fundraising, and on-the-ground/Market staff and supporting teams pay a big price for lack of consistent leadership in this area. Staff are taking a big hit for mistakes made in spending, and for the lack of accountability at a leadership level. Many of us are very excited for a new president/CEO and are eager to have this position filled with a strong leader.

I truly wanted to love working for March of Dimes, their mission is near and dear to my heart. I must warn that this is not the organization to join if you're hoping to make a meaningful impact in the world or be part of a supportive team that challenges you to grow. Senior leadership can be best described as toxic. It is not uncommon for senior leaders to to openly gossip, blame and shame other people & departments, rather than collaborating, creating shared goals, and holding each other accountable. Development staff are talked about about as the "problem" , as though they just need to listen to what they are told and not use their brains. Even with the recent housecleaning of leadership, many of those that remain in senior positions are guilty of the toxic behaviors previously mentioned. While there are small pockets of pleasant leaders, they are complicit in the toxic and destructive behavior by not having the courage to speak up and do something about it. There are a slew of questionable behaviors that trickle down the organization that stem from the lack of credible leadership at the helm-- which ultimately is impacting the organization's bottom line and ability to drive their mission. For anyone that takes pride in their personal values, I encourage you to look elsewhere for employment.

Like many orgs, this place is run by clueless, incompetent, mean, and overpaid executives. The staff who work their butts off are drastically underpaid and they just furloughed a bunch of people with no promise of backpay. They paid out their PTO but this was after everyone was encouraged to burn most of it over the holiday so from folks I've spoken to, they didn't get much.

The benefits are not great, it's a culture of micromanagement. People watch your zoom dot all day to see if you are in a meeting, pretending to be in a meeting (with a calendar block), or if you are active, inactive, or offline altogether. Some people sit on zoom calls by themselves all day to prevent being harassed by management. You pay quite a bit for subpar healthcare plans. No real on the job training or resources provided. Read the 990. The organization has last revenue every year since 2009. Never recovered from the 2008 recession, and just did another round of layoffs in January of 2023. They've spent more than they've brought in year after year. No CEO, CFO, and the interim CEO is only on board part time. It used to be a $250M organization, which has declined to $100m a year.

Another ‘reorg’ is unraveling now (Jan and Feb 2023) and it’s the 5th or 6th in 7 years… the CFO is gone and the CEO is gone - both within a few months of each other and before the end of 2022. The current leadership lacks knowledge and understanding of how to successfully raise money and focus on relationships. This organization fosters and rewards mediocrity. Remaining C-suite/Senior Leadership does not accept responsibility for the current financial situation. They all continue to blame previous leaders, while congratulating themselves and promoting people who would be considered a joke at other national non-profits. There are some standout staff, but they are few and far between. The bureaucracy is off the charts, and nobody knows who to trust. It’s a ‘kill or be killed’ culture and there seems to be little long-term vision or planning behind the decisions that are being made. I would strongly recommend that any seasoned event fundraiser PASS on this organization - whatever they offer, it’s not enough until there’s a new a CEO and you know the direction and what they actually want to accomplish.

No raises, no clear direction with leadership. Poor work morale. They furloughed 1/4 of the company 3 months ago. They do not care about individuals and are doing everything they can to make money... even when it goes against their mission. They let go of the VP of Volunteers, all health equity roles, and Chief Diversity Officer. They are in the hole and continue to lose money. All internal employees are leaving - do not join right now.

Company is full of extremely talented, but also extremely humble and real people. I have never worked for a company where values actually play into everything they do - even behind closed doors. Our values drive our leaders and our leaders live our values day in and day out. The people make Thumbtack incredible and the culture here is second to none. TT is a diamond in the rough when it comes to working in tech. You won't find a better employer.

They have a very ethical and professional approach to things and hold themselves to a high standard that I admire. They give their employees autonomy in their jobs and it’s fully remote permanently. The culture and environment is not something you can put a price on. The topics discussed behind closed doors consist of empathy and strategy to be better leaders than already executed. Great place to work and amazing career opportunities. This place clearly cares about its employees and it chooses a mix of personalities for leadership with different perspectives to make a complete and sensible picture.
Work from home, great team, fair pay, good medical benefits, and a lot of company holidays.
allCons: Not a lot of cons at Thumbtack.

The Trust and Safety Department is a sinking ship and I'd highly urge anyone to NOT consider employment here. Though it might not even be an option for you, because they are taking the cheap route and offshoring everything to the Philippines lately. What used to be a role with autonomy and the freedom to make the best choices for our users has now become a robotic non-personal department that cares more about standardization than about the individual user experience. It's hard to take a Quality Department seriously who is located in the Philippines, does not understand the culture of the United States and our customers, and who has never actually done our work before auditing us and telling us how to work. It's frustrating to have Senior Leaders support the Quality efforts, and not stand behind the specialists who have been loyal to Thumbtack for years in hearing and taking our concerns seriously. Our managers can only do so much for us. Overall, the lack of support, heartless standardization efforts, and "quantity VS quality" efforts of moving the majority of things over to the Philippines leaves little to be desired of the Trust & Safety Department. I am actively seeking other employment opportunities, and I know I am not the only one.

As an AE you use to just sell a pro and pass it off to a success team member (15 minutes and on to the next). Now you have to fully activate and train the pro on your sales call which has taken up to 2 hours. Quota is the same as when the sales call was shorter. Daily KPI’s have increased and the managers like to shame those who are struggling. It would be better if quota was adjusted and we were paid better. Compared to other sales gigs this is on the low-end unless you work at a mall kiosk. Also the leaders think they are being motivation but really it just gets old because none of them have ever sold during the activation period. Thumbtack also puts a lot of red tape around who you can and can’t sell. Sometimes you run into a grey situation where you think you are doing the pro a solid and benefitting Thumbtack but honestly they will do whatever they can not to pay you on an account sold.

The whiplash felt by the recruiting team caused a great deal of stress. After going through layoffs in 2020, it happened again in 2022. Yes the market is strained but it felt hypocritical to have a very costly offsite 1 month prior to the layoffs.

That ambiguity I mentioned previously. If you thrive in ambiguity, you will thrive here, if you do not and you need to be given direction constantly, TT might not be the place for you. It's been said many times before but a 401k match sure would be nice. Hopefully after we go public.

Company runs "pilots" all the time without systems and tools in place before implementing. Endless Zoom calls hinder a days work. High level of micro-managing. Transparency is not really transparency as manager's are constantly having side discussions about changes that affect your direct role and responsibilities.
It’s still a private newer company (last 12 years) sales department is even newer so there are lots of changes and pivots. To work here you just be flexible and able to embrace change.

No 401k matching. There is no longer a work-life balance. You will need those company holiday closures because taking PTO isn't really an option unless you want to get even further behind. Workloads have significantly increased for junior and mid-level employees since the December 2022 layoff. Most of those laid off were junior managers and below. Leadership was not impacted by the layoffs. This has resulted in as much, if not more, work being done by a much smaller workforce. It's not sustainable. I hear complaints related to this from peers across the company. I'm personally putting in excess of 12-14 hours a day during the week and a few hours every weekend. I also worked during my recent PTO. Unfortunately, I continue to get behind. As a side note, I have consistently received above-average performance reviews so it's not that I can't manage my time or am unproductive. I used to preach the praises of working at Thumbtack, but I can no longer recommend working here. I'm currently looking for a new opportunity.

There were lots of good things about this company when I started. By the end, the bad out weighed all of those factors. The purpose of this review is to tell my story as objectively as possible to help someone else make a fair choice. I don’t think this is a safe place to work and I don’t think it ever will become a safe place. Upon getting employed here I started making a reasonable rate. Starting pay was $17 an hour. That was life changing for me. I’d never made so much money before. I’m a go-getter jack of all trades type of person. If you put me in a position I’m going to do my absolute best to figure things out. I had never worked in a warehouse before but quickly I realized some things could use improvement. There was minimal training involved but I’m used to that. I’ve been thrown into several jobs, this wasn’t any different. So I offered my ideas and I felt listened to, valued. Everything was great at first. I felt like I could take ownership of my own projects and the money continued to pour in for me. Here’s the thing. I’ve never liked people who could be bought, but I became one of those people. At six months things were escalating and I saw the signs. The trans girl who quit unexpectedly, the subtle way people were treated. I ignored it because I was making money. When I suddenly was asked to start treating people like less than, I complied. When they laughed at someone, I laughed, and I was terrible. I hurt people at that job, lost friends, and yet they’d buy us lunch and I’d ignore it all. So many times things were said like “anyone can do her job, let’s just fire her.” “Anyone can do this job.” “They’re replaceable.” Slowly I started seeing more and more girls quit. The turn around was atrocious and through it all I stayed. I worked so hard and I put so much of myself in that position. I worked through an injury, through illness, and then things changed. There was such a lack of guidance because their expectations were all over the place, and at that point everything that went wrong was suddenly my fault. I had fallen from their graces which was obvious by the belittling meetings they hold to pressure people, and yet I still clung to my position. I suddenly felt replaceable as if everything I’d done for them meant nothing. I was so terrified of leaving because of the pay decrease I’d take and there are still people there terrified to leave because of the exact same thing. Over my last few months there I had come to truly see what they were like. I didn’t want it to be true, but how could I ignore it anymore? OSHA violation after OSHA violation, mold in both warehouses, a complete lack of safety training, and the very blatant nepotism in the HR department. The handbook, where policies were changed with a drop of a hat. They never told the team either, just changed the rules and went on their merry way. It became this violent circle of will they won’t they, -take my benefits away, decrease my pay, or fire me? I’d watched it happen to several other girls during my time there, and when it was finally my turn I realized I was a terrible human being for having stayed so long. I had let them buy me. Another trans girl was hired, and the way she was treated was the last straw for me. You can not have a company with values of empowering women when you treat people the way I, and so many others were treated. Some girls were even threatened for trying to speak out. No one should be afraid to go to work. No one should wake up everyday and think ‘I’d rather die than go there.’ So if you have no ethics, are transphobic, and can deal with someone who is incredibly disorganized, this is the job for you. If you’re willing to join them, then the pay might be great if it’s not reduced for behavior. Benefits are subpar but okay for what you’re doing if you don’t get them taken away. And yes, I did take a pay decrease when I left, but you know what? I can sleep at night. Instead of daily nightmares they’ve become less frequent. The vibe in there felt very high school, and sorry but I’m a grown up. If you’ve read this far I hope this sheds some light on an experience that happened at this company. I hope it helps you make the right choice.

Hi I started working for A Shop Of Things in Nashville just last week. I got fired for minor inconsistencies in my work and a few technical errors/ misreads. It was my job to photograph their inventory, make graphics, do email campaigns, manage social media, etc. for both A Shop of Things, and their sister shop Burning Love. Two businesses in one all for the same pay of $18/hr pre tax. Anyways, my boss from the get go was cold and hardly approachable, creating a feeling of walking on eggshells, which makes someone like me who has anxiety even more prone to making mistakes. She sat me down privately the morning before firing me and said, in so many words, that she did not have the time to keep correcting me on my mistakes. No warmth, barely any encouragement, just criticism. Zero compassion for someone starting a new job with no previous job experience in the field. I had only been working there for 7 days. Nothing I had done was so unforgivable that someone would have needed to fire me. I got the sense that she wanted the new hire in my position to know exactly what to do from the get go with little to no guidance. I also get the sense that she doesn't want someone who thinks for themselves working for her. I had training in the warehouse which wasn't my job. That time could have been used better for my growth and improvement. I took amazing photos and graphics for them that were worth way more than how I was being treated and talked to. FYI - there were a ton of mistakes on your end that I caught and didn't tell you. Maybe had your directions and "copy" not been so confusing I would have managed better.

Unfortunately, the other negative reviews on here ring true. The department has fundamental organization & communication problems. It’s been clear from the start of my time at PH that this department has operated in the same regimented yet arbitrary, inefficient, and counterintuitive way for decades. That could take years to undo despite recent leadership changes. If you are coming in from another conflicts department, know that this one doesn’t utilize Intapp or probably any technology you’re used to. The Relationship Management System (RMS) has been this department’s database of matters/corporate hierarchies since the 80s. This interface is extremely tedious and ilegible. Its outdatedness presents so many problems (i.e. data not saving correctly, poor organization of important notes). Our management hasn’t been proactive about fixing these persistent bugs. And instead of Intapp we use the New Business Intake System, which is less problematic than RMS but very outdated nonetheless. Sadly, the management isn’t very proactive about finding solutions in general. On the contrary, they tend to get defensive when given any kind of feedback about the many problems that arise. If you point out inconsistencies or a lack of clarity, they will not take accountability, nor will they take your input seriously. They will take offense and belittle you. In doing so, they discourage employees from thinking critically about their work, asking clarifying questions, and being proactive about their development. The training in general is severely lacking. To preface, the “training” for conflicts research is an extensive process that typically takes 1-1.5 years to “graduate” from, but there’s no rubric or structure. There are three trainers, who are also senior researchers and are thus the point people for nearly everything urgent in the department. As such, these three trainers are stretched so thin and barely have time to balance their own work, let alone review all of someone else’s. If your schedules don’t align or if they’re working on urgent checks/projects in general, it’s difficult to get your work reviewed on time, much less to find time for a discussion or tutorial. Essentially, your “trainer” approves your work, but you have to figure out most things on your own. I’m an incredibly self sufficient person, so while this doesn’t bother me in principle, it does irk me because the work is so niche, and the management is easily annoyed if you don’t know something, even if you don’t have experience with it. I believe the managers are under the impression that the trainers spend more time with us than they actually do. The trainers are also very inconsistent in the way they analyze, write, and determine results for conflicts checks. It’s one thing to have basic human variation, but these individuals have pretty fundamental differences in the way they approach the work, which leads to a lot of confusion. Something that one trainer would advise or approve will be deemed incorrect by another. The trainers should really be talking to one another to develop a consistent curriculum, but as I said, they’re overworked and really have no incentive to do so given how little the managers value communication and directness. On that note, communication is almost absent in the department. Feedback is only given formally a few times a year, and asking for more casual/passing feedback ends up being a production. And it’s common to get hit with negative feedback on something your trainer has never critiqued or even made you aware of. This is obviously not effective, especially because employees have already developed certain practices and understandings of concepts by the time the managers tell them it’s wrong. In general, there’s a disparity between how the managers treat conflicts employees vs attorneys. They’re passive aggressive to conflicts researchers, but they’re overly accommodating if not groveling to the attorneys. Time and time again, I’ve seen my managers bend the same rules they’ve drilled into us so that an attorney doesn’t get vaguely upset or impatient. There’s one particular attorney who’s supposedly a big deal and has a conniption every time we copy him on something, so he gets granted lots of special shortcuts and exceptions. Many attorneys walk all over the conflicts department and expect instant gratification (even if they’ve been ignoring our requests) because it’s been established that they can do it without consequences. I’d say this is a decent starter job, but not worth staying long-term— and most people do not. In the year and a half I was at the company, 6 people including myself left. 6 out of a department of 13-15 people at any given time. It will take a massive overhaul of the department to change these fundamental problems.

Perhaps the most significant advantage of Forever Living Products Company is the fact that it is free for anyone to join. As long as you have basic education and possess the ability to convince consumers, you are ready to go. You do not have to have prior experience in sales. In fact, you do not need to have learned sales or marketing for you to succeed in the job. Generally, you obtain the products and market them to various consumers in exchange for money. Part of the profits goes to the company while you retain the rest. This means that the more active you are the more money you will earn. It is therefore no wonder that the company has grown exponentially from the ashes 36 years ago into a global powerhouse. Another benefit of joining is that you can dictate your own schedule of work. Unlike formal employment where you would have to work strictly from 8. A.M. to 5 P.M., you are your own employer. This way, you set targets for yourself and work without supervision, coercion, or intimidation. The fact that there are no educational requirements means that the company can employ those people who have failed to find jobs elsewhere.
