Hire Velocity is a company that I unfortunately cannot recommend. My experience working for this company was incredibly negative, and it is clear to me that the issues I faced are systemic within the company. One of the most striking issues with Hire Velocity is the way in which leadership treats their employees. The turnover rate at this company is incredibly high, with people leaving after only a few months. This is due in large part to the fact that leadership uses scare tactics and threats to ensure that employees meet their metrics. This creates a very negative work environment that is simply not sustainable in the long run. Furthermore, the pay at Hire Velocity simply is not worth the anxiety and poor treatment that comes along with the job. The leadership is poor, there is no upward mobility, and it often feels like the company views its employees as disposable. There is simply no reason to put up with this kind of treatment when there are so many other companies out there that will value your hard work and dedication. The problems at Hire Velocity are not limited to poor leadership and low pay, either. The company is incredibly unorganized and unprofessional, with no moral compass to speak of. I had several different supervisors in a very short period of time, which is indicative of just how poorly run the company is. Additionally, the highest turnover rate I’ve ever seen only serves to reinforce this idea. One of the major issues at Hire Velocity is the fact that they show favoritism, which leads to good people being fired often. This is a major problem, and it ultimately hurts the company as a whole. Furthermore, the upper management seems to be there not because of what they know, but who they know. This creates an atmosphere of incompetence and unprofessionalism that is simply unacceptable. The recruiters at Hire Velocity are highly overworked and underpaid, which is yet another problem with the company. My advice to anyone considering working for Hire Velocity is to watch out for everyone and everything, because it truly is a game. The company needs to start promoting people who actually have leadership qualities and skills, and they need to give recruiters the chance to give their team leads reviews. This would help to ensure that the good team leads are recognized for their hard work, while the bad ones are held accountable for their problematic behavior. In my experience, the managers at Hire Velocity were fine, but the team leads were often micromanagers who made the workplace unpleasant. It is ironic that the company accuses employees of not putting in the work when they spend so much time spying on them and scrutinizing every move they make. This is not leadership – it is simply someone who is power hungry and has no life outside of work. Another issue with Hire Velocity is the fact that they praise toxic workaholic traits, such as working through breaks and late hours or weekends. This creates an environment where hard work is equated with sacrificing your personal life, which is simply not sustainable. Additionally, the company is plagued by nepotism and dishonesty, which only serves to reinforce the negative work environment. Overall, my experience working for Hire Velocity was extremely negative. The company is poorly run, with unprofessional and incompetent leadership. The turnover rate is incredibly high, which speaks volumes about the kind of work environment that exists at the company. The pay is not worth the anxiety and horrible treatment that comes along with the job, and the lack of upward mobility makes it a dead-end career path. I cannot recommend this company to anyone, and I would advise anyone considering working for them to proceed with extreme caution.

allCons: Elkay used to be a great, inclusive place to work with a good company culture and leadership that truly cared about the people working there. BUT THEN THEY MERGED WITH ZURN IN 2022. Since the merge closed (yes, it was a merge, not an "acquisition" like some other reviews may lead you to believe) and Todd Adams became the CEO, it has become 100% clear that he and all other C- Suite executives only care about the shareholders pockets and everyone who works for them is just a number on a page. They make decisions - like laying off half of a department - without thinking about the consequences. They claim that "people" are one of their core values, then show that by removing the flexible work-from-home policy, reducing paid sick days from 5 to 2 (DURING A PANDEMIC), and slashing all other benefits in half. When employees tried to reason with management about why these changes were harmful to them, they were met with stupid catchphrases and no one willing to advocate for them. I'm not sure how Zurn managed to be voted a 2022 best place to work, but they definitely did not retain the title for 2023 - and not because "people from acquisitions don't like change." Zurn's company culture is simply "stress." The leadership team is completely disconnected from what actually happens day-to-day and will fire anyone without a thought, like picking names out of a hat. Then they somehow expect the people who are left to magically have the same skills/knowledge as the people they fired without any time to train or learn. And when they obviously do not, they fire them, too. Those of us left from the original Elkay will mourn it - it was great place to work with truly the best people who were all incredibly talented and excelled in what they did. But that company - and it's values - are gone. What stands in it's place are the charred remains of a trusted brand name, slowly being disintegrated until there is nothing left but corporate greed, a soulless CEO, and the ability to trick unsuspecting jobseekers into thinking its a company that will value and support them. It will not. Please don't make the mistake of working here - I know I will be getting out as soon as I possibly can.

Elkay was successful and profitable, with a difficult year that resembled many similar companies given supply chain challenges and runaway inflation coming out of COVID, yet Zurn leadership seems to have capitalized on painting the COVID-aftermath challenges as the norm for Elkay and that they "rescued" a "distressed" company. They did not. In speaking with many former Elkay senior leaders, it was apparent that there was no interest in collaboration on much of anything. In speaking to people outside of the companies, I have experienced little positive feedback on Zurn, its management style, its tools, processes, etc., where I frequently would hear positive things about Elkay from some of those same people. Can't tell you in the only 9 months since the merger how few people remain from the Elkay side (most voluntary departures) and most of them are something significantly less than happy. People (particularly good people) are a commodity these days, and Zurn has shown me nothing that shows it will be able to attract and retain quality people who can "play well with others". I absolutely loved working here, but unfortunately I was laid off along with 10% of the company during an economic rough spot in 2023. Employees are passionate, knowledgeable, and everyone was very easy to work with. I wasn't even aware of the official job titles or degree histories of most of my coworkers-- everyone was treated equally and scientific contributions and ideas were valued regardless of who proposed them or their educational background. The atmosphere was also highly collaborative and communicative, and I was allowed to pursue some personal research projects to investigate things that would have been nice to know but weren't strictly necessary for our work. There's a very strong culture of maintaining a good work-life balance. Nobody works weekends and working late is strongly discouraged, though I sometimes did stay after 5:00 to finish up something I didn't want to carry over into tomorrow. A good proportion of people leave early on Friday. Work hard, play hard basically. My leadership was pretty hands-off and extremely flexible as long as you got work done. They were also very understanding of emergencies and family commitments, even last-minute ones. Working from home if you didn't have any reason to be on campus was standard, with zero expectation that you show up just to show up and warm a seat/lab bench. The campus is beautiful with food trucks visiting multiple days on the weekends. There are great events and happy hours for the employees, the gym has a cardio room and a weightlifting room, and there are delicious cafeterias with vegetarian (and even vegan) options available at every station. allPros: Guaranteed 40+ Hours a week. During peak season, 1st and 3rd Quarter you can easily work up to 60 hour weeks. For OSC, there are ZERO GUARANTEE of Full time/Benefits for new hires. Hiring process is from "Temp" to "On Call" to avoid FL labor laws, letting them work for more than 32 hours on average without giving benefits. Due to which turn over is constant and most people do not stay for longer than five to six months. Management guilt trips labor into overtime, with absolutely no quality of life in mind. Management refuses to hire quality people, being unwilling to interview for "lack of time". Going through Express is the only way to get a foot in the door. Benefits per health insurance were recently cut so you're paying the same rates for less coverage at the doctor's office (40% increase out of pocket). Skyline is in the middle of a rebrand. They are trying their best to push the company with family values and workers appreciation. But at the end of the day this is just another corporation who's only goal is to protect their bottom line and take advantage of skills without promotion or equal opportunity.

I cannot tell if they're making lives miserable because they're malicious or just incompetent. I'm leaning towards weaponized incompetence. If you want more details: "Communication is key" was the very first thing I learned about the company yet in various crucial situations the company fails to meet the minimum requirement to maintain transparency and professionalism. Do proper research about the average compensation for your role/experience and speak up about actually receiving it, because if you don't say anything they will make sure you earn the bare minimum, or not even give you a proper contract at all. Multiple project managers with different management and task delegation styles will make it unbearably awful for work to be done. "Don't worry, just ask us!" is not a solid nor viable advice because no one should be wasting their time trying to figure out what they need to do instead actually doing it. Assigning tasks with just the title and due date filled with zero context is beyond useless. Full-time employees also aren't treated that much better, with the team being under-staffed it's likely you'll end up working overtime without being properly compensated. Be diligent with tracking your hours, and make sure you know what/how/when to submit your invoice in case they decide to add extra rules they never bothered to tell you in the first place. Be prepared to have them push our payment just a few days shy the legal limit stated on your contract, or just pay you late regardless of what they've confirmed through writing. You're not paid as an intern, which is unfortunately not surprising, but you're also (supposedly) not invited to any of the social events. You still see the rest of the team planning fun activities on slack anyway, so just ask to be invited and they won't have the guts to say no.

As a driver without experience, you’re hired in the auto hauler program. It is presented as a role where you learn the basics but they literally just show you how to load trucks and send you out on your own. You’re told that you will be eligible for double hauler training and the accompanying pay after 30 days. You get to orientation and they tell you that was incorrect and you’re welcome to leave if that’s the expectation. I’ve seen guys wait 5-6 months on their turn to go into training for the double hauler. In the meantime, you make a little over $3 per car loaded. You have to average about 14 loads per day, six days per week (which is their requirement) to get a thousand dollar check. This is very demoralizing since the double haulers make around $70 per load doing the same thing. Three loads per day and they’ve out earned you after you have literally run at a sprint for 8 hours. Equipment is horrible and very outdated. The maintenance shop and supervisors tell you NOT to write up the trucks using the electronic log but to use a paper dvir. This is so they can not fix it and put it back out to use on the next shift. I’m sure that if DOT regulators were to show up, not one single truck would pass inspection for one reason or another. Major violations all around. General Motors is close to ending their contract with Jack Cooper due to their refusal to invest in their fleet and will buy their own vehicles to deliver their own SUVs and will probably take many drivers from Jack Cooper. Generally you don't alert anyone as to when you go out, or when you come back. You complete payroll at the end of the day and transmit your work, and are given discretion as to how you organize your cases and which area you work in each day. You may work 2 hours for a case or two that are nearby, or you may spend 4-5 hours in drive time depending where you are and how far your cases are from you home. Also- you "rent" your desk for the day so you sit by someone new a lot and that seems okay but you do not get the comfortability of knowing the people around you. Makes it feel like you are just a number, just a desk, and not playing into a community feel. - Lack of leaders: Electrolux is a room full of managers and no leaders. (Maybe a handful but not a lot of them). There is no managerial leadership training, and a lot of the managers are hired off the streets due to turnover, so they do not know the company culture or how electrolux wants teams to be led. - Little to No Training: Training and Development was HUGE when I started at Electrolux, and I was promised a lot of things. Nothing came to fruition, and when I brought this up to my manager (who was also new to the company) I was told in a very dismissive way: "I am figuring it out on my own too". I left that 1:1 extremely discouraged. - Lack of Buy In from Upper Management: My team had the unique opportunity to build and develop an area of the business, but with the lack of resources and technologies to do the job well, we were left treading water but still feeling like we had to prove ourselves. We really needed upper management to get align with the work we were doing to build a robust demand plan. Every meeting felt like we were moving 2 steps backwards and half a step forward. - When you do leave voluntarily, they do not care about your thoughts or concerns. I have been waiting for 6 months for someone to give me an exit interview (which I have requested multiple times). This is why I am finally posting on here. - Extremely unclear growth opportunities: because management is as new as their subordinates, there is no clear path to success...this was a big red flag for me.

I have thought positively about all my other jobs, but management in the Call Center (mainly customer service) is oppressive! Calls come in automatically without having a chance to answer, and you only have 8 minutes a day to turn off calls at all/take a break. That is not enough time to even breathe on some nonstop days! After talking for 4 hours, you would think you need a drink of water or a little snack or to run to the bathroom, but nope! No allowed time for those things. They also get you in trouble if there’s more than 6 seconds of “dead air” in the call, and they monitor everything on your screen (which is understandable, except they criticize every little thing that is not exactly “their way”). I’m a damn good worker and was recognized well by one of my managers, but the other ones would only jump in to pile on more work or say that you took a 9 minute break that day instead of 8 minutes. All for $10 an hour. I thought this was going to be a great opportunity and I went in so excited just to be treated like this. I worked there over 2 years ago and I still cannot believe that I did that to myself and worked there for 7 months. I am so happy in my new job and it makes me sad looking back on how poorly we were all treated. Never work in their call center if you don’t want to be controlled and micromanaged to the max.

The culture at Melaleuca is very toxic. It is built on fear. Company meetings led by Frank are meant to scare employees so they don’t leave. They talk about not laying people off but in the same sentence they said “if people aren’t performing, let’s remove them and just not replace them.” The departments are working with limited team members. One person ends up doing the work of 2-3 people. Turnover in the marketing department is extremely high. It has changed almost entirely since I have been here. Employees are told they are high performers but are treated as expendable. Pay is low compared to other companies unless you’re higher up. Speaking of management, most are all white, middle aged men. The main customers of Melaleuca are women. I have seen many times when management rejects advice from their female employees and makes assumptions about the customer. They often ignore the data, going with their own agendas. The strategy is changed often and makes the lowest people on the totem pole do all the work. It is often a lot and the other departments aren’t understanding that this comes from top down. There is lots of tension between departments. The culture in the marketing department is full of gossip and secrecy. You can’t trust very many people in the department. It can consume you. I’ve had people tell me that have left Melaleuca that it is so freeing and that you don’t realize the weight it has had on your shoulders until you leave. There is so much more to say but it is challenging to capture it all. The other reviews are from marketing executives that aren’t working in corporate. They are our customers that are putting in reviews for the company.

Your mileage is really going to vary. If you are one of the lucky ones who get established here, you're going to learn a lot about bankruptcy law and have the potential to make a big difference in the lives of desperate clients and make some good money doing it. The problem is, management is losing money at such an alarming rate due to structural problems that pre-dated the pandemic, and the urge to get cases filed drowns out every other impulse. If you get hired as an attorney, you will be pushed into the deep end of the pool and be expected to swim. You won't be trained and you'll be minimally supervised with a very big case load. As a result, it will be very challenging to do your job in a competent and ethical way. This format breeds bad lawyering. I raised ethical issues many times and was actively shut down. This company only learns when they get sanctioned or threatned with sanctions, which has happened several times. Some people might be able to thrive in such an environment. Indeed I did for many years. I eventually quit because I found it impossible to meet the demands of my case load while still being the ethical attorney I wanted to be. I think the biggest problems are 1) the case load is too big for their level of staffing and they won't increase it 2) you are given minimal training 3) You won't be rewarded for being a good attorney, only for being a profitable one. 4) Odds are you won't survive the selection process and you'll be one of the tens of lawyers that have worked here, been chewed up and spit out. Statistically, you're gonna start here, be worked to death, feel like you are harming your clients and quit in less than a year. Or you could rise in the ranks, make good money but still be worked to death and be driven to test the limits of your law license. Do you feel lucky, punk?

Compensation and benefits, pt. 1: Cash compensation (base + bonus) is mediocre, and equity compensation is absolutely dismal. Most employees - and everyone at the individual contributor level - are simply not eligible for long term incentives like RSUs. Virtually the only people getting long term incentives are Director level or higher. In the middle management levels, you are only eligible for equity if you have an exceptional performance review, which they force-distribute at less than 5%. Since stack ranking, forced performance distributions and concrete budgets are used, your boss almost has to be a jerk to get equity to anyone actually doing work; an excellent review must be balanced by a bad review. Compensation and benefits, pt 2: Health insurance is embarrassing for a company working in healthcare that, depending on the day and the stock price, could be the single most valuable healthcare company in the world. Employer only pays 68% of costs, and they use Aetna, which is in a constant battle with United for worst healthcare network in the country. The only saving grace is they have a Kaiser HMO option for folks in California, so you can avoid having the absolute worst provider. Compensation and benefits, pt 3: There is a pension program, but I couldn't even list it in the Pros. I did the math once, and, basically, it's like if you took a single year's raise (~4% of base salary), and invested it in a conservatively weighted / borderline poor performing 401k. You only get this benefit if you stay with the company 5 years, so at best, this benefit is like getting a bonus cost-of-living raise once you hit the 5 year mark. I think a much higher impact on potential job candidates would be to offer 4% higher base salaries and just scrap this program. Compensation and benefits, pt 4: Parental leave is generous, and the fringe benefits are competitive -- think tuition/home exercise reimbursements, the little 'thank you' awards you can use to buy gift cards or a toaster -- stuff like that. The internal education platform is also actually useful and worthwhile to use in your free time. Compensation and benefits, pt 5: The 3 year vest on 401k company matches is ostensibly in place to incentivize people to stay, but you don't have a policy that vests the people who were laid off before 3 years, even if they were caught up in broad, sweeping, non-performance-related layoffs. You're basically stealing benefit money from your employees when you do this, and it's shameful. Compensation and benefits, pt 6 (final): As a result of this overall approach to compensation & benefits, you often find people working here who are either phoning it in, playing it ultra safe, or are a little...behind in their careers. I'd like to point out how I haven't just said "management bad" here. It's everyone, the level 20s, the level 30s, and everyone in leadership. I'm sorry to everyone reading this currently at J&J, but, come on: you know it's true. The only reason I took this job is because I wanted something stable as I have kids. The Credo: Unfortunately, J&J can't just be a company, they have to be one of the 'good ones,' and they have this credo which you can google in 2 seconds that explains how they're going to try and be good. It's like a more longwinded 'don't be evil.' In the past, this meant that J&J thought a bit more long term, valued employee retention, and hesitated to do layoffs. The J&J I work at, however, is just like the rest of the corporate mob. Layoffs are a constant threat and short term shareholder value is prioritized above all else.

I feel ambivalent about the behaviour of local management. There are regular mood check-ins which everyone can participate anonymously and have an impact, in theory. There are vast differences in the positioning of the different members of the management team. Sometimes there is a lack of direction, or one almost has the feeling that it is expected to be given by the employees. This sometimes feels good and empowering, but more often the lack of direction feels unsettling. There is a lot of talk about and badmouthing individuals, both current and former team members. On the part of management and among the wider team. This sometimes dampens the otherwise good mood and creates anxiety as to whether it will be the same about yourself as soon as you turn your back. The treatment is also not always equally fair to everyone. Those who don't question or criticize fly under the radar. Those who do or unexpectedly step on the wrong person's toes quickly end up on the persona-non-grata list. Sometimes the popularity factor with management and the "inner circle" is the deciding factor. Unpopular employees are ignored or marginalized and abandoned in personal emergencies. I observed this twice and finally experienced it first-hand, to the point that official processes were not adhered to and support I was entitled to by law was not provided. In good times, the new management style is positively very concerned with flat hierarchies and participation. Unfortunately, when it comes to difficult topics or discussions, it tends to shift to conflict-averse to passive-aggressive.

allCons: Too Much Overhead, Exec Mgmt Top-Heavy, Slowing Growth

Company direction has been taken over by vulture capitalists. Expect to see regular layoffs yearly going forward. Stacked ranking has been introduced (although they softened the terminology…it’s still stacked ranking.). Culture is starting to turn toxic as employees and managers jockey and backstab to avoid layoffs and pips. Risk-taking was previously rewarded even in failure…that’s unlikely to continue. Pay raises, bonuses, and stock grants have been reduced considerably and further cuts are likely to become regular occurrences. Internal bureaucracy is becoming overwhelming, slowing down development and customer support to a crawl. Management is aware of and sympathetic to the toxic changes but are powerless to do anything. Even Marc Benioff seems to be fearful of losing his title and is taking positions unthinkable even a year ago. Fast growth culture is over. It’s all about profit margin now. Ohana is dead. Company will live on but as a traditional IT company not unlike IBM or Oracle. Path to $50 billion in 3 years is unlikely.

1) Fake "Ohana" culture (If you're ex-oracle, white, or a bully you'll thrive here). 2) Toxic sales leadership (no WLB, nepotism at its finest, racist & sexist leaders are protected despite ES/HR complaints filed, patches/territories are inequitable, lack of accountability and tons of deflecting, and inauthentic "team selling" is encouraged). 3) Hypocritical (Budget Cuts don't apply to leadership = pressure clients to attend Dreamforce but AEs can't attend due to budget cuts + force AEs to remotely watch SF leaders waste thousands of dollars for a lavish week in Hawaii for non-client facing Laulima + build Trailblazer ranch that exclusively only SF leaders visit + prioritize paying celebrity $10M despite layoffs | Digital HQ = publicly say the future of work is hybrid/remote work + force remote SF internal teams to report back to office +3x a week). 4) Facade of DEI (Equality Report is inflated to reflect # of hires but not transparent on URM/women retention & career progression = high attrition rates, false sense of belonging, microaggressions, gaslighting, & cultural appropriation)

It has become too bureaucratic. They divided teams into ever smaller teams by Industry and some of the newer less mature products suffered for it in terms of competitive edge and innovative enhancement releases. Perhaps they'll get back to their roots and focus on innovation of their core products. Too many acquisitions without a proper assimilation program created a chaotic onboarding for acquired companies and no clear direction for selling the salesforce way for them to be successful and introduced channel conflict.

They preach work-life balance, but they are/ were so under-staffed - you work all the time Under-staffed because lots of promotions from within, but no backup for gaps - and hiring too slow You work on a lot of sales deals at the same time - supporting 6 salespeople at once Very long hours and weekends of working Lots of office politics

Managers are just that, they are not leaders, all they are worried about is what deals are coming in. Managers also strongly played favorites on teams, and it was clearly seen when accounts would be assigned to AEs. Overload on resources so it is often hard to find out where to actually get help. AE's are often so pressed on their own numbers they don't want to stop and help their own teammates. Horrendous bro culture, a lot of AEs will do/say what they have to in order to get a deal to close, because accounts refresh every year they don't care about the downstream impacts on broken promises or poor customer experience. There is no boundary for work/life balance. Managers will call you over the holidays or late on weekends for updates on deals, they will expect you to put personal life on hold in order to hit your numbers. The company does not breed a positive culture, this is an incredibly toxic place to be.

There’s an unrelenting amount of bureaucracy, constant notifications and trainings and such that are not beneficial and that are in conjunction with a really high level of expected utilization which makes it harder to meet your goal. The promotion process is awful (1-2x a year and challenging) which makes moving up painstakingly slow, and we are definitely underpaid in the industry by a LOT. This makes me feel very under appreciated for the amount and quality of work that I do. It’s also hard to meet your utilization goal AND keep getting certifications unless you’re doing it in your spare time which is awful. It’s hard to imagine being able to stay here for a long time without being a “boomerang” employee in order to get an actual decent pay raise. While many of the senior leadership is pretty good, Marc often delivers extremely tone deaf messaging which is not great for morale either (latest being his response to layoffs and him going back on his previous statements around remote work)

With the new investing partners there is a sentiment that more layoffs, more cuts to benefits, and restructuring is coming. Acquisitions of Slack and others hasn’t panned out. Salesforce is a business first, the coming years will prove that out. It’s about increasing product margin, the stock price, and pushing operating costs to customers, and the employees are simply numbers. The culture is a huge facade and it’s becoming anything but a family/ Ohana. If you’re thinking about joining, just lower expectations. It’s an average job, no different than the next tech company.

1. Toxic Work Environment: The work environment at Cafe Nero was toxic and demoralizing. There was a pervasive lack of support from management, and communication was poor. Shifts were often understaffed, leading to excessive workload and stress. The lack of teamwork and cooperation among staff members created a hostile and unfriendly atmosphere, making it difficult to enjoy coming to work. 2. Substandard Compensation and Benefits: The compensation and benefits provided by Cafe Nero were below industry standards. The wages only reached the minimum wage, and there were NO benefits offered to employees. The lack of proper compensation did not justify the high workload and stress levels experienced by employees. 3. Lack of Employee Care: Cafe Nero demonstrated a complete lack of concern for the well-being of its employees. There was no effort made by management to address the numerous complaints and concerns raised by staff members. Requests for time off or schedule adjustments were often denied without consideration, and employee feedback was dismissed or ignored. The company showed a blatant disregard for the physical and mental health of its employees, leading to burnout and dissatisfaction among the staff.

The café I worked in was run with increasingly strict controls on our behaviour and these controls were also arbitrarily enforced and differently for different people. If one member of staff made a 'mistake' the whole team was subject to threats of disciplinary action. Management claimed that they had high standards but this was not evident at all in their behaviour towards members of staff. Speaking for myself, I was personally insulted a number of times and subject to random pseudo-disciplinary procedures that were not explained to me. I was also made to feel threatened in store, in front of customers and other staff. I was told that my training was not a priority and members of staff who were hired after me were promoted ahead. Everything is brushed under the carpet in favour of profit, a maniacal and exploitative drive to up-sell the premium coffee to customers, and there is a lack of understanding by management about almost any issue in store.

The QA score system is all subjective and is not a hard and fast checklist that is easy to evaluate how a particular call went. You have to rely on whether or not the reviewer thought you were being friendly enough with the customer while also getting them taken care of in a short amount of time and also nailing certain processes and asking specific questions about the products or try to make a sale. Also be prepared to take on more than just your current role if they think they can squeeze it out of you. I was subjected to being place on "Backup" teams for other parts of Customer service for if they needed coverage or needed help. Be prepared to not get paid for that extra work and to merely be recognized as one of the backups because they can't find it in their budget to hire on more full time members of those teams. Be prepared to lose those backup assignments if you were like me and hoping that those would pan out into a promotion because your stats took a dive because of all of the backup stuff you were doing and then not get it back. In summary my experience is similar to most who worked there during my tenure, especially toward the end but I would say if you are looking for a job to have between other jobs then go for it but don't hope to start in Customer service and then be stuck in the same role for 7 years.

allPros: You’ll have control of your time

GRA positions offer an opportunity for graduate students to gain valuable research experience and develop skills relevant to their field of study. Students who are awarded GRA positions typically receive a stipend, tuition remission, and health insurance, which can help offset the costs of pursuing a graduate degree. GRA positions can help students build relationships with faculty members and fellow researchers, which may lead to future career opportunities. By working on research projects, students may have the opportunity to contribute to the advancement of knowledge in their field and make a positive impact in society. Clemson University's ME department is ranked among the top mechanical engineering programs in the country, which can enhance the value of a graduate degree from the department.

The workload of a GRA position can be demanding and require significant time and effort outside of coursework. The research focus of a GRA position may not align with a student's personal interests or career goals. I think the downside is the pay. Again, depending on your department, they come up with a lot of excuses as to why you can't make more in the Admin role. I was told that I am pretty much maxed out where I am at in this position ($38,900) even though there is a pay range posted on the description that can be up to the $50,000 not to mention that other admins in different departments make anywhere from 45,000- 56,000. If applying for this job, be sure to ask about pay and the room for growth in pay.

There is very little opportunity for growth, and it shows with the motivation of the staff. Because you are stagnant in positions and there is not incentive to work harder to gain better access to positions or increased salary there is little-to-no motivation to really try. For my first two years I tried very hard to innovate and implement new systems that could increase my productivity and success, however this was a complete struggle to implement as most of the other staff and faculty were very siloed in their colleges and had little interest in doing something new that would shake up their current routines. Clemson is the very definition of "if its works then why do something different?" which breeds a plateauing creative environment. Unfortunately there is next to no opportunity for pay increases, and the finance and ops team will use the excuse of state pay band structures to justify this. Often times HR will make what feels like a generous offer at your initial agreement, be warned that this will be the last time salary will be offered to you so fight for every last dollar you can get because there will be no further discussion on salary increase during your tenure. You will also see a lot of favoritism and internal politics play-out at the executive levels of each division and college. Most of the people in these positions act as figure heads for larger fundraising efforts from the university, they have little insight into what you are actually doing. Middle management is often very good here though, so you can count on good direct managers. There just seems to be a widening gap between leadership and actual employees that CU is not interested in addressing.

Applicants, beware. When you leave this company, you might experience a sort of professional PTSD for a while and wonder what happened to you, your self-worth, your ambitions, your self-confidence. That company will siphon it all out of you. This job could be the perfect job, except it's hell. Low salary and barely any annual raises. It is a shame that this company does not seem to value and/or retain the many smart, dedicated, and talented people it hires. For example, most editors have PhDs (managers/leaders don't necessarily) and are very smart and willing to work hard, but they are de-professionalized and made into sweatshop workers. Editors are supposedly hired because they are specialists in their fields but are constantly provided with papers to edit in random unrelated fields. It does not seem to matter to the company who you are, as long as you are a warm body who can go through a task. The company has a revolving door. People at every level are constantly leaving. No matter how long you have been with the company, you will always find yourself forced into an obligatory training for something that's changing and that you have no interest in. None of these training opportunities are career-building; they are only about specific internal processes and only aimed at making it possible for the company to expand business. Training is on your own time, as are the numerous meetings. Extra demands/training are not usually matched with a decrease in your workload, which is allocated on a daily and weekly point basis from which you cannot deviate without consequences. Expect to have to catch up on most weekends. The company relies heavily on AI for many processes and it seems that it places its trust and faith in metrics, not in people. Deadlines are unpredictable; I never knew my deadlines but a few days prior. The job was only "flexible" because I had to be flexible. It is sad to say that many people working there have probably lost confidence in themselves to get out and do something else with their skills. Employees are micromanaged and drowned in daily data about performance. Objectives are revised upward when you meet them. Editors, who should be the heart of the company, are not listened to. Micromanagement/surveillance includes asking you to record yourself while editing; data generated per paper you edit are compiled weekly, monthly. You will be asked to install on your computer software that records every keystroke you make while editing a paper and films your screen during the process. Your dignity as a person and as an educated professional will reach a zero level. Even though you work from home, the company is ever more present in your space than any supervisor would be in a face-to-face job. The surveillance and patronizing culture is often disguised behind the language of “support”. We were constantly reminded to embrace a company culture that exists only on paper and, in my experience, is a smokescreen for a toxic and distrusting environment. The company seems to consider employees as highly replaceable, and creativity, talent and critical thinking is often crushed or ignored. Most papers the company receives are extremely poorly written/translated. Currently, editors are expected to work at a rate of 2800 words per hour minimum, and the company recently implemented a close to 4000 words per hour average for a compulsory percentage of papers each week. Editors cannot choose the papers to edit and salaries are not increased when the workload increases. The pressure of keeping with pace is extreme and constant. You will be told to leave errors in papers (so called “low priority” errors) and to mostly focus on “low hanging fruits”. In summary, if you want to keep your dignity, if you have ambitions and self-worth, if you expect to be treated like a professional with an advanced degree, only consider this company as your last choice and a temporary solution to unemployment. The level of patronizing and control is unseen in most academic professional environments.

Micro managed, overworked, feels that I was replaceable, underdog, and culturally backstabbing each other. I worked for Kaiser Permanente for 13 years. I was proud being a Kaiser Permanente employee before, and this was when I was in my late 20s to 30s. Kaiser was great then as I was a single woman, and starting to build my career. After three kids, and two Workers Comp's case for my work permanent injury, Kaiser was not so worth it anymore. Management blamed everything on me, as we all know we always under staffed and very difficult to find help to reposition patients. Colleagues and charge nurses would help, but they wouldn't like me so much afterwards. I often heard that colleagues would talked about other colleagues in a negative way. Not to make the situation worse, I was transferred to another department after my leave of absence, and the Department Administrator accused me of a lot of things that I did not do such as "missing for hours" while in fact I was sent to Flu Clinic by the Charge Nurse to help out. and what a good leader should do, was investigate and verify right? no, she went straight to write a corrective action and pushed me to sign it. Like what others had mentioned, the Union was a joke. I never asked for help other than when this happened, and they replied that I just came back from a leave and I needed to prove myself. Again, it just felt that I was nobody, I was just a robot doing whatever they asked the staff to do/ fill out, and that my critical thinking was not appreciated. Pretty much, just be quiet, do whatever the checklists were, and I would do just fine. I was in grad school as well, and the Department Admin said that this department was not suitable for me then. I was shocked as I thought as a great leader, we supposed to encourage and motivate our staff to reach higher in life. I reported it to HR for investigation, and..... nada. Again, I was nobody for them, and I was not an asset to them, plus with everyone wanted to work for Kaiser, they probably glad I was out their company. I finally resigned after 13 years considering my mental health and my family well being is more important than staying in Kaiser for a great pay and salary. By the way, I worked in other company as well during the same time I worked for Kaiser (and still do now), and I felt my professional nursing expertise was valued and appreciated. Of course, they pay much less, but being happy in the work environment, make a better quality of life.

'They're friendly' dog-owners will casually say, whilst their rat of a pet does their utmost to try and tear your throat out. This sounds dramatic, but being chased and bitten by a dog is. I like dogs, but having been attacked, and bitten, I now I have a healthy respect for their unpredictable nature. There is a 'training' session on how to deal with dog attacks, as there are numerous instances every year. Posties have had life-changing injuries. Google it. The leading technique is to use your satchel as a barrier. FYI if you're a dog owner and your dog attacks a postie, and the postie can decides press charges, your dog can be put down. I was badly bitten, but didn't press charges as I'm a dog owner myself. I had to inform my manager, and RM legally had to stop delivering post to that address until they installed a postbox outside the gate. I was told I could no longer work that route as the same house had a vendetta against me, believing me responsible for this... When you're new you get the worst days off. If you work in accounting, IT or marketing, odds are you spend more time complaining about your boss and the toxic environment than you do being productive. Our watercooler jokes are about who has the worse boss and why. The managers of these departments clawed their way into these positions, and I promise it wasn’t through meaningful experience, and will do anything to stay there. It’s no longer about teamwork but instead being a person on their team. Most of us just put our heads down and do the work because we’re scared of getting on the bad side of our boss. We have seen what happens to individuals who do speak up. We take surveys and everything and they come back with negative results but there isn’t much being done to resolve the bad leadership we are faced with every day. They’ve come up with things like a culture committee, but I’m sorry, letting us wear casual clothes on Fridays and having more snacks in the kitchen is not going to address the toxic atmospheres these women create for us daily. It puts us in a super unfortunate position because we all love our company, but the leadership at corporate is awful. Do I continue to stay and hope for the best and that the board will finally see what is happening here, or do I just cut my losses now knowing that things like “snacks” and “premium coffee” are their answers to our problems?

There are early signs that the culture is heading towards profit-first at the expense of its people, which is being felt in a several ways: Pay increases have significantly lagged behind inflation for years (despite two raises, I'm paid $7000 less today than I was 2 years ago when you account for inflation - BOY am I feeling it, and I'm not alone) New people are being hired in at higher salaries than the experienced team members they are joining Any attempt to negotiate salary is shut down immediately. Managers are powerless to support their people when it comes to fair pay; HR has total control over new hiring and salaries The process of industry benchmarking to determine fair wages does not appear to be conducted in the light of required responsibilities and skills. The focus seems to be on basic job title. This leads many employees to be benchmarked against lower skill positions compared to their actual duties, and paid less than they're worth. Employee performance assessments by department are required to conform to a bell curve, where most employees must be rated as average, but a percentage *must* be rated below or far below average, and a few must be rated as above or far above. Managers are routinely forced to downgrade the high ratings they gave to deserving employees in order to conform their department to the bell curve. It's insulting both to employees and the science of statistics, and it keeps merit-based raises low. It honestly makes me consider intentionally hiring some low-performers that will be rated low, so I can preserve the ability to rate my rock stars accordingly and try to get them what they deserve. Performance-based bonuses are limited to certain classes of employee As a result of all this, amongst most people I talk to within and without my department, morale is presently at an all-time low - and I've been here more than a decade. The general feeling is - why work hard, why be "intrapreneurial," when no matter how hard we work, we're rated middle of the road and can only watch as inflation eats up our stagnant wages.

About 4-5 years ago the company shifted focus dramatically toward DEI. On the surface, not a big deal but in reality it represented a shift away from VMware as a technology leader and toward VMware as a social justice company. Given that VP bonus was tied to DEI metrics, I found myself restricted on who I could hire for positions. This meant that I had to engage in discrimination in who I was able to consider for roles, and found myself "dumbing down" my hiring criteria due to lack of applicants who fit the "correct" DEI requirements. For a variety of reasons (and covid was a huge catalyst), general morale and work ethic seemed to decline greatly over the past few years. It became increasingly difficult to get anything meaningful accomplished in day-to-day work. The products themselves became increasingly bloated and buggy, plus the overall business strategy became muddled (specifically the cloud strategy). VMware recognized the need to transform from a "product" company towards a "services" company but simply lacked the ability to successfully transition. Major transformations require agility and ability to adapt products quickly, which is simply not possible for companies that have allowed themselves to become complacent.

In other restaurants, customers usually buy an entree each, and maybe an appetizer or bar drink, with the possibility of them grabbing something for dessert. Not at the Cheesecake Factory. Almost everyone orders dessert of some type, and most of the time they just get it to go (order it in a to-go container, take a few bites, then just close the lid). Each cheesecake slice is ~$10. That's 50% of what an entree averages, and it's almost assured that everyone gets dessert while they're there....and the best part is, even if they order it to go, they usually tip 20% as if they were eating it in-house. The money is amazing....IF you are hungry and grab it. There's always shifts to pick up, too. Just know, serving is the best way to make money there. As an example: today was Monday, and I worked 4:30-10pm. I made $200. I could have left at 8pm, but probably wouldn't have made more than $150 if I had left earlier. The money's there, you just have to be hungry and grab it.

In many companies fulfilling OKRs are the main goal and it was the same here. What was genuinely frustrating was when management refused to acknowledge, let alone put efforts to fix roadblocks in achieving them. It seemed as though senior management was in a competition to show the best numbers to the CEO, who has constantly enforced the notion that outcomes and ROI need to be seen, regardless of the effort that went behind it. While this is the norm, it is my opinion that it is not effective in the long run when there's actual process issues that need to be fixed. If you're required to reach the airport at a certain time in India, and there's a huge herd of cows blocking the road, you're not going to reach the airport on time magically, even if you believe with all of your heart there are no such animals as cows. I cannot Thanos-Snap my fingers and make the herd disappear (get the analogy?). Epic levels of denial, and this of course resulted in a huge mistake, that affected over 50% of the workforce in January (mentioned later). This ignorance was replicated across the management, as they displayed total disregard to frustrations relayed by actually dedicated and loyal employees who want to do their best. They would rather give them criticism and ironically, a false sense of job security (maybe because they themselves don't know how to fix the problem without making themselves seem incompetent to the CEO). I have read case studies about great CEOs going down to the grassroots to know what's exactly happening or checking in, but I am amazed at the levels of obliviousness across the leadership. I don't really blame the CEO for trusting his management, but I do blame the values and criticisms that enforced this ignorance. I believe that he should have enforced working for the company-first rather than working for individual departments or personal achievements. But what do I know, it's his company, his rules. So, what happens when the numbers are rosier than they actually are? Mass hiring, and when it clicked that they were way off with what was relayed and what strategy they had for the future, they decided to lay off 150+ team members, many of which would've given their complete self to better company results accepting way less in return. A decision without clear logic behind why and how people were chosen to be laid off, done in the most abrupt fashion, as shocking as it would be if a family member died suddenly without cause (of course the grief isn't the same, unless your company is unfortunately your only "family"). So, what's your lesson or take-away? Join the company, like you would any company. I loved the team, but you should keep your CV updated, contacts ready, job opportunities saved. Don't give your blood, sweat, tears or your peace of mind to this or any company. Ask for the goodie bag if it is still there, because I cannot promise that the goodbye kit will be the same. I got to keep my Mac, I guess as something I could sell if I don't get a job during this amazing recession. Take criticisms from one ear and send it out the other. Prioritise yourself no matter if you join here or somewhere else. And, don't spend all your money. So with that, all the best potential future Skitter, you will definitely learn a lot.

The new folks don’t know internet culture or Gen Z or even what seems uncringey to the average young person, but they’re often delivering mini TED Talks about their insights in these arenas to literal Gen Z coworkers, longtime online community experts, and trendsetters. Don’t get me wrong, some of these new folks are nice and trying their best, but there are a few of these marketing directors who just see OG Discorders as competition that they must sabotage so that their own (very out of touch cheugy) ideas can shine through. The culture here has shifted over the past few months. It took me a while to realize it, but now that I see it, I can't unsee it. I was hired about 15 months ago. When I first joined, I felt welcomed. The work I was expected to do was fair, and while it was difficult, everyone offered me help where they could. These days, me and my team are on our own completely. We've asked for more help, and we've been turned down. Everyone is burnt out. Every company All Hands meeting ends with someone asking what leadership is going to do to help with everyone being overworked. And every time we get a dispassionate "We're working on it" response. But no help comes. I can't afford to leave. The economy is in shambles and I have a family to support. But I've reached the point where I am looking into medical leave. I took this job because Discord brags about how wonderfully they treat employees, and I was sick of being walked over by employers. And I think that once upon a time they *did* care. But they don't anymore. Or at least, it feels like they don't. I was promoted while the rest of my team was not. Why? Because I was hired first. My teammates do the same amount of work as me. They as just as burnt out as I am. When they were first hired I did my best to take care of them, but they don't need that anymore. We're all on the same level. Only difference is that I am properly paid for my stress and tears, and they are not.

allPros: I will say that the owner is fair with pay and will never mess with or play games with your paycheck.
allCons: I was with the company for over 7 years and implemented the products they sell today (University Magnets). After being in a car wreck and going through rehab I was allowed to come back to work but I had to start all the way back at the bottom, which isn't unfair, so I went to work and did what was asked of me. Shortly after I was promoted to project setups and even given a 10% raise within 60 days, so I was basically on the same trend I was when I first started working there. Not long after that I started taking care of customer complaints and chargebacks, which is what I was doing as Operations Manager. When I went to the owner to discuss my responsibilities and pay, we spoke on the phone for quite some time and he told me what was expected and would discuss a pay increase at a later time. After we ended the call he promptly called me back to inform me that he decided to let me go because the conversation we just had didn't sit well with him. When I asked for a specific reason why he said it would take too long to explain it to me. That was not acceptable to me so I pressed him for a reason and that resulted in him yelling saying "I don't need to have a reason to let you go" (I omitted the swear words). That technically is true in the State of Texas, he even said I could claim unemployment and he wouldn't fight it. I understand business is separate from personal situations but when you are told you are family and invited over to someone's house for almost every major holiday that kind of mixes business and personal life. If he is willing to let someone go for no reason knowing that the employee is now disabled and trying to get back on his feet then he will do that to anyone. Even an employee that has been there since the beginning is treated with disrespect. The way he talks to the people that do the most for his company is very disappointing. Find a company that is willing to invest in you as much as you invest with them, not just chew you up and use you for however you can profit him then spit you out.

Nothing is guaranteed except for what is in your contract. Leadership is not hesitant to work you overtime. In some places, you can work 60-70+ hour weeks. No one mentions duty prior to you joining the Navy unless you have a good recruiter. Duty is mandatory overtime without additional compensation. Advancement is based on quantity of additional things on your annual evaluation and not work ethic. You can be the highest scoring advancement test taker and be the hardest working person in the boat or command, and the person that scores lower on the test, volunteers a few hours a week, takes an art class, and leads PT once in a blue moon will get advanced. Sure, we travel but we have a curfew. What grown adult is required to be back home by 10pm when traveling? I'll let you take a guess. The one's that are ok will all the noted items previously mentioned end up staying in and continue the toxic traits of past leaders. We come across few and far in between good leaders which is unfortunate. I came into the navy with a different attitude and planned on doing 20 years minimum.

If you don't agree with government / DoD / service branch policies and will not compromise on your beliefs / morals, you will have one heck of an uphill battle standing your ground, and very possibly might lose (i.e. be dishonorably discharged... over, basically, a difference of opinion). So in other words, your life is only your own in the military if you make it so, and doing that just might cost you your military career and have lasting consequences on your life once you're out. Clearly I'm speaking from a personal experience, that almost resulted in my separation from the Navy, but by the grace and will of God I'm still serving. Despite my more difficult experiences in the Navy, I would join all over again. I didn't have a lot of life experience prior to joining, and I certainly do now. The majority of my adult life has been spent in the service and the good, bad, and ugly has all culminated in a positive learning experience that I will carry with me for the rest of my life.

I find it regrettable that I have to pen down my experience at this organization with such a negative perspective, but it's important that others gain insight into what's truly happening behind the scenes. At the helm of this organization is a leadership structure that channels fear, rather than inspiration, as its primary motivator. Rather than fostering an environment of openness, respect, and empowerment, the powers that be exploit vulnerability and foster a climate of intimidation. It felt less like a professional workspace, and more akin to a twisted game of survival where every day was an uncharted expedition through a minefield of high-pressure demands and irrational expectations. The culture, or what they refer to as "our way," resembles more of a cult than a cohesive and collaborative unit. Dissenting opinions are not only discouraged but treated as heresies, creating an echo chamber that drowns out innovative thoughts and stifles any semblance of personal growth. The near-totalitarian obedience demanded is not just disturbing; it's dehumanizing. The leadership's relentless demand for conformity goes against every tenet of a healthy work culture. As for direction, the organization seems to be navigating blindly. Strategic planning appears to be an alien concept, replaced by spontaneous decision-making and a distinct lack of foresight. The everchanging policies and constant shift in goals created an aura of instability and uncertainty. It was a frustrating experience to invest time and effort into projects only to have the direction abruptly change without clear reasoning or communication. Moreover, the benefits package, or the lack thereof, is another glaring flaw. The absence of health benefits is not only a blatant disregard for employee welfare but a stark deviation from standard industry practices. In a time where health is paramount, such negligence is nothing short of appalling. The constant attrition rate is a testament to the unbearable conditions. Each week, faces disappear and new ones take their place, creating an environment of transience and instability. It was disheartening to witness talented individuals driven away by the toxic atmosphere and lack of support. In conclusion, working here was a profoundly unsettling experience. This organization has a long way to go in terms of cultivating a supportive and nurturing environment that values its employees' wellbeing and promotes growth and development. I cannot, in good faith, recommend this place to anyone seeking a healthy, constructive work environment. I only hope that this feedback catalyzes a much-needed transformation.

They also pay you, so make sure to button up the details of your pay when you start, and if you believe you have something more to offer than you're worth, Biogen may be desperate enough to negotiate for that. The team you're on will truly treat you the same as a salaried hire which is respectful of them. At the same time, it is difficult because you may work just as hard as full-time employees but not be compensated as well. Also, your team may not be great so being treated the same is not necessarily good. The chances are high that your manager will be very cagey about if they can offer you a full-time position, so if you end up doing good work and are there for a while it will probably be frustrating. The other con is that because you are employed in this weird zone you'll feel "siloed" in your team, in a situation where no one outside your team wants to interact with you. All this amounts to a bad employment structure, so no, I do not recommend contract work.

Labcorp has people development at the forefront of all organizational goals and areas of focus. It's part of everything. Employees are consistently supported in their career growth endeavors, so much so, that it is a part of line manager discussions, is embedded in performance assessments (developing self and others), and at the top of mind during assessment of new business opportunities and assignments. In addition, there is a strong line management and mentorship network to allow for support and guidance. Personally, I have felt encouraged and appreciated since the day I chose Labcorp. My career has grown significantly over the years and this couldn't have happened without the mentorship and support I received from colleagues, line management, and leadership.

The "unlimited" PTO (or flexible time off as they call it) is a great benefit. While this may be a "scam" at some companies, I generally take time off every 6-8 weeks. I've never had a problem with getting my FTO requests approved and it's great knowing I can take time off when needed. Additionally, it's very acceptable to step away for a medical appointment, etc during working hours if needed. Medical benefits are good as well. There are things you can do to greatly reduce the amount you pay in insurance premiums which is nice. They also offer an HRA program that the company pays into. 401(k) matching 100% up to 5%. The managers I've had are all very supportive. No blame game if something goes wrong, just trying to figure out how to move forward. Managers are also receptive to concerns about workload and will work with you to help offload tasks.

In addition, I found out during my discussions with my supervisor about this issue that Camping World recently reduced PTO for new hires from 10 days to just 5 days. Disgraceful.

They don't care if the end user's are receiving good quality work, they only care about how many tickets you work in an hour or day. You'll be expected to work projects while doing tickets, and expect the project to be completed ASAP, even when the ticket volume is high. They will tell you that there is no deadline to get a project done, then they will question you on why you haven't completed it yet and then ask you every day. If you work an on call shift, expect to somehow be on call during the day and when you work 8 hours on a weekend while on call, don't expect to get any comp time like normal companies that care about their employees give. Managers and employees routinely work nights and weekends with no comp time, and are ok with it, which shows that if you want to have a work/life balance, don't work here. Just because it's remote, they expect people to work 10 hours per day a minimum. They say they have unlimited PTO, but that's a scam and you end up having even less vacation than if you were given 2 or 3 weeks since people feel compelled to not abuse it and end up taking even less time than if they were just given a set amount per year. I have disabilities, and even though they said they accommodated them and the doctor's appointments, they despised me for trying to take care of my disabilities. I gave a 2 week notice as a professional courtesy, and on a slow day, even when there isn't much work to be done, they fired me, completely expecting me to work like I'm trying to go for a promotion rather than leave. No one is going to be working with 100% effort during their 2 week notice, but CW does! I wish I had just quit instead of trying to be an adult and a professional, so if you do work here and don't like it, I would refrain from giving a two week notice, especially if you expect to have an income to provide to your family with. This is easily the second worst job I had, and couldn't even stand a month before I realized I had made a grave mistake and started looking to replace this one. Luckily I was able to find a job before all my hair fell out!

allPros: People are great. Collaborative and lots of independence and trust from others. Fun being part of a venture firm that is emerging as a top firm. Fun working with startup founders amd finding ways to help them.

Mission and Employees: HackerOne is a reputable company and brand that is committed to its valuable mission. As a startup, it has experienced both successes and setbacks, but has used each as an opportunity to learn and improve. The founders are dedicated and unwavering in their pursuit of the company's mission, and the leadership team has undergone changes that have propelled the company's growth. The employees, who are passionate about the mission and embody the spirit of the hacker, are what truly make HackerOne exceptional. Benefits: Unlimited PTO, Wellness Wednesday, etc. were great.

allCons: None - Really enjoy being here.

HackerOne places its mission above employee salary. This is unfortunate as the cost of retaining quality employees may be less than the time and resources spent on recruiting and training new ones. Additionally, HackerOne should consider implementing a more equitable compensation structure, like eliminating location-based salaries, to remain competitive with other technology companies that offer equal pay across the board.

It's hard to describe HackerOne and the many things happening in a set of bullet points. On the one hand the business is focused on providing what people need to feel integrated and get on with their jobs, on the other hand it's highly dysfunctional and prone to burning employees. At the core of it is a company that thinks it's a startup but really, is increasingly more corporate with all the dysfunctions of a startup. Things keep ticking and on paper look good because there's a collective of people who are grinding hard on goodwill and a sense of belonging. The company has no way to identify and thank these people as staff are told that "everyone is expected to work hard as a default". On the other side a lot of people are coasting and are instead putting their energies into standing out as personalities. Success at HackerOne is 60% work and 40% managing perceptions, if you just want to focus on work then this isn't the place for you, or at least don't expect to get recognised for it without taking some billboard signs out advertising your achievements. The company is US centric and you really feel it. HR have a poor understanding of local issues (outside the US) and make egregious mistakes that can cause serious problems to employees. Unfortunately they go into "Dark HR" mode and will burn anyone in an effort to preserve themselves, which raises another problem; There is a lot of lip service paid to company values and self improvement but this is selectively applied as and when it suits the business. You're constantly asked to evaluate yourself against company values and some unspecified performance metrics, you're constantly questioning yourself. This keeps you doubting yourself and putting ever more hours in without really looking at your work situation and how it's affecting the rest of your life.

Poor management, no support, toxic environment. As a phone rep, you're on the front lines with shareholders. You're the person they talk to when there's a problem with their account. With this company, no one does their job properly. As a result, you will encounter a high amount of frustrated shareholders who did what they were supposed to do to accomplish their transaction, but because an employee failed to follow established procedures, the transaction was denied--and, in general, the company will double down on the mistake rather than fix what was done wrong. So, expect a high amount of angry callers who will berate and abuse you--and you WILL have to sit there and take every bit of it unless the caller uses foul language or slurs. When that happens, you'll have to take the abusive behavior 3 times to give 3 warnings before being allowed to disconnect the call. You will constantly field calls from frustrated callers who were told the wrong thing by other reps. Accept this as the way it is. There are two reasons for this: 1. poor training and poor resources (see below), and 2. other people do not do their job, so even if you tell the caller the right thing, someone else drops the ball and makes you look like the one who was wrong. No, there is no recourse for this. Get used to callers thinking you're an idiot, even when you know you've given them the right information. As a CSR, your performance will be reviewed by people who do not fully understand your job, which is odd considering the company likes to brag about how CRSs are promoted to other positions. It will then be YOUR job to do a thorough check of all of your reviews to make sure the person reviewing you has done their job accurately. If you don't do this, YOUR performance metrics suffer. So, not only do you have to know your job, but you also have to know the quality team's job (who make more than you) so you can make sure they're reviewing you properly. However, catching a mistake does not guarantee your review will be adjusted. You will be expected to meet insane call handling times. While you're expected to keep your calls under a short amount of time, the company heaps on procedures that greatly and negatively impacts your ability to meet your metrics. Filling out a fraud report used involve filling out an email, which used to take just a few minutes. It now requires filling out a form and filling out an email, which takes about 7 minutes. Need assistance with a call? You used to just ask in chat to your team lead and assistant team lead. Now you have to go to the "resolution desk", where you will either post in a chat and HOPE you get a timely response--or any response at all, OR you'll have to put your caller on hold and CALL the resolution desk, which frequently has staggering (15 minute+) wait times. You'll be required to call them for something as simple as getting approval for a sale. Rather than posting the account info in chat and waiting for the approval while you do other things in the caller's account to be efficient, you'll be forced to give the account information verbally and wait on the phone (with your caller on hold, who you must check in with every 2 minutes--and res desk will hang up on you if it takes longer than a few seconds to check in with your caller so you'll have to start the approval process all over with a different resolution desk rep who answers the phone) while they verify the info and give the approval. It's important to note that while these changes are being made that make it more difficult to do your job efficiently, absolutely no allowances are being made to account for the additional time these changes require. Rather than have support, you will have team leaders who tell you to "check your resources" rather than help. And they will be condescending about it, even when the info you need is NOT in the resources they're telling you to use. Those resources? They were organized by a toddler, and they get changed frequently with no notice. There is no rhyme or reason to how the information is organized. The resources contain dead links, so even if you manage to find what you think you need, that crucial link isn't going to take you to the information. You're told everything you need to know to do your job is in the resources. (Spoiler alert: that isn't true.) You're also told not to waste time looking for something that isn't there. (Because, "efficiency" metrics.) Sound confusing? Good. You're getting an idea of how you'll go through your day, not knowing if the info you need is there, whether you should look for it, and if it's not, good luck figuring out how to help your caller. Finding some of the less commonly used info that you know is there is fun too, because the index isn't really an index, and searching pulls up a bunch of information that is outside the resources you need for your calls. You will constantly be told you are not meeting metrics. You will be threatened with "corrective actions" which can result in you losing your job because you don't meet metrics. All the while, you will have more responsibility put on you with no additional compensation. You will be forced to handle special clients who have procedures that vary from the general clients. You will be expected to flawlessly shift from a special client to a general client and back again without making a mistake. You will go from handling a few clients when you first start to handling many clients within a few months. But as long as you aren't meeting metrics, you will NOT get any raises. You'll be in a constant state of not knowing if today's the day you'll be fired. Or if today's the day they're going to force another special client with complicated procedures on you. You'll have no say in that--you either do it or you can quit. You'll receive no appreciation for anything. If you haven't uncovered the trend here: you'll constantly be told you're not good enough (and the metrics will be used to support this) so they don't have to give you a raise or promote you, but you'll be good enough to handle the special care of those special clients and additional responsibilities. A big dose of cognitive dissonance that keeps you off balance because you won't know if you're actually doing a good job. More responsibility would indicate you are, but the lack of raises and constantly being told you're not meeting metrics indicates you're not. (Hint: you are, they just want the work you do without having to pay you what you're worth.) This company's culture is "acknowledge the bad, ignore the good". You'll spend your time off decompressing after the abuses you faced during your shift and the overall stress of the job, which cuts into your ability to have a true work life balance. The system is rigged to prevent quality customer service. Reps are forced to be limiting with their information in order to keep calls short to meet metrics. If you're someone who believes in helping people, don't work here. You won't be appreciated, and you'll be punished for the effort you make to provide quality customer service because it takes too long for you to also meet the metrics. You cannot provide excellent customer service, taking care to meet the needs of each caller, AND meet metrics. If you're meeting metrics, you're taking shortcuts on the customer service.

I worked at NetApp for a few years and it was one of the worst work experiences I have ever had. The company's frequent layoffs and workforce reductions made it a place of constant instability and fear, where employees were more concerned about their own job security than working together to achieve shared goals. In such a toxic work environment, employees tended to backstab each other, spreading rumors and sabotaging each other's work to gain an edge in the constant competition for job security. This further eroded morale and made it almost impossible to build a sense of team spirit. The frequent layoffs also led to a lack of continuity and stability, with projects being started and then abruptly abandoned, or teams being restructured and reshuffled every few months. This made it difficult to get any meaningful work done, and employees were constantly worried about whether their jobs would still be there the next day. Overall, NetApp is a company that seems to prioritize short-term profits over the well-being and development of its employees. The constant layoffs and workforce reductions create a culture of fear and mistrust, where employees are more likely to backstab each other than collaborate to achieve shared goals. I would strongly caution anyone considering employment at NetApp to think twice and carefully evaluate the company's track record with layoffs before making a decision
