There's a ton more to say and if Glassdoor allows me to edit this, I'll try to update this review as I reflect more. But generally, I *highly recommend* giving Credit Karma a try if the high-level looks okay to you. I've heard of many horror stories of other large tech companies and FAANG and it always made me relieved to work at Credit Karma. The years I worked there were the best in my career so far and if they were open to remote work, I'd probably still be working for them. Much love to my fellow Karmanauts!

Financial Advisors, avoid. You will not be the Financial Advisor for your assigned branch(s) unless you enjoy working with "Retail" clients. Private Banking and Kalai clients out of your branches are all going to go to existing Financial Advisors, at the discretion of the bankers who are "in charge" of the relationship. They say it's because they want to make sure the client is going to the "best" advisor for them, but that just means it's not going to be you. The only inexpensive option currently available to clients with <$100M are Annuities, and unless you want to write $30-50M Annuities all day, you're going to have a difficult time making your sales goals. Their "rep codes" are in the 50's, and they've got a total of 12 Advisors left. Do the math. There's a very limited amount of support offered, and you'll be given an exhaustive/inexhaustive list of "all" possible scenarios to complete a transaction, and if yours isn't on it, expect weeks to hear back on how to get it completed. Asking for help will get you no where; you'll to often need to wait a week or more to go through a meeting where they'll be answering questions that you didn't ask, and never discussing the ones you did. Be ready to be treated like a second class citizen by people with less education and experience than you, and aren't licensed to do your job. Your leash is very short, and held by people who could never be described as a "Fiduciary." At the end of the day, it's your license you put on the line every time you advise a client, and the bankers are just interested in making their B360 goals. Not set up well for Advisory-based Advisors; limited to "Model Portfolios," and nothing else in your Advisory Accounts. Great place to work if you're more interested in Annuity based business, they're very experienced in that. If you bring new ideas or mention something you've seen as standard practice in your past working experience, be expected to be viewed as selfish, ungrateful, and mocked for it. Asking for something to be "escalated" will just result in asking the same person over and over about it instead of it being moved up the ladder. Highest-valued clients aren't even handled by the Financial Advisor's, they all go to the mysterious "Trust" department. They've got all the options and the kitchen sink, too; discretionary rebalancing, individual securities, Treasuries, and primary operate on an Advisory-based approach rather than Broker/Agent/Advisory. My experience was so bad that I'm going to leave the industry entirely. The job was killing me, and I have a whole host of new health problems directly related to stress that I've got to address now.

I don’t hate anyone enough to encourage them to work here. The only people I can imagine enjoying it here would be faculty, since they typically aren’t involved with the administration of the running of the organization or its schools, departments, and order offices. With tenure and hands-off leadership, I imagine that faculty tend to enjoy a pretty laid back and relaxed life. Everyone else? Not so lucky. In fact, it’s often the polar opposite! Let’s dive in: Chronic turnover: Having to wear 3-5 different hats in addition to your actual job with little to no recognition and minimal pay would drive any sensible person away. Add that to an organizational culture where people can lash out slanderously false accusations at will without any basis, and you’ll understand why this place seems to only be able to hold on to most of their staff for about 2yrs. If you survey the place, you’ll see most offices are composed of people that are pretty new, and this happens all the time. Most people opt to leave the madness and migrate to better opportunities. Chaos and confusion everyday: It’s true. Because people aren’t treated right, they leave. Because they leave, operational KSA’s leave with them. Additionally, most leaders don’t really lead. They just want. But more on that later… Discrimination: It’s insanely obtuse and flagrant. I call it “Minnesota Racism”: it’s where people know how to smile, nod, and carry themselves out in public with decorum — always keeping a front face of appropriateness — while simultaneously communicating that you don’t belong, aren’t respected, and aren’t wanted. Because of their brand new DEI initiative - a direct response to the social upheaval during the lockdown of 2020 that was surfaced by students continuing the university’s administration - it seems they are trying to hire more people of color in leadership spaces. But it feels more like checking a box then actually informing and reshaping they’re perspectives. From my observation, these leaders of color are applauded during their welcome to the university and during Black History month, and then muted and politely tucked into the background. Even as a middle-manager, I have frequently seen and experienced prejudice and discrimination first hand. This has led to and included false allegations, accusations, and hostility. Depending on the department, many coworkers who are also new can be polite and sincerely warm. But in other spaces, not so much. Despite your resume and the reasons they hired you, people here tend not to believe or trust your expertise and can be quick and avid about finding fault with your work. You lose Bernie you can even get started. Poor/Absent Leadership: The leadership seats might be filled but they are not leading. This is why people experience so much burn out: leaders can have a list of things that they want but no solution for how to attain their desired end. Even worse, they are unwilling to be a part of the solution generating process. They have an extremely hands off approach to leadership, which is very problematic because there’s no one to definitively have or make a final say on matters. When they are asked to do so they get frustrated, annoyed, and sometimes even attacking in a counter-punch kind of way (even though no initial punches were made). None of the leaders seem to have a foundational “why” or vision for the units or teams they are in charge of, other than their own grandeur. There’s a lot of technical plays, pomp and circumstance… but no substance or engine of driving forward with clarity, absolution, definition, and purpose. There will always be politics in academia, so that goes without saying. But this institution is something else altogether! It is, in my view, literally directionless. Empty speeches are occasionally made without any follow up or results and it’s acceptable. It’s grandeur merely for grandeur’s sake, and the staff and administrations pay for it. Not only does it make being able to execute the functions of your job severely difficult, if not impossible, but it sets you up for open and chronic “attack.” There’s no foundation here.

My name is Maarva Carassi Andor. I'm honored to stand before you. I'm honored to have been employed, and honored to have been worthy of a Nice Pak bonus even if it was a long time ago. Strange, I... feel as if I can see it. I was six, I think, first time I started working for Nice Pak under the table. Heard the bosses screaming, felt the disappointment in my bones as they crushed my hardened soul for no reason. Holding my sister's hand as we walked all the way from the broken overcrowded parking lot to the main building not fit for minimum wage workers. Where you stand now, I've been more times than I can remember. I always wanted to be lifted. I was always eager, always waiting to be inspired. I remember every time it happened, every time those that were fired or left that dreaded place lifted me... With their truth. And now I'm fired. And I yearn to lift you. Not because I want to shine or even be remembered. It's because I want you to go on. I want the good employees of Nice Pak to continue. In my waning hours, that's what comforts me most. But I fear for you. We've been sleeping. We've had each other, a paycheck, our work, our days. We had each other, and executive management left us alone. We worked insane hours with no direction, and they left us alone. We took our measly salary and ignored them, we kept their engines churning, and the moment the weekend came, we forgot them. Because we had each other. We had a job. But we were sleeping. I've been sleeping. And I've been turning away from the truth I wanted not to face. There is a wound that won't heal at the center of this company. There is a darkness reaching like rust into everything around us. We let it grow, and now it's here. It's here, and it's not visiting anymore. It wants to stay. Nice Pak is a disease that thrives in darkness, it is never more alive than when we sleep. It's easy for the unemployed to tell you to fight, and maybe it's true, maybe fighting is useless. Perhaps it's too late. But I'll tell you this... If I could do it again, I'd wake up early and be fighting these b@$t@rd$ from the start. Fight Nice Pak!

Review from a salaried position, but similar for all positions throughout the company: Just like other reviews, it's hard to find a place to even start to list of the things wrong with this company. My background: This was my first full-time job out of college and was here for a little under 3 years. Position at FIC was Production Engineer. For starters, the pay isn't competitive at all and raises are hard to come by or don't happen at all. 3 years into this job and I was making $15K under the expected for my position/experience, and had observed many other salaried employees quit and find jobs of similar seniority/position immediately making $10K to $20K more than at FIC. FIC has yearly "merit increases" which are a standard percentage increase across the board for all employees, no matter what position or seniority level, and this increase barely covers inflation for each year. The work environment. The work environment is horrendous, both the physical, working environment and the culture of the overall company. While the plant does a lot of welding which is expected to cause fumes and weld splatter/dust, regular cleaning just about never happens. The air in the building is horrible to breathe and work in, and the floors are always slippery of oil that is not cleaned up from the presses. The building houses nearly 300-400 workers per shift, and each building (Carol Stream and Bloomingdale locations) rely on one single janitor to take care of the entire building on their own. From 5am til 5pm, these janitors are working they're butts off and barely making a dent having to clean bathrooms, break rooms, and walkways. Worst of all, if one of the two is off a day or two, the one janitor has to clean both buildings in the same day, leaving both a complete mess because they can't keep up. Why FIC never thought to hire a third party company like many other manufacturing plants is beyond me. The culture. While the name "FIC America" can fool you into thinking its an American company, it is not. FIC is owned by Futaba Japan, run by Japanese, and employing Americans. But, at FIC America, all the executives are Japanese and put themselves above everyone else. They preach that all employees are equal and deserve the same respect, but this is never practiced. If several managers of departments such as QC and Production Engineering agree on a change that needs to occur to better the output of products or better the work environment, one of the Japanese executives can step in and shutdown the entire idea just because they don't agree with it, and those who came up with the idea are forced to just accept it. Lies, deceptions, more. Everyone knows the saying "Practice what you preach", and this can be said everyday at FIC. Every executive and most managers sit behind their computer screens all day, dictating everyone under them. Before every meeting, they all declare their "Safety Commitment" and "Quality Commitment" while none of them actually practice it. Executives will be aware of issues that are occurring on the plant floor and do nothing to solve it, and in turn risk the safety of their employees and potentially sending out bad parts to their customer. The plant manager, at the time, was the only executive ever seen actually assisting on the floor because he's the only executive with true knowledge about the workings that go on outside the salaried office. Working the machine operators like dogs. To tie into these working conditions, hourly employees are expected to work 12 hour days, 5 days a week, and expected to come in every Saturday and sometimes Sundays. Being a salaried employee, I see that these shifts are 12 hours, but I cannot speak for what they're told during their hiring process like other reviews have stated. Either way, the turnover rate is insane here. There is always a shortage of machine operators because they're worked like dogs for a less rate than a starting position at say, Aldi. I've seen and heard, over the 3 years here, more than 20 instances of new hires coming in their first day for orientation, and not coming back after lunch, with many of them going down the street to a different plant with a better starting pay and much better working conditions. These same issues are translated to the office and salaried employees as well. The turnover for salaried employees is horrendous. Between the 2 buildings, there are roughly 80-100 salaried employees, and have seen someone new in nearly every position. During my time working here, I saw 35 salaried people quit, most of which don't even stay for 3 months before realizing they'd be doomed to stay any longer. For the Production Engineering Welding department that I was apart of, things got significantly better when a manager who actually had the knowledge and leadership skills was hired for us. He fought for a better pay for us, dictated the work accordingly, and didn't force us to do jobs that put us in bad or uncomfortable positions. He fought to try and break us away from the normal of the rest of the company, but with too many Japanese executives above him, and a dictator like old man who had gotten into the position above him through seniority, he still has not been able to better the department despite his best efforts. If he's reading this, I want him to know that without him, I would not have stayed as long as I did, and I truly appreciate all his efforts and everything he did for us. If you're still reading this, I know you're actually concerned about working here. If you're engineer and reading this, DO NOT TAKE A POSITION HERE. There is no where for you to move up, you will be stuck at the same level you started at (when I was leaving, my manager at the time was trying to implement engineering levels to help us move up, but at the time of my leaving, still hadn't been implemented). There is very little for you to learn here. The machines run on outdated PLC's that are very rarely used in other industries, and you will fall far behind in knowledge and skill by the time you go to switch jobs. The pay will be nowhere near competitive to other jobs of similar positions for the Chicago area, and you will never get to that point no matter how long you stay here

I started work and was giving a task, on completion told they tabled it. I sat in my role told to review work. I have an expectation as to what that means but was given no feedback as to the company's expectations. I worked for a department where the manager was never in the office in the mornings and left around three to take care of his kid. Day to day from him was minimal so tasks of the audit were left to seniors tasked. The only feedback was what audits were to be planned. First nine months on the job was no feedback. I was told that failure to complete the original assignment would affect performance reviews, so I revisited that work and set up a power point presentation which I was thanked for and told later was tabled again. Two months before the end of the second year there everyone in the department including the other senior that was doing a lot of the work and I was left alone. My performance review was weird, half of the review revolved around the manager asking me why the other individual left. I did not know. The other half was vague references to managerial paperwork functions regarding completing all jobs that was expected. Functions I was never shown how to do. They hired two kids out of college and it was left to me to train them because the company did not send them to any training at all and I was essentially the only one in the office for half the time. I did so. At this time I started to find myself in strange pushback and was being condemned for talking to load once or other petty things without any understanding from them what or when or who was making the complaint. It was coached as random people going in secret. I then stopped talking in the office and started using conference rooms for phone calls mostly out of fear. This was never an issue before but I made corrections. I started also to perform all these other functions which was demanded of me, figuring out the arcane system set up before which I was told to do. Again never asked this of me before and it was not an issue then. Now it was but I agreed without complaint. At these time the manager would make snide gossiping complaints in my presence in front of others undermining me to the people who were supposed to be working for me. About a month and a half after this in February I was on phone with a client and making a request. He blew up about some mundane point and started swearing at me. I was conciliatory and apologizing because as an auditor for 20 years I had seen this tactic by client management before. At this time one of the individuals I had working for me had also had a problem because I asked her to redo a piece of work. I calmly explained what was not completed and why and did so with the intent of teaching her how to do the work. Now, if I approached it in the wrong way that is on me but I was not angry, I was very conciliatory and tried to be helpful. The woman got angry that I would dare to question her and went off in a huff. At that point I get called in and given a four page writeup which was completely biased and untrue stating I was aggressive and nasty (absolutely not one incident mentioned and that work was not done. What was referenced was an audit at the end of the year that was discussed but never assigned. I offered to help work on it and at the time told that no we would table it for lack of manpower because three individuals quit. I should mention at this point I was having trouble with my hearing. In this session I was berated, I was told a laundry list of gossip said about me from well over a year before as the reasoning for this but no specifics given and was shut down with vitriol when I inquired. I should note that I had received two formal year end interviews at this point and this was never mentioned. I was also told "no one liked me". Now I was taken aback from this so I did not push back and it was obvious that nothing I said would matter. In discussion I explained that part of the problem was I was having this issue with my hearing and that might be why I was talking loud on the phone to which I was told "I don't give a damn about your health issues". I don't talk gossip in the office, maybe I should just to be informed so I called this other lady, the senior who quit before. I had normal formal talk with her like how is your wife, how was your weekend kind of stuff but mostly her and I focused on the tasks at hand. I had an open conversation with her and learned a couple of things. People in the office did have an issue with my reviews because essentially was doing them. I am older and an old school auditor so I was brought up in the day where your work was redlined to the hilt in order to cover any error because end of the day the reviewer we all feared the most was the lawyer for opposing counsel if there was ever a legal dispute so it had to be perfect. This sticked with me. She did tell me though that she appreciated my doing this because up until that point the work was a rubberstamp by this other guy. She had never seen that before. She explained she felt she was doing most of the work and not getting the promotion she was being promised. At this point recruiters were calling me and I stopped blowing them off and decided to get another job. I was told to only supervise work at this point by this manager as well instructed not to do work. Odd, we only had three people other than him . He also assigned audits to me and audits to him but it was the two new hires that would perform all audits to learn. His audits were getting completed first and when mine fell short I took up the slack but I only took work of this young girl he seemed to be protecting and spending a lot of time in meetings alone with when he was there. It got weirder and more awkward for me in the office. When I finally accepted the job I had a month's notice. I did not tell management right away. I waited till Wednesday the second week before and that due to the fact this manager was never in the office and I had to email my resignation anyways. They made a big show of giving me a full week off with pay and sent me to a exit interview but I was told by online videos no matter what never tell them anything negative. I expect nothing of this and truth be told this is some time back now. I am just placing this here mostly just to get it off my chest because I never had any opportunity to say anything about it. It was one of those situations where I was just glad to be out of there. I accept there could be things I did that attributed to this but I cannot truthfully say to you what that was as the people involved in this were extremely fake!

I have devoted considerable thought to the recent all-staff meeting and the remarks made by our CEO regarding the value we purportedly bring to the organization. While I appreciate hearing such affirmations from our C-Suite executives, I am hesitant to accept their sincerity. My reservations stem from the observation that our leadership, exemplified by individuals such as Katie Bynum, tends to disregard subordinates who do not occupy high-ranking positions. Despite having attempted to exchange pleasantries with her on several occasions, I received no acknowledgement from Ms. Bynum. Unfortunately, this behavior is not limited to her, as the host of the all-staff meetings also overlooks less influential members of the team. It was rather disheartening to note that Sarah Hirshland acknowledged this individual and signaled that she truly doesn't know how these people can be to others. C-Suite members have very different perspectives of the people they work with and unfortunately, those who get the closest to them tend to be putting on airs the most. Furthermore, our organizational culture appears to promote the idea that employees are not crucial to the company's success. For instance, the decision to cut out people from games and award the remaining roles to tenured staff members who have a track record of being difficult to work with in the organization and their preferred colleagues is not conducive to fostering a sense of value among all employees. Additionally, when Kate Hartman responds to feedback with insincere explanations, it creates a lack of trust and further undermines the perception of employees' worth. Finally, it is my belief that leadership is currently out of touch with the needs and concerns of their own teams, and this has resulted in employees being treated poorly on a day-to-day basis. It is imperative that we shift our focus to reward merit and to cultivate a work environment that combats hostility and aligns with our core values. Mere affirmations of our worth are insufficient, and I implore Sarah to take concrete steps to identify and eliminate toxic elements within our organization. At the end of the day we're all here for the athletes but the organization's greatest asset is its staff but that staff is hardened and calloused. At our next big meeting, I want to hear plans to make working here better for everyone and I want to hear about how promotions for those who have deserve them are on the horizon. If that isn't a plan, these things need to be on a very very short roadmap.

I want to remind everyone to not fill out their culture pulse survey. The best strategy for this organization has always been to keep your head low and not try to get yourself into any situations. People and culture are not your friends, things WILL get worse if you talk to them.. The culture pulse is not as confidential as you might think and I promise you, people and culture will ostracize you or worse if you are negative in it.. If you have positive things to say, go for it.. However, if you have any grievances, I encourage you to post a review here instead. Games surveys are the same.. never be honest on these surveys.

Ok, the review titled "Wish people would stop complaining!" was so bad that I had post my own review despite not wanting to ever do this. It perfectly exemplifies the hostility and invalidating of actual issues that are present in this organization. Oh and no, I am not part of a small group of people posting negative reviews. This is a bad take based on nothing concrete or factual. I'm going to break down why their review was bad and give you a taste of what is going on here: Limited Perspective: The individual claiming that disgruntled coworkers should appreciate their current workplace may have a limited perspective since they have only been with the organization for a year. It's important to consider that different people have different experiences and perspectives based on their roles, departments, and tenure. The fact that one person has had a positive experience does not invalidate the negative experiences of others. Further, it doesn't mean there isn't a larger grouping of people with opposite perspectives just because they have positive experiences. Validity of Glassdoor Reviews: While it's true that some people may use anonymous platforms like Glassdoor to vent their frustrations rather than addressing them directly, it does not necessarily mean that all the negative reviews are baseless or exaggerated. It's important to acknowledge that Glassdoor can provide valuable insights into the work culture and experiences within an organization. Dismissing all the negative reviews as the work of a small group of complainers may be oversimplifying the situation. We have had issues in the past with our internal P&C department becoming frenzied when our surveys were submitted with negative results. I have personally had leadership mention exactly what I have said on my surveys verbatim, angry that I had these comments. Also, it's simple Psychology...People keep talking about Glassdoor reviews like a new Taylor Swift single just dropped so of course they're going to want to be on a platform that is clearly being paid attention to. Subjectivity of "Good" Work Conditions: The individual emphasizes the positive aspects of their current workplace, such as flexible work arrangements, free swag, empowerment-focused meetings, and time off. However, it's important to recognize that what one person perceives as "good" work conditions may not be the same for everyone. Different individuals have different priorities, expectations, and needs. Some employees may value other factors such as career growth opportunities, work-life balance, or a supportive team environment more than the perks mentioned. Also, just because other organizations are worse, doesn't automatically mean this organization is good...This is a false equivalency. Confirmation Bias: The individual's positive perception of their workplace might be influenced by confirmation bias, which refers to the tendency to seek out information that confirms one's preexisting beliefs or opinions. By focusing only on the positive aspects and dismissing the negative feedback, the individual may be overlooking potential areas for improvement or failing to empathize with the challenges faced by their coworkers. This individual could also be in a position where they don't have to deal directly with the culture like some people do or maybe they have a rank that motivates people to be more respectful to them. Lack of Long-Term Perspective: The individual mentions the benefits and positive experiences they have had within their first year. However, it's important to consider the long-term sustainability of these positive aspects. Workplaces can change over time, and what seems good initially may not be sustainable in the long run. It's essential to consider how the organization's policies, practices, and culture may evolve over time and whether the current positive experiences will persist. Individual Experiences vs. Systemic Issues: While the individual may have had positive experiences personally, it's crucial to distinguish between individual experiences and systemic issues within an organization. Just because some individuals have positive experiences does not negate the possibility that there may be systemic problems or areas for improvement that affect a larger group of employees. It's important to consider the overall work environment and the experiences of a diverse range of employees before making a judgment on the validity of the negative reviews. In summary: Telling people to "move on" and going on to invalidate a group of people for having negative feelings and perspectives is part of the toxic culture of this organization and this individual exemplified it perfectly. Also, FYI, I know a group of the people that posted reviews here; Many are no longer with the organization but it's a much bigger group than you are insinuating. A little extra: Paris planning is underway and people are learning the reality of their games statuses. What Kate Hartman has been saying is only half the truth; Many newbies are going to the games because much of the staff that has been here longer had their games opportunities revoked for one reason or another, usually to do with leadership at the games. Process behind the picking process has needed to change for **years** and we have changed quite a bit, but I don't think that sweeping this under the rug is the best course of action [the send the newbies plan]. Negative reviews are going to come in droves because people are rightfully unhappy and that's ok. Let's do something about this instead of disregarding it like the individual I referenced in the bulk of my review.

The average employee is grossly underpaid for the work they do which is why the turnover is so high. Although, their internal numbers will never accurately reflect that because they'll classify someone's leaving reason due to salary as "Mutual Agreement" or "Other Opportunity" instead so their QBR numbers look better. It seemingly takes an act of God for any title corrections, pay increases, or other administrative action to be taken. But if a high enough level employee threatens to quit they'll magically come up with the money to bump their salary and change their title. While they can't do more than 3% salary increases (if you're a top performer), they can find the funds to do extravagant parties (only in their Hoboken or Israel locations, of course), send gifts to employees around the world, and do contests with wild prizes like sending entire families to Disney for a week. Their culture is basically boiled down to "do more with less" and "do what I ask, and don't ask questions about it". Communication is awful across the board. DE&I is a joke. Their only focus is on improving numbers related to women, and even that feels like a marketing ploy to fill in their LinkedIn postings. In my opinion, this is largely affected by having Israel native leaders who are not as familiar with the history and culture in the USA and who refuse to take feedback from those who ARE familiar. Attempting to have a global approach in this area is a huge miss. Senior Management is completely out of touch from their employees. Work life balance is all over the place. Many employees put in well above 40 hours a week on a regular basis, but with everyone being salaried they don't have to pay overtime. And after they spent 3 years with everyone working from home (quite successfully), they are demanding employees come back to the office 3 days a week for a hybrid schedule. Where this REALLY doesn't make sense, is that most teams have employees all over the country or even the globe. They'll never be in the same office with each other and will do video calls, so what's the point?

Many other little nit pick things, but this is the best, concise gripe list I can come up with.

*****Intel has a strong work culture of being paranoid***** that consistently works against it. Intel HR policies and management promotes this culture of paranoia in every employee of Intel. There is too much overthinking on plans that never happen to the point where questioning a project seems irrelevant. The attitude towards customers and competitors is often arrogant. Pre-pandemic, the culture remained reliant on cube culture and no one dared to pack up to leave before 5pm. Post pandemic the cube culture has dissipated BUT management is increasingly trying to get employees back in office by passive aggressive actions such as holding on-site only meetings. There's very little comradery within departments, and this has a disheartening effect on employees over time. Work culture is confrontational and harsh. Lots of pressure on engineers to solve problems with very little training. The work pace is fast and high stress. It's mostly an ethnocentric workforce which is great for diversity but ultimately hurts culture through the social cliques it forms and creates massive divides within groups. You are pitted against your team members as there is a culture of usurping your colleagues' work - expectation of attending meetings at ridiculous hours - some of the worst managers I ever had. Do better Intel.

The reason the company is struggling is because they have strapped themselves down with bloated systems that slow everything down. Nothing can get done without 6 layers of red tape and process. You'll probably have to have lots of overseas meetings, there is not consideration for time zones

On top of this, strategy around projects is non-existent, never proactive, always reactive. It will take weeks to get anything moving, and when it does the lifers in-charge will act as if they've never heard of the project or budget and prompts weeks long re-review. If you are lucky enough to start a project you then get to go through the 'personal agenda' phase. All the lifers want to push their wants onto the project and will bring it to a standstill with them trying to get their way.

Culture of "need to know" is confusing to people that function best when they understand how everything works. If you can be told to do a thing and repeat it and you aren't compelled to understand things beyond the scope of your position, this is fine, you'll love it. Feed your family and you are good to go. But if you are inquisitive, this job will be tough. Without the bachelors (if you don't have), they won't pay you much attention. You won't get training beyond what they want you to do and it will really confuse you when you interact with other departments. It is a very chaotic and siloed organization. The actual work onboarding was very poor. The org seems designed to be as unwelcoming to new hires as possible. Many teams have secret code names that give no indication of what they're responsible for, and the team names change regularly. The majority of the people I needed to collaborate with had generic titles of Product Manager or Software Development Engineer in the employee directory so it was impossible to figure out who was responsible for what product area. The wikis are hopelessly messy to navigate and contain a ridiculous amount of outdated information that is never removed. I was left to navigate all of that without much support. The culture is not friendly. Few people were outright UNfriendly, although there were a handful who were condescending and hostile on a regular basis. But I was mostly shocked at how few people seemed to enjoy their work. I'm used to laughing, joking around, and/or enjoying the company of my coworkers. I found Audible to be a cold and inhospitable place. There were a few gems who were genuinely sweet and helpful people, but on the whole it's a culture of "I'm not responsible for that, good luck figuring it out on your own, here's a link to a wiki with 500 pages to read through." One of the mantras is "move fast to make it real." There are of course benefits to trying new things and failing (and learning) fast. But too often "moving fast" at Audible means "doing absolutely zero due diligence and plowing forward with a half-baked plan that will ultimately waste time and effort." There are many Amazon-proprietary tools and frameworks that you have to learn. That's fine if you plan on a long tenure at Audible or Amazon. But if not, you will spend a lot of energy learning what will ultimately become non-transferrable job skills.

companies.name: Code Ninja
allPros: There was a very good culture here.

I have been working at Code Ninja for less than a year, but I confidently can say that the company is fantastic. Here are some of the reasons why I love working here: (a) People. The people are wonderful, everyone is very helpful and friendly so you wouldn't get intimidated to ask questions even as a new hire. The team is diverse and talented, and there is a lot of collaboration and support among colleagues. The managers are also supportive and approachable, and they give clear guidance and feedback. (b) Culture. The company fosters a culture of realtime feedback which is very important to create an environment that is safe and always striving for excellence. The culture is just like any other startup, where processes are scrappy and agile. This means that you have a lot of autonomy and ownership over your work, and you can see the impact of your decisions quickly. There are, as in any other organization, some challenges with scrappy processes such as lack of documentation or standardization, but for me, it works well because it allows faster turnaround time and removes unnecessary bureaucracy. (c) Opportunity. Code Ninja gives us the opportunity to have exposure with leaders, even directly to the CEO and top officers of business partners. This means that you can learn from the best and also have a voice in shaping the direction of the company. The company also encourages learning and development, and provides resources and support for personal and professional growth. (d) Work-life balance. The work time of 7am to 4pm works perfectly for me because I still have at least 2 hours remaining every day with daylight which I can use to work on other stuff; this is something I couldn't have in a regular 9 to 6 schedule. I also love that our setup is mainly work-from-home, with once a month face-to-face meeting in a coworking space. This gives me flexibility and convenience, and also saves me time and money from commuting. The company also respects our personal time and does not expect us to work overtime or on weekends unless absolutely necessary. (e) HR. HR is always ready to listen, and while there may be minor disagreements over policies sometimes, just like in any other organization, it gets resolved through open communication.
They are concerned about employee's growth in their respective fields. The work environment and culture fosters a safe space for everyone.

Wow, there is so much. I worked my way up from a collector to a collections manager to an accounting supervisor for TAFS in a short 3 years. So believe if anyone has a valid and honest perspective I do. I took over as the Accounting Supervisor due to the previous one quitting for being over worked and understaffed. I walked into a Department exhausted, unmotivated and most of the Team quit within months due to this. We never stopped working that hour of OT. I often worked over 120 hours for the sake of my Team to be able to leave at 5pm (1 hour AFTER they were supposed to get off) and us still be current on cash. I built up a new and amazing Team over the next year and we withstood every storm upper management threw at us. New Cash Posting System which was a huge mistake (and believe upper management knows this), they were slow to react to resolve the issues even though I let management know on a daily and weekly basis of how the team was doing. new process changes at the same time within different areas of the Team with little to no training or support. But best believe we adapted and made it work, because of me and my Team. Not the Company. Me so worn thin my team hindered growth and opportunity they deserved. I constantly told them the numbers may look good but it’s not just about the numbers. You provide feedback and great communication and visibility of issues that get ignored. Instead of listening and understanding they brushed it off with an “I get it” , “I am drowning too” or even more entertaining the Controller tries to have a talk with you and instead of wanting to talk it’s a premeditated conversation she planned in her head with her favorite phrase being “bottom line is” but then when you make a valid point it flips to we are working on it, just communicate with us, like I haven’t been?!? They are reactive instead of proactive. They outsource team members through an out of the Country Company and they want the stateside staff to work harder and longer than the remote team. Allowing the remote team to make mistake after mistake for months and months but when it’s talked about I end up being the one in the wrong? The same remote team I fought to get a raise, supplies and things to be successful, I am all the sudden rude to because I expect progress, self accountability and reliability. I had the CFO, Controller and my Manager on an email saying they were my biggest fan just 2 weeks ago. I have given everything to that Team and I built one heck of a Team and because I questioned the nonsense and raised a blind eye to what was dragging TAFS down they made up some crap to write me up and then two days later fired me!!! Hahaha, like you gonna write me up for lies even though I have never been in trouble and then two days later I am fired? Fired because I was rude to my team in tone and made them unmotivated. The one thing I do walk away with is almost everyone on my Team reaching out to me telling me how amazing I was as their Boss. The same Team I was supposedly so bad to had nothing but love and support and I have the screenshots and messages to prove it. Gotta love TEAMS. You may have fired me for lies, but I will rest well knowing I did a great job for that Company and I impacted the people I worked with in a positive and meaningful way that they will carry forever. You were wrong and you know it and I hope you do right by my Team cause I know they will still be doing a great job for you, because I trained them. I supported them. I had their backs and I made them best they could be. I told you many many times the numbers might look good but it could be so much better. Look where my passion got me. What because I spoke up and stopped working all that OT, now all the sudden I am not good enough for your Company. They don’t want better. They want those numbers to look good. Too bad they are cleaning up so many messes from others that “played the games” and smiled their way to the top. Wish I could send the screenshots! But one messaged copied below from one of my staff to prove this isn’t some angry review. This is truth. And I have so much more proof. “Hi Shantel, I hope you don't mind me messaging you, but I couldn't just not say something to you. I and all of the other cash apps here will miss you dearly. I will never forget how you would stick up and defend me when I was training and not getting as many other things cleared. It's not just that you were a great manager, it's that you ARE a great manager, and they lost out on one of their most valuable workers in the company period. You made working here feel passionate, and you deserve so much more than what happened. Things won't feel the same without you, but I will do whatever I can to make sure that passion stays alive here. Whether gone or not, you will always have left your working ethic and spirit in me and the team. I wish you all the best, Shantell. Thank you for everything.”

allCons: There are always going to be growing pains in leadership transitions. There will be a period of getting to know others and how they work and thrive in the workplace and the best way to support a wide variety of professionals. The return to office announcement could have been handled very differently, however leadership has also gone to great lengths to help make that transition back to office easier. I am a firm believer in time will tell how this change will overall impact the company, but I am going into all this starting at curious and doing what I can in my role to make that transition, both the RTO and the leadership changes, as easy as I can for those I come in contact with on a daily basis. This company will constantly boast about great work life balance, interesting and empowering work, and career advancement but when you start working, they'll constantly warn you to not take PTO, work extra hours to improve the company's utilization rate, and cast you to projects that aren't even for the role you were hired on as.

I have over 20 years of software development experience, and I have worked at many different companies on many projects. And I will say without hesitation that the working environment at the Church is the best anywhere I have been as a software engineer. We rarely work more than a 40-hour work week (occasional, but rare emergencies might be the exception). The management stresses it - they truly want us to work an eight-hour day and then go home to be with our families. It's wonderful. Yes, bureaucracy, politics, etc. exist at the Church like anywhere else. But it is far less than most other places in my opinion. Almost everyone is simply trying to do the right thing most of the time while putting team needs and the purpose of the Church ahead of personal egos, self-centered views, etc. Agile and software development processes, while not perfect (it never is), and it varies from project to project, are for the most part what they should be: team-focused (without ignoring individual needs/wants), light-weight, flexible, and the teams are allowed to be self-organizing - more so than anywhere else I have worked. The net result is a much more productive work environment. I can get double the amount of work done in a 40-hour week at the Church than I could somewhere else in a 60-hour week. Everywhere else I have worked in Corporate America stifles productivity/innovation with their never-ending focus on heavy-weight Agile nonsense (SAFe anyone?) and Agile dogma. This is nothing more than inefficient waterfall processes that are wrapped in an Agile label so that the executives feel good about "doing Agile". Not at the Church - these things are done the way they were intended to be (with minimal exceptions here and there.) Training is good, as long as there is budget for it, which there usually is. The technology stack is good - not always "bleeding edge", but they try to keep up for the most part. It is interesting to work on projects that give me a greater understanding of the Church's purpose and inner, organizational way of doing things. Working on projects that I feel a strong sense of purpose enhances the productivity, and enjoyment of work. Working remotely is the preferred way of working for IT professionals at the Church - although some people work in the office, most work from home. Video chatting/working with other team members is efficient and works well. Most teams have occasional team activities and occasional in-office team meetings to ensure that team members see each other face-to-face on occasion. The benefits are good. Health insurance (DMBA) has many options with low monthly premiums and no deductibles for in-network healthcare. (One negative side effect of this is the lack of health savings accounts - low deductible plans are not available for this. There are the FSA health savings spending accounts available, however.) Low co-pays also. Dental insurance is good also. Vacation/sick leave are excellent. I never have a problem requesting vacation time. Retirement benefits are very good. They have a 4-percent 401K match and an 8-percent additional that you are just gifted. Not much beats that.

I mean the consistent lack of consideration and respect that is afforded to the "inferior proletariat" regardless of their work ethic, experience or intelligence. There are a handful of people in managerial positions that are entirely unqualified and lack the obligatory professionalism that should be illustrative of the Firstenergy Code of Conduct. We as skilled and unskilled laborers are irrevocably held to those standards when management can behave disgracefully and without regard to the well being of their subordinates let alone exhibit some moral rectitude and kindness when speaking with their employees. Unfortunately, that is not the case: my personal experience has been with a supervisor who DEMANDS respect rather than earn it. As an employee, I show respect as a professional courtesy but when that is not reciprocated and I'm treated like a pawn in their own personal struggle for power and I'm expected to stroke their ego while being berated, yelled at, swore at and denigrated purposefully to others, it's a little much to handle. This is a culture where people are so very used to getting away with whatever they wanted regardless of the callousness or immorality of their words and actions. Job security: While a large portion of our competition engages in the hire/fire cycle, ADI works to maintain our talent pool. While no job is ever invulnerable, I feel much more confident in my job stability here than I would with most other semiconductor industry employers. Lateral movement: I've heard from old college friends how they eventually felt pigeon-holed into smaller and smaller niches as they developed more focused expertise. At ADI I'm encouraged broaden my expertise and to shift into dissimilar roles over time. This is expected to keep employees interested and engaged, and in my opinion it works very well. Culture: There is an extremely strong culture of collaboration here. Walk around the office, chat up any random engineer, and learn what they are working on - this is deeply encouraged (and a primary driver for trying to get folks back into the office post covid). In this process I've engaged with dozens of engineers, eventually collaborating with most of them on secondary projects (work other than the primary focus of our roles). A primary expectation of senior staff is that they help accelerate development of younger engineers, e.g. through mentoring programs or just plain old conversation.

In addition to this the center has pretty much eliminated the technical promotion pathway in favor of saving the available GS14 and 15 levels for our over abundance of management roles. Labs are generally empty as we don't hire anyone capable of doing hands on work anymore in favor of contract managers and oversight roles. Most of the strong technical talent is being pillaged by the growing space industry across the US and especially in the local Huntsville area. Also there's a ton of infighting and territorialism at every level: center level, lab level, division level, and team level. Honestly I'm surprised anything was ever accomplished by all the arguing and stovepiping on who is "allowed" to do what.

I work in a research staff position that works closely with colleagues in identical jobs in Wash U Neurology and Psychiatry. It's an open secret among staff and among faculty in Radiology, Neurology, and Psychiatry who are writing grants that Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology/MIR pays less than comparable staff positions in other departments. In many cases I've seen, a LOT less. I've talked with multiple junior faculty members who are making anywhere from $10-30k less than people at their same levels in Psychiatry and Neurology. These are high-performing new faculty members in Radiology, in many cases POC and/or women, who are collaborating closely with, performing identically to or better than, and in a lot of cases winning actual identical grants to their colleagues in Neurology and Psychiatry. These people are bringing in a TON of grant money for MIR and MIR refuses to pay them what other departments say they're worth. It's wild. In my own case and in the case of other staff colleagues at my level, research staff in Radiology are making $10-20k less than those with identical duties in Psychiatry and Neurology. In a few instances I've helped to train people in collaborator groups in roles just like mine who are making more than me as a baseline. It's frustrating. I'm aware of a Radiology colleague who was given a promotion and received new promotion-based duties 6 months before their salary was actually increased - and their request for back pay was denied. Trying to advocate for yourself or your team to MIR leadership sends you through a labyrinth of impossible challenges to justify exactly what the cause for change is ("pay equity with people who do the same thing I do" is not a good enough response for them) so ultimately nothing changes. Turnover at MIR is fairly constant for reasons like this, which means we are constantly training new people in our own department and spinning our wheels. MIR leadership is entirely uninterested in working for pay equity at any level and shuts it down right away if you broach the topic- they very much want to hide this information, but as I mentioned it's pretty common knowledge among staff and new faculty in various departments that they pay a lot less and are generally less flexible on things like promotions and remote work arrangements (MIR won't budge on this even if you are dealing with health issues or caregiving duties - I know someone great who is going to have to leave their MIR job over this, it's heartbreaking and I dearly hope they can transfer to Neurology). There's an upcoming window where they might make changes when a new chair of Radiology is chosen, but from my discussions with faculty the general feeling is that it's unlikely that any material changes will happen, and if so it would be incremental pay adjustments for faculty with no updates at the staff level. We'd all be very surprised if MIR goes for actual pay equity with other departments for either faculty or staff. If you are looking for a research staff job at Wash U and you have skills and experience to offer, try to avoid Radiology if you can. Turnover is fairly constant and they have repeatedly demonstrated aren't interested in making any changes, pay-based or otherwise, to encourage faculty/staff retention. If you are trying to get your foot in the door, it's fine, that's what a lot of us are doing here, just make sure you stay aware of your worth while you are here and leave when you have the experience to get a better deal.

When I left, most cutline crew members and especially supervisors were overworked. Supervisors spent less time overseeing their crew and spent the majority of their shift rotating Destacker operators and Saw Tenders while overseeing the new automated scanners through all breaks and lunches and even Finger joints. Then they had to squeeze time for their own breaks and lunches (if they took them) in before they start rotating through the next break or lunch period while having to mathematically update production reports numerous times in a day. They didn't have enough time to monitor job performance of less experienced crew members on Split and Swing shifts. After I began 5th year (Going into late 2004 and into 2006) in the department I worked in, crew members rotated through all breaks and lunches and belts were getting clogged after the first break and the rest of the shift. We were shorthanded and overwhelmed as I could see and experienced that tensions to elevate at a very high level. After deciding I couldn't go on like this, in the Fall of 2005 I made an investment into a small business and scheduled to leave out of state in April 2006, Sadly, I tore a left rotator cuff a few weeks later 2005 from repetitive overuse. A manager diagnosed my tear as a "left arm strain" but didn't write down that I was overwhelmed from repetitive use, proclaiming "we don't want to be negative". The managers all understood the machine, I operated could shut all 3 cutlines if I didn't keep up. But I wasn't given the needed help to rotate through lunch. So I was skipped a lot of breaks and lunches to avoid my line from shutting down all the Cutlines, whether banding up 7 or 8 units or clearing the belts enough so the cutline belts could continue to flow. This occurred on a daily basis. (I didn't have the help to stop and band, so I did it during my breaks and lunches) After my injury, I was put on lighter duty and after 2 weeks I was sent to the company Doctor who without thoroughly examing my shoulder, determined that I had "left arm strain" and ordered some PT during my off time. I was still going to work and later put on a machine that still required proper use of both my arms (but my left shoulder wasn't getting any better) and later I broke my right knuckle after which I was on a cutback belt using my bad arm/shoulder. After about a couple of weeks the PT told me (and documented) there is something wrong with my shoulder and to call a lawyer. (Which I didn't do at first) The company Doctor still wasn't going to issue an MRI, until I told him I was going to my Primary Doctor when he became disgruntled and issued the order. About 3 months, my shoulder injury was finally diagnosed as a torn rotator cuff. I tried to get my medical records, but he refused and later left town permanently. Because I was obligated to leave by April of 2006, I was on my own. When I pursued a settlement, California comp. law payout was a maximum of $10K for a rotator tear and no money for a broken right knuckle. (The knuckle is sore to this day) SPI wasn't willing to settle, which forced me to get a lawyer. I found this frustrating because as a whole, SPI were really an awesome Company. Keep in mind that I wanted to work at SPI for 30 years before the madness began in late 2004. When I got injured, my overtime disappeared, and I couldn't make my house payment, so I cashed out my pension until it ran out and ended up losing my home anyway, because I wasn't fully functional to work my new business. The plant operates smoothly fully staffed, but with 500 crew members it was nearly impossible to be fully staffed, with at least some employees calling in sick (and some on vacation) so it wasn't unusual for the plant to operate shorthanded, unless they called in an employee or two to partially pick up some of the slack. (Of vacationers) My advice is work hard while trying to discover your own physical limitations as you will be pushed to your limits. Find a "bid" that you can do in the long term in an area of the plant that runs relatively smooth and with a supervisor that is present. In my case, I had a supervisor occasionally check on orders, but when they began rotating other machine operators (except me) supervisors stopped to check performance and orders. How is a company going to know how far they can push you, unless you either get hurt while skipping breaks and lunches just to keep up or simply let my belt fill up and shut down all the production on the cutline? You have a choice, get chewed out or get hurt. I unconsciously chose to get hurt. (My 5-11 frame's healthy weight is 170lbs and I was a stick at 152lbs, when I left and wasn't properly compensated for my injury causing me to lose my home)

A lot of the reviews here have some very different takes about this company, but I'm just going to speak to my own experiences working here. I've been in the tech industry for several years and worked at a few different places including other start-ups and this is unquestionably the best place I have ever worked. That's not to say it's literally perfect or that there isn't room for improvement, but Amperity is far better than the vast majority of places to work in tech. They pay competitive salaries for the roles (at least in engineering). They have great benefits, especially if you live near an office, but even if you don't there's a huge amount of flexible vacation time, and you're strongly encouraged to use it, a company-wide three-day weekend at least once a month, the standard array of health benefits, parental leave, etc. As a person belonging to multiple marginalized groups, I think their DEI efforts could be improved, but again, they're doing a much better job than most of the industry, and most importantly, management is very much open to feedback on how to improve. I've felt very safe and respected the entire time I've been here, which honestly should be the bare minimum in the workplace, but unfortunately I can't say the same about a lot of other workplaces. My overall take: Honestly, I love this company, I care about its future, I actually believe in the product we're making (which really is just a bonus), and I highly recommend it. If my experiences start to change the longer I'm here, or management or direction of the company change, I'll be back to update this review, but until then
- Kind, intelligent peers - Flexible work from home options - Strong software with long-term potential to become a market leader
allCons: The space we operate in is changing quickly and some parts of the company are more ahead than others.

Working in the software engineering/technology organization at Amperity can present several challenges. Decision-making processes lack transparency, and it can be challenging to have a voice if you did not join during the company's early years. The team prides itself on its complex software architecture, but it fails to recognize that the same complexity is hindering its growth potential. Additionally, there is a lack of documentation, and early employees, who possess extensive knowledge and experience, often dominate conversations. Operational incidents are often unintentionally bottlenecked by these same employees. The leadership also presents some obstacles, with a high turnover rate at the C-level and no pay transparency. Furthermore, career paths are not clearly defined by division, although they're a bit clearer within the technology team. I don't know what the plan is for the company. Nothing is really ever shared broadly. Amperity's processes and ways of working may have worked when it was smaller, but they no longer support sustainable growth. Early employees appear to cling to old ways of working and outdated opinions and often overlook the hindrances they pose. They also recently laid off junior engineers due to a lack of capacity to ramp them up, which is not a wise investment in the company's future.

The company seems not to have a sense of move fast and break things. The general feel I got was everyone wants to only keep the lights on without introducing too much innovation/ new products. The company mindest is keep things working while trying to sell the same product to more clients. The teams are usually so small that there are very few leadership and growth opportunities (unless you are one of the old gurus who has been there since early on and have a ton of legacy knowledge)

- Lot more talk than action - Surprisingly top down for a start up - Difficult time cutting through noise to grow - Compensation can be higher - Most likely will get hired into a level lower than you are at already

- product is visibly losing it's market share to other competitors and still struggles to find P/M fit. No innovation at this point - the product is basically just playing catch up. Product team clearly struggling to make the right decisions on what to build and focus on next. Losing existing customers and struggling to find more while sales teams try to shove the same product down everyone's throats and try to convince them to buy Amperity. The company is really blind to it's flaws and keeps pushing a false narrative to it's own employees that it's the best. No real path to IPO, will probably be acquired - Management is incredibly toxic with unreasonable expectations to deliver with little to no guidance while not even having their own stuff together. They're always pulling the "well it's a startup" card even though they've been around for 7 years with a Series D valuation as justification as to why you're failing, or are not a good fit, and it'll never be anyone else's fault except yours. Your manager will drag you down with them, and it will ultimately be you who's affected. - If there's anything wrong with your performance, management will not say anything until you're basically pushed out the door, given no real chance for improvement. They struggle with having active conversations on expectations and performance, and choose to just get rid of someone instead of working on improvement together. The "we're a family" values are pretty much just for show when it actually gets ugly. - Leadership doesn't even reach out to you at all anymore, and the company is genuinely losing the endearments of a startup and replacing it with the worst parts of bureaucracy. - there's definitely favoritism towards certain employees who can never do wrong, and the nepotism is strong.

The leadership team at Amperity has two skills: 1 - Optics. Making things look a certain way regardless of reality 2 - Firing people with a spine who won't be a sycophant Working at Amperity is like playing a game of Russian roulette. One day you're the best thing that ever happened to the company and the next you're being shown the door because you knowingly or unknowingly became a thorn in the wrong person's side. You never know who is next. It's fear based management. One example. Amperity is the least inclusive company I've ever worked for. Yet they are masters at making it look like DEI is a priority. Amperity's product decisions are made in the worst echo chamber I've ever witnessed in my many years of working in tech. Only members of the inner circle get to influence product decisions. Anyone who has the spine to point that out and/or present any data that contradicts the opinion of someone in the inner circle can expect to immediately be shown the door. That bias is very evident in the product itself. I've witnessed several people get fired and none of them were cis hetero-normal white men. not.a.single.one.

There's a high barrier of entry to work here, especially in engineering. It was one of the harder interviews I've had, and the work here is definitely not easy. But that's just the space we're in, and there's no expectation ever to work overtime or weekends--we're just building a complex piece of software. It's still a startup-like company. Building the airplane in the air, etc. Things change quickly, there are not years and years of documentation and processes in place yet, so you have to be prepared for less stability. Not necessarily a con, but important to consider if you're coming here.

- Understaffed technical teams & surprise layoffs - The company prides itself on having a startup culture, even though it’s 7 years old. companies.name: Wacker Neuson
allPros: Pros I have been working as a design engineer at Wacker Neuson 1-2 years, and I would like to share my experiences and thoughts about the company on Glassdoor. Wacker Neuson is a global manufacturer of construction equipment and machinery, and it has established itself as a leader in the industry. Here's my review based on various aspects of the company: 1. Work Environment: The work environment at Wacker Neuson is highly professional and stimulating. The company encourages collaboration, innovation, and creativity among its employees. The design engineering team works on exciting projects and is provided with the necessary resources and tools to excel in their work. The management is supportive and open to suggestions and feedback. There is a surplus of resources on the team. Mark Lang and Don Knutson have extensive knowledge. Both are willing to help. 2. Compensation and Benefits: After a raise and the annual bonus, I would consider the compensation to be average. However, the less tangible benefits are impressive. Vacation starts at 3 weeks paid for salary employees. Additionally, the company provides various employee perks, such as health insurance, retirement plans, and employee assistance programs. 401k vesting is not tiered, though. 3. Career Growth and Development: I was able to learn a lot at my position. However, my understanding is there are few formal opportunities such as GD&T classes or other certifications. The company provides ample opportunities for learning and advancement. Additionally, internal mobility and promotional opportunities are available for those who demonstrate exceptional performance over extended periods of time. 4. Work-Life Balance: Maintaining a healthy work-life balance is a priority at Wacker Neuson. The company excels in this area. Company has flex hours with core hours of 9-3. Optional “Summer hours" means you can take off Friday after noon, assuming you reach your hours for the week and have completed your workload. The company understands the importance of personal well-being and encourages employees to manage their time effectively. There can be occasional project deadlines and workload spikes. Salary usually means you work 40 hours per week, but you are expected to go over 40 hours per week at times. 5. Company Culture: The company culture at Wacker Neuson is collaborative, inclusive, and diverse. Employees come from different backgrounds and bring unique perspectives to the table. The company fosters a culture of respect, teamwork, and integrity. Regular team-building activities and social events contribute to a positive work atmosphere. 6. Innovation and Technology: As a design engineer, I appreciate Wacker Neuson's commitment to innovation and technological advancement. The company provides engineers with the tools and resources needed to stay at the forefront of the industry. This enables us to work on challenging projects and develop groundbreaking solutions. 7. Communication and Transparency: Wacker Neuson promotes open and transparent communication channels throughout the organization. The management encourages employees to share their ideas, concerns, and suggestions. Regular team meetings, department updates, and feedback sessions ensure that everyone is informed and involved in the decision-making process. In conclusion, Wacker Neuson provides an excellent work environment for design engineers to grow or advance. I expect the company to make a compelling overall offer to new hires if you consider the entire package. With a focus on innovation and technology, Wacker Neuson provides an exciting platform for design engineers to thrive and contribute to the construction equipment industry.
