companies.name: Northwestern Mutual
allPros: great culture and company - lots of growth opportunities

The pros of being an advisor at Northwestern Mutual would start with the great training program and support of the office staff. They make sure you have all the material you need to learn about the industry and hit the ground running. They also cover the cost of your investment license exams which is a nice little perk. I really enjoy the San Jose office because I can bounce ideas off other advisors here who are willing to help me out in any way they can. It is a very "self motivated" type of job but having a lot of support feels nice and makes it a little easier. Also the ability to grow your income through both insurance and investments is great.

This internship is a great opportunity for those that are willing to put in the work. I have always wanted to start my own business and never had a clue how, so this internship allowed me to do just that, and I have been able to make a significant amount of income while still in college. It's a very rewarding career when you put your all into it, and work to help your clients.

There are a ton of amazing people in recruiting in the organization nation-wide willing to help you, because they know it is challenging. That is #1 Pro about this company. Another Pro is the stability of the company. Recruiters are not laid off like in other industries or companies. It's also because the Partners of an office literally have to recruit new people to grow their income. After a year or two, you can make good income. After that, zero growth or professional development. Another pro is literally no one looking over your shoulder, no micro-management. It is a great job right out of college if you can commit your life (not time necessarily, but volatility and stress) and have no family to take care of. Hours are very normal, and will be a little less than recruiting positions at a major financial firm or bank, which is great. Prob 8-9 hours a day instead of 10 like most big bank recruiters who generally work more hours per week. The recruiting role itself is difficult, so it can be hard to find new recruiters, especially at the starting salary. They will keep you on board if you are halfway decent and you boss gives a reasonable goal for the year (which varies greatly office to office). Some offices have extremely supportive Partners who try to keep and develop their recruiters. Some have no issue with a revolving door every year. The recruiters in the company support each other coast to coast even though they work in different offices. Some offices will offer an opportunity to get licenses and certifications, but probably won't pay for useful expensive ones like SHRM. They will let you get insurance and series 7, which is useless for recruiters. Many recruiters become commission based Financial Advisors just like the ones they have to recruit, because it is literally on of the only options for income growth. Great overall culture and networking. This works out well, because you can network with all the other recruiters who leave NM for other Financial firms every year. (very strange pro, I know)

You get to own your practice. You can do the career your way and they allow you freedom to experiment. You get out what you put in so if you are a hard worker and enjoy the field or work, you will make a lot of money and have a good time.
Decent pay and benefits, and they were generous with swag.

Northwestern Mutual (NM) hires full-time Recruiters and Financial Representatives when all other SF Bay area companies are looking to lay off "non-essential" employees, ask for unattainable metrics, or seek only to hire contract or part-time work. NM is financially stable, has not had layoffs, and is always striving to grow local branch offices. Thus there is always work for recruitment teams. Each local branch office is a mini-start-up, allowing Recruiters to grow into future leadership positions and earn more compensation. The people in the office are friendly, and I am surrounded by incredibly hard-working professionals who want to succeed in their careers and business.
Plenty of autonomy, free to approach things how you want.
allCons: none that I can think of

The hardest part of the job would be finding enough people to talk to and building up your book of business. Also balancing the work load with continuing education is sometimes tough but overall not that bad.

It's not for everyone, in the sense that a lot of my peers couldn't handle the work, and didn't feel comfortable dialing the phones. You have to be accountable for yourself, no one is going to hold your hand and tell you exactly how to spend every minute of your entire day, so you need to stick to your calendar and make sure to get ahead to keep appointments on.

While the people are great, the system just isn't set up for long term success. The longest running recruiters will be in rural or small cities where opportunities are less. You will make far more money recruiting for a major bank or other financial company. They will most likely start experienced and non-experienced (in recruiting) people at a very low starting salary until you "prove yourself". Zero growth in any agency staff position. NM has over 600 recruiters. There are probably under 40 with more than 3 years in the role. Hiring commission only roles is hard enough, but the company gives no help, leads, or much support to the people you hire. Too much rests on whether they get a Director (manager) that actually cares about them. The Directors are top individual contributors with no leadership or coaching training or experience. If you get a great one, it makes a huge difference. There are some great ones! Essentially this role will get stale on income and stress after about 2-3 years. Get into a bank or a large financial company after that. Remember, you DO NOT work for Northwestern Mutual (Fortune 100 company) as a recruiter. You work for a small agency staff that the Partner pays all the bills personally. Normal 2023 benefits such as paid maternity are non-existent, except those required by law. You will get standard health insurance. Another really weird thing is their strange titles. Everyone is either a Coordinator or a Director. There is no hierarchy that makes any sense whatsoever. Many recruiters are referred to as "Director of Recruiting" which confuses the hell out of people when you are trying to interview elsewhere . It is NOT a Director position like another financial firm. It is more like "Analyst" or "Associate" level. Great job to jump to a bank after a few years to hire for salary roles. Also, a lot of Directors will ruin your recruits who start training , and you will not get credit for the hire. They quit before they finish, because their "mentor" is horrible. Remember, the mentors are not managers. They are glorified individual contributors who can't be fired. They will just go back to being an individual contributor. Most don't even listen to the Partners, Training team, or Recruiters.

You have to own your practice. This means a lot of work and no base pay. You have to scrap for every last bit of your pay because it's all commission. This can be daunting for some as it ended up being for me. While it is nice to have the freedom to do the career how you want, it can end badly just as easily as it can end positively.

The culture is extremely political and work moves at a snail's pace. Every meeting requires pre-meetings, and every project requires approvals from leaders in every department. I was unproductive a lot because of the number of meetings I had to schedule just to move to the next step. And because they love all these meetings, it's very hard to get on anyone's calendar because they are always booked. People are nice, but the work moved so slowly. It was boring. Be prepared to be inundated with all things DEI, every, single day. I understand the value, but being beaten over the head in every class and company-wide meeting gets old. They are not proponents of remote work either even though they were extremely successful while everyone was remote due to the pandemic.

The position the recruitment team primarily recruits for is challenging and hard to describe in an initial conversation. Most candidates will not understand the compensation structure if familiar principally with a traditional base income. Thus, leadership provides a ton of training to recruitment to better inform them about the role and to explain the position to prospects clearly. Moreover, the interview process for candidates is extensive for an entry-level position, and most candidates will self-select out of the process if unable to move quickly. Further, those professionals used to hybrid or remote work will ideally not like the in-office work culture, but there are exceptions to the work policy. On a positive note, the firm has an incredible value proposition and truly impacts people's financial lives. Lastly, anyone seeking a new opportunity, eager to learn, has grit, and is comfortable earning a performance-based income will flourish here!

Less of a financial planner, more of an insurance salesman. 100% of your comp is commission, and the commissions are peanuts unless you sell whole life insurance. During training you are assigned to producing a list of 200 contacts. Once training ends your job is to call, and continue calling, these people to set up a meeting. The meeting is ostensibly to get to know them and develop a plan, but the comp structure means you'll be squeezing whole life insurance into every plan (because you make pretty much $0 if you don't). Bottom line: Unless you can sell whole life insurance you will make nothing. I think I made $400 over 3 months. Maybe I just suck at selling insurance, but if you aren't confident you could sell insurance (policies with premiums of several hundred dollars a month) to at least 5-10 people stay very far away. If not, don't give this a go if you have rent to pay.

I believe that the welfare and satisfaction of employees are crucial to the success of any organization, and that it is the responsibility of the management to provide a supportive and healthy work environment. If the club is firing employees for quitting, this sends a message that they do not value their staff or prioritize their well-being. It also raises concerns about the club's compliance with employment laws and regulations. I urge you to take this issue seriously and to take steps to address it. You will often not get assigned enough work to meet your metrics (4 closures a day when working remote and 3 when working in the field). You then have to either save some closures for rainy days or ask other adjusters if they can give away some of their work when they're too busy. System is definitely setup against the adjuster to succeed. I will often only get assigned 1 or 2 claims in the field when I am required to close 3 a day and will have to go searching for a 3rd claim to close. Some people never get deployed and work exclusively from home (this is usually due to developing some skill that separates them from the rest or they're really good at closing claims virtually, so Allstate tries to keep them in a virtual position). The management team is a serious issue. Three C-levels “left” in 2022 among several individuals in upper management. It’s a boys club of white men running the company. Lots of forced prayers at company events. Everything that created the company purchased by Blackstone has gone down the toilet. It is not powered by people. The morale is at an all time low because employees are not allowed to work remotely even if it’s a desk job. Employees get 52 days a year to work remotely and are required to log those days in advance and management runs badge access records against those logged days at home. This company doesn’t value work life balance or family. You are expected to always be available 24-7 no matter the circumstances from PTO, evenings or weekends. DO NOT WORK HERE

The Fresh Market is EXPENSIVE. Your PTO hours are accrued throughout the year. Only 40 hours can be rolled over to the next year. Give us our allotted hours for the year all up front on Jan 1. Give us an option to sell unused PTO if only 40 PTO hours can be rolled over. OR just get rid of your 40 hour roll over cap. The volunteerism is a great idea but don’t hold it against employees who do not take advantage by withholding Eagle Club. I would be more inclined to actually volunteer if it wasn’t tied to a religious effort. DCO and CET (electrical and mechanical) were combined into one role. Let me repeat that: Three careers, three different trades, were combined into one. What makes it even worse is, you have 18 months to become competent in all three careers, get a success profile book signed off, for a 2-3% raise. No one really knows how much of an inventive this will actually be, because they won’t disclose the pay scale for this new position, which they have termed “Jack of all trades.” Who would really want to learn 2 other careers for anything less than 10-15% salary increase when one could easily find another job for 5-10% salary increase for way less responsibility? DCO gets a 3% raise in order to close the pay gap between DCO and CET, but if you were making less than $30/hr, that 3% does not close that gap. CETs get nothing with the restructuring. They have to qualify as a COT1 first before seeing any monetary incentive. I don’t think one person from the manager level down was ever consulted about this restructuring. When this business plan was introduced and we were given an opportunity to ask questions, someone asked if we (techs, leads and supervisors) were going to be asked for our input. The answer was “this going to happen sooner than later.” So the answer was basically a resounding NOPE. This restructuring was rolled out with very little thought and no plan of action as to how we are going to make it work. FacOps is left trying to figure this out on the fly. Former DCO Team Lead and DCO Supervisor career paths were destroyed. This applies to all QTS sites. Their next level for career path was either DCO Supervisor or DCO Manager. With this new organizational restructure, they were demoted to COT1, expected to keep their daily Team Lead/Supervisor responsibilities, and now have to climb the ladder all over again. They have to qualify for COT1 first, then cross fingers a miracle happens to get promoted to COT2, COT3, COT Supervisor, then COT Manager. But wait, they already transitioned CET supervisors into COT supervisor, so their ceiling now stops at COT3 until a Supervisor or Manager position opens up. DCO has always been an after thought when it comes to FacOps. There were 10 DCO techs with half the customer base just a few years ago. Before this restructuring, there were 4 DCO techs with twice as many customers. (Guess what, another DCO tech just quit for greener pastures, so that leaves 3 DCO/COTs to keep the site running, learn electrical and mechanical, and cross train the electrical and mechanical techs - all the while maintaining a 24x7x365 data center. Have you heard of burn out?) Diversity and inclusion is non-existent. The majority of people in Site Director positions, all the way up to Chad Williams, are mostly white males. There is an apparent love and bias toward those who served in the Navy, especially on a nuclear submarine. I respect our veterans but when a veteran is hired or promoted without the qualifications over a current employee with the qualifications, then I have a problem. I’ve seen capable and qualified employees get passed over for open positions for a Navy Veteran, or an outsider. I’ve also seen Navy Veterans get promoted 3-4 times within 2-3 years when our policy for promotions is 12 months in your current role to be eligible for a promotion. If you are a minority, your ceiling for career growth is low. Powered by People is nothing more than a catch phrase. It’s more like Powered by Veterans and God.

QTS's leadership is lacking diversity in both gender and color - the C Suite is all white and only one woman in place (HR role). As published in their ESG report (available online) 65% of their workforce is white, 12.9% Black, 9% Hispanic, 6% Asian; additionally only 22% of QTS’ workforce is comprised of women... Their lack of commitment to creating a diverse workplace puts into perspective how behind and out of touch they are with the gen-x/millennial/gen-z workforce wants and needs. For example, QTS' version of work/life balance is offering a Flex Program that offers 52 days a year remote which needs to be logged in their system and approved by management. QTSers want a Diversity and Inclusion effort (to include a C-suite role) at QTS but the CEO couldn’t stomach a group with such a name and in turn had it renamed to "Community in Action" the day the program was launch. Every effort to pull QTS into the 21st century is met with resistance by the CEO and leadership, making QTS a place where ‘disruptors’ and individuals who question the status quo no longer welcome, and the few remaining who refuse to toe the company line are being silenced quickly. In addition to the above, the CEO leverages his Christian ideology in almost every All Hands, Sales Kick Off, and People Rally meetings. For some, that behavior can be ostracizing and uncomfortable which doesn't seem to affect him or other leaders. Additionally his conservative political ideology is manifested in the types of QTSers that are hired and are in leadership positions, further curating a homogenous workforce. QTS in 2023 leaves current employees and prospective employees with much to be desired. Like this review's headline stated...you can do better.

- Lack of communication between teams. Israel teams are doing one thing and New York teams are doing something else - There is a lack of culture. It's truly deceiving. The office is very open and there's always good music playing but employees feel like they're always being watched by senior leadership. Recently all employees were forced to have mandatory hours in office 9:30am - 7:00pm. Employees need to get permission to come in late or leave early - Very little to zero discussions on career growth and trajectory. Since there's no HR to formalize a process or leveling no one know where they're going. - Junior/young employees are not offered equity. Some younger folks are told they're entitled to equity in their offer negotiation but managers do not follow through. Additionally, junior employees are paid below market (very below market). Many are not paid a living wage to be in New York - Employees are often yelled at or harassed by the company's cofounders. There is a huge cultural gap between Israel and the US. Communication is different, mannerisms are different and NY employees are always forced to appease Israeli team members/stakeholders - The company employs many international new graduates who NEED the sponsorship to remain in the country. The company takes advantage of this vulnerability since the long hours and poor treatment make it extremely difficult to recruit on the side. - Recently a top performer was fired in front of the entire brand during an all-hands. It was extremely inappropriate, uncalled for and the co-founder treated her with such disrespect - it was truly demoralizing. - Most employees who are promoted are only promoted in title. Raises, bonuses etc are out of the question. - This company has the highest turnover I've ever seen in company. - The co-founders look favorably on the New Ventures team, so if you are dying to work here, join that team.

Terrible culture. As mentioned in other reviews, 9:30-7pm mandatory hours in office (have to ask permission to leave), in office 4 days a week. Career growth is not prioritized - you have to fight for everything from taking a day off to getting a bonus. The "finance" team is one person who is so overwhelmed that sometimes people don't get paychecks. Equity is not offered and salaries are low. Many contracts include a 2-year non-compete barring you from working in any area of the beauty industry (I even heard of one employee being threatened by legal once they left because of this). International students/people are hired so that they are essentially forced to stay with the company for visas. Management is focused on squeezing as much out of people as they can (and have bullied / screamed at employees). Because of all of this, morale is low and people are constantly complaining and gossiping around the office. Not to mention, much of the company's selling strategies also have the same unethical/shady vibe, which is not fun to be involved in (for example -- promoting a "Primer Quiz" which redirects all consumers to the same Primer, retouching marketing assets to no end). Teams are kept in silos so you will never get to learn about other parts of the business. Management acts as if the company is a rocket-ship headed towards space; but it is in fact a dumpster fire. DO NOT DRINK THE KOOL-AID.

companies.name: Ulta Beauty
allPros: Good schedule and works with you when needed
My only pros are the others I worked with and the free product.

Positive work environment, this stems from the solid work ethic of the general manager. She does not play favorites. She puts in get hours and does the work. I feel like the rest of the management team at this time are working well together. This isn't a "us vs them" club like in the past. Appreciated the individual company product education for our monthly product line of the month. The gratis is a definite perk
Easy job that doesn’t require a lot of physical work.
Nice discounts, great insurance and health benefits.

Pretty easy going job if you're a fairly comfortable cosmetologist. Great clients, great tips... usually. Benefit Cosmetics gratis is amazing, $300 a year or so to spend on their site. You also get full sized products of new products. Great co-workers, no "mean girl/boy/them" politics when I worked there. I met some amazing people. Management was decent although District Manager for Ulta itself at the time was kind of rotten.
fun environment, great employees, discount
allCons: Doesn’t offer Over time or weekends off

We were supposed to get a bonus for hitting our yearly sales goal, never got it. I was expected to bend over and let customers do whatever they wanted and accept returns, even for items we didn't carry, because our GM "didn't want to fight" with them. I was told by our GM to commit fraud (I refused) when processing returns. The store was dusty, messy and we NEVER had enough hours to have enough staff to get any of the work done that was expected to get done. The salon staff were rude, unhelpful and called off work CONSTANTLY and the GM didn't care and would alter their timecards. Our GM was fired for timeclock fraud (her own timecard), and we were all told to basically pretend it didn't happen. I worked over 75 hours in one week because we didn't have enough staff and no one cared enough to do anything about it except make the managers fill in. I would NEVER recommend anyone work here. You're underpaid (cashiers barely made $10/hours and we were encouraged to offer them basically pennies), customers get free reign to yell at you, and you watch people steal product all the time and you cannot do anything about it.

We are supposed to get gratis on a weekly basis for watching our weekly training videos. I feel that many of the employees aren't watching the videos which is keeping the rest of us from getting our products to try out. Either that or the managers are keeping the full sized products for themselves. I've seen a few managers with full sized gratis and I haven't received any gratis for those weeks. Sometimes I've made appointments for the salon and been bumped for a non-employee guest who has made an appointment. That's understandable. Sometimes when I've done something incorrectly I'll be coached on the fact I've done it wrong by three different managers. One is enough. They push credit cards heavily. It's very stressful sometimes. To the point that they make you feel horrible if you didn't get even one during your four hour shift when you weren't on the register.

Very much a high school atmosphere at this particular location, favorites and clicques prevail. It's horrible, the women there need to learn to support their fellow sisters & coworkers (and the sprinkle of gentlemen as well). After all, beauty comes in all shapes, sizes and past experiences. Definitely dropping the ball there but the captain of the ship let's it sail. 5 manger changes during training period which made it difficult to stay on company training deadlines and lack of support to try new techniques and machines on fellow coworkers for the sake of learning because of the clique supporting and referring clients to one coworker more than another - which was unfair to a newbie to reach their weekly sales goals. Hate pushing products due to price, not everyone has the same bank account so I flipped it to educating every customer on the product ingredients and benefits of what my clientele was wanting to achieve results for.

Consistently hires new employees at higher rates than old ones and doesn’t give long-term employees raises to match. They encourage you to quit and get re-hired to get a raise because it’s easier than actually getting HR to approve it. It’s a decent short term job, but long term you’ll be stuck making close to what they hired you for, while newer employees are making anywhere from $1-4/hr more than you. When you ask them to adjust it, they’ll tell you it’s a long process and that HR will deny it a few times first and tell you it will take a lot of patience. I’ve been told a few times that they are aware of the issue and that all the other long-term employees have had to deal with this as well. They also tend to cut hours for the older employees in favor of scheduling the new ones for training. They often change your schedule by adding, changing or taking away shifts without notice. This can happen anytime from the week of to the same day as your shift. They expect you to check WorkJam daily to see if your shifts have changed rather than scheduling for 2 weeks out and leaving it as is. This makes it very hard to make plans outside of work, or have multiple jobs.
Ulta has ability to pay employees what they’re worth but often don’t. You have to sometimes fight for your associates to have an adequate wage. Point system is dated. People aren’t numbers.

Walker, MI location can be a bit zany at times, however. Due to the set up of the brow bar, customers often interrupt you during a brow service as you're in an open area on both ends. Which, is not good, wax is finicky and needs to be just the right temp for pulling. Oh, and people really need to teach their kids to stay out of the wax. lol. The only bummer is working weekends, where you have significantly less clients than your regulars during the week. Sometimes felt pointless to work weekends as the beauty advisors had clients on lock for getting them product and you don't make commission on Benefit products, so there isn't a lot of incentive to push their products.
poor pay, management can be too demanding depending on what area you work in, operations team does a lot of work for making less than prestige BA's

If an in-office environment is what you've been craving for since 2019, there's only one place and that's Verkada. The thriving office is filled with passionate employees that build human connections beyond work. The office is beautiful, workplace just launched our very own hot-food cafeteria with multiple options for lunch and dinner. You can tell, we really care about the fast-paced culture and have off-sites and in-office events that make my own friends who come wish they worked here. Top leadership is as experienced as they get and there's a clear biased to promote from within. We have a high-performance culture, I suspect most bad reviews are from employees who are underperforming or have been recently terminated.

Verkada is one of the very few places in silicon valley that understood this, the result is that we're thriving now coming out of the pandemic and not having to do any massive layoffs in 2022 / 23 Knowledge sharing / Real-time feedback: My teammates and I still have access to ELT quite easily, (my CMO is just three desks away, and I can go up and see our CEO / Co-Founders without much fuss.) It's been immensely helpful to have an engaged leadership team that shares the same trenches with my team and me, we are able to tackle problems and build fast. Opportunities for growth and professional development: Verkada's unwavering support, belief in talent, and willingness to take bold steps have been instrumental in our team's impressive growth of 400%. Frequent confusion in the workplace. The work environment was unnecessarily stressful due to poor communication between departments and capricious changes in direction from upper management. Sample volume in context of the laboratory's production capacity did not justify the rushed pace of workflow. Staff often went without lunch breaks due to under-staffing and poor distribution of training. Holidays were not observed because upper-management did not want an increase in turn-around-time for the few samples that arrived; this was also the rational for requesting production staff come in during extreme weather events and hazardous road conditions. Interpersonal conflict was rarely escalated to management or HR. Some difficult employees were let go after their pattern of poor behavior was known and documented; however, staff favored by management had all criticism of them ignored. This resulted in the perpetuation of a hostile work environment by management-favored staff against those who complained, specifically by denigrating their targets in private conversations to weaken job security and jeopardize possible promotions. Cliques were common, people frequently talked behind each other's back. HR has an unconscionably weak definition of what constitutes severe or pervasive sexual harassment. Of the incidences I know of, including one that I witnessed, the perpetrators remained employed while those who filed complaints were either terminated or quit. The company likes to boast about the diversity of their workforce and the number of women they've promoted and placed in leadership positions; this is hypocritical considering the gravity of their failures toward those who were brave enough to report their experiences of sexual harassment knowing the risk, and ultimately the cost, they incurred.

With the growing role of Electronic Logs, and its relation to Hours of Service; as well as the business opportunities and working environment in the Covid and Post-Covid world this has become a growing internal issue. Operations Mangers and Onsite Sales Professionals are responsible for all real world implementation of Health and Safety, Transportation Compliance and Business Development. If you are looking to work directly with field personnel in a role related to Health and Safety, Emergency Management, Trans Compliance or another auxiliary group apply for a position specifically mentioning OPERATIONS. If you are looking for an office position and or remote position apply for a position described in a more traditional manner to those titles. The company can also be very reluctant to accept internal applicants from other business lines into divergent lines, instead recruiting from external companies or just out right purchasing the company. Unfortunately, my experience in the sales role at Leyton UK was marred by a toxic culture, especially reflected in senior management. There was a lack of support and guidance from leadership, and the company's strategic direction was generally indecisive. This often led to confusion and frustration among the sales team regardless of being top performers or not. Furthermore, the targets set did not reflect the current market, and if you were unfortunate to fall behind on numbers, we were often performance-managed without any proper support or training. The commission structure was extremely poor compared to other companies, despite what management will tell you, with commission percentages being pushed down annually, making it difficult to stay motivated. It dropped from 5% for the life of an engagement to sub 3% of the first year's deal only in the time I was there. The company always presented itself as the market leader for customer engagement when in reality, it was subpar compared to its competitors. This is reflected in the client churn rate. While there were some positive aspects to the role, including a good team dynamic, the negative aspects outweighed them. I would not recommend this company to anyone looking for a supportive and positive work environment.

Mayo is a big organization so your experiences may vary. These comments are specific to Clinical Research within Mayo Clinic. Clinical research at Mayo is fairly dysfunctional. Most of the research leadership are from the Rochester area and have never worked outside of Mayo Clinic. The organization is very top heavy, with way too many managers looking to justify their salary by making up unnecessary policies and programs ultimately preventing investigators and study teams from doing actual research. This results in highly bureaucratic culture where feedback is not welcome. A rigid (almost military) hierarchy ensures that information flows through gatekeepers so nobody is held accountable. Read Catch-22 or watch office space for a taste of what it will be like to work in research at Mayo Clinic. TLDR: - highly bureaucratic - rigid hierarchy - limited opportunities for growth - out of touch leadership

Any potential IT candidates, filter the Glassdoor reviews by job role and choose Information Technology to see the overall satisfaction amongst just IT staff. This will help you make an informed decision if you’re looking to change jobs. All reviews are accurate. Low wages, burnout conditions, backstabbing, lack of promotional opportunities. You no longer can just be promoted for working hard, there has to be a business justification and then the position will be posted for everyone to apply for. This means you have a bunch of coworkers scratching and clawing their way up. The result is people hoarding work, backstabbing others to make themselves look better and sucking up to anyone in a position that will help them get promoted. If you do get the “promotion”, you’ll still be making far less than others in the same industry. They say their health insurance is top notch, but it is far from that. You’d think that a large healthcare organization would have amazing insurance, but that is NOT the case at all.

They what to be number one but they don't want to pay employees like they work for a number one company. The benefits are there but only some people get to use them. This is driven by the staffing or lack of staffing from department to department. Some areas are staffed at dangerously low levels but there are multiple layers of management who contribute little while constantly at "meetings" that improve nothing.

I ultimately left because Rochester as a city is not a place to thrive for extraverted people in their 20s & 30s. I ended up driving to Minneapolis almost every weekend just to do something. Mayo is great for a thriving career but outside of that, Rochester is a damper in my opinion.

Not a good place to grow your career. IT leadership is secretive and falling behind the center for digital health (another IT org) not good if you aren’t an older Caucasian man. I worked here for 5 years and lost track of how many times I was interrupted, talked down to, etc. Pay is low which is so sad because Mayo acts like it’s a world class organization but keeps their IT professional pay low. They also ask analyst titles to do engineering work but then don’t pay them like engineers. Need more in person collaboration and team building

Pay could be better, not very many holidays, PTO is generous but must also account for the fact that you must use it for certain holidays that are not paid by the company. Also, using it was an issue. In the summer months, only five consecutive days of PTO could be approved. You may not even get all five days approved because it’s based on seniority and certain number of people taking off and if a certain day is already at a max for people taking off, you will get denied. I asked for 5 days for a trip and only had 4 days approved. I ended up leaving Mayo 6 wks before my vacation for a job that gave me the full week paid. Tuition reimbursement was also non-existent. Employees were very overworked and overwhelmed during the pandemic. Half the staff were furloughed for the summer while the remaining half of us did the work of the full department. When the staff came back from furlough, we were given a $1,000 bonus that everyone received. I think those that continued to work should have had an additional bonus, whether it was monetary or additional PTO as so many employees were completely burnt out at this point.

Everything from the on-boarding to receiving your schedule is incredibly efficient. I did my 1st 2 days of training virtually at home with a manager leading the classes and the Assistant Manager had my hours punched in before I confirmed. Nothing (from clocking in, to giving a discount to doing a return) is difficult, and the way they do things just makes logical sense. There are several leads and supervisors so the 2 managers are free to do their jobs and keep the store running efficiently. The store has all the details dialed in (example: we have soap, and pens, and bags are stocked in size order). They have this "1 is 3" mentality; essentially that 1 great employee equals 3 mediocre ones so there's minimal negativity. Work/life balance is easy because you can trade shifts in their app, and/or request to take more shifts in the same app. Another value they have is "Win-Win" and they believe another person/team doesn't have to lose for another to gain. It's the least toxic place I've worked in probably 2 decades. Store Manager leads by example. Assistant and all leads are always actively assisting on the sales floor and have a wealth of knowledge. They offer part-time benefits including 401k, dental, medical, and vision. Employee discount is generous and starts on your 1st day. There's transparency with sales plan and there's open communication. There are thousands and thousands of SKUs, so the mobile device we use allows us to type in things people ask for and we can show them photos. The device will also tell us if it's in stock and what department it's featured in. The device also will tell you the next date it'll be replenished if it's sold out. There's no guess work, so communicating with customers is genuine, accurate, and concise.

If you are a female looking at a possible job with EQT, I urge you strongly to reconsider. I am a female who has worked for this company for a decade +. Due to personal restrictions, I am unable to leave this job at current, though I desperately wish I could. This company is not one I would recommend to any female looking to advance their career. The nepotism and sexism I've experienced at this company is both mind-boggling yet unsurprising. There have been countless times over my decade with this company where I have been the only female in a meeting. There have been countless times over my decade with this company that I have been talked over and/or ignored by a male coworker. I have seen other male coworkers in my department promoted faster than me, even though I receive glowing quarterly reviews. When asked why I wasn't given a promotion, my male supervisors and bosses are usually vague. It wasn't always like this at EQT. There was a period of time about 5-7 years ago where there was a broad push throughout the company for more diversity, especially at upper levels of management. In my opinion, it had a broad but successful reach to try to allow other voices to shine through in the workplace. However, since the new management has come in around 2018 this notion to include more diverse voices seems to have been shelved. If you need proof, simply look at the company website and the people running EQT. With one - ONE! - exception they are all white males. There's a lot that other comments say about EQT on Glassdoor that are both good and bad. I could touch on a lot of it, since I've been here so long. Most of what is written on this site is true (especially the negative reviews). But I wanted to lend a voice to the lack of diversity in this company, because any prospective employees need to be forewarned - if you are not a white male, you will not find success here. I hope to be able to leave this company soon, so that I can have serious discussions with HR about what I've experienced through my career here. Until then, I can only hope that this message serves as a strong warning to anyone who doesn't fit the cookie-cutter EQT mold.

Also because of this 1099 setup, there were no benefits. The biggest con was the crazy proprietary time-tracking software I had to install to clock in and out. It would track keyboard strokes, mouse movement, websites accessed, and take webcam screenshots of me every 10 minutes (some people's were even more often than that) where my face was required to be visible. If any of these things weren't on point, at best I might not get paid for that 10-minute stretch -- or at worst, company policies threatened that I could be fired me for "fraud". Better still, they cared way too much about where I got my work done. The other biggest con was that the work was absolute drudgery. As a "manager" my job was merely to learn all the characteristics of a high-quality support ticket, and when my agents didn't meet the criteria in one of their tickets, I had to write up a coaching document explaining in GREAT detail (yet also as succinctly as possible) what they did wrong and how to do better next time. Then I would send it to my agent as well as my supervisor who would review it and then coach me in the same way.

I worked at this company for 7 years and witnessed its ups and downs. It used to be a cutting-edge company, a leader in remote work, but over time it started to decline. During my time there, I met many great people and professionals from various fields. Unfortunately, most of them no longer work for the company. The reason for the decline is twofold: 1. The business model is to acquire dying software products, provide minimal support, and make money from a shrinking customer base. It's important to note that there's no focus on selling good and profitable software. 2. The top management's poor behavior trickles down to all levels of the company. Employees are treated as mere "resources" and their well-being is ignored. They can suddenly duplicate workload without adjusting compensation, switch employees to a different project in a day with a different technology stack and expect the same results within two days time frame. They deceive and manipulate, for example, by saying "shrink to grow" when there's no actual growth. KPIs are always aggressive, and even if you meet them, next quarter they will be increased, without any compensation for sure. The consequences of this for you as a new hire are unfortunate: 1. You'll mostly work with outdated and irrelevant technologies. 2. The software and codebase you'll be working with are outdated, have poor quality, or are technologically limited. The knowledge transfer process is also lacking, leaving you with a "black box" that nobody knows how to manage. 3. The size of the team is adjusted every quarter according to the shrinking customer base, and because this happens across all projects, they'll let you go instead of reassigning you to another product. They call it "shrink to grow", but it's a lie - there's been no growth in 4 years. 4. The remaining employees are left with an overwhelming workload, but their expectations and compensation remain the same. For example, a product that was once supported by 3 engineers (each was pro in his area, and supported a set of product parts written in c++, Objective-C, C#, java), may suddenly be supported by just one person who is expected to have the same level of knowledge and output for the same compensation. 5. The team environment is hostile. Each new member is a survivor of previous downsizing and views you as a threat. If your performance surpasses theirs, they'll be fired. Professional or emotional support is non-existent, and senior employees often do performance/PR reviews, using subjective reasons to decrease your delivery rate and decline your work. So, for those who consider joining this company: I strongly advise against anyone joining this company. Unless you're in dire need of money and are willing to be treated poorly, having your brain manipulated and wasted and have your hard work disregarded. FOR CUSTOMERS of products under the ESW CAPITAL umbrella, my advice: RUN!!! and plan your migration to an alternative product as soon as you hear that your product has been acquired by this company. You will experience declining quality and support, as well as increasing costs if you stay. Because the company business model is to let the product die. So anyway you will switch, sooner or later.

I very much appreciate and take advantage of all the great campus perks, from the on campus diner and cafe to the medical clinic and fitness center and most of all the positive energy and frequent on campus live music.

My time at Sweetwater has been nothing short of amazing so far. The development culture here is very collaborative, work/life balance is good, and there is a very real sense that employees are cared about. I've never heard people talked about as "resources" like I have at previous jobs. SW really does pour into and invest in people at the human level. There is no shortage of opportunity for someone hungry to do great things at this company. The amenities at Sweetwater are a major plus for me as well. The fact that we have so many great services right here in the building make it very convenient. Over the past several months, I've seen a concerted effort from senior leadership to bring the shining examples of great leadership and culture over into the IT side of the house, and really attempt to break down some negative historical leadership practices.
Good discounts on gear, good facility to work out of, lots of like minded musicians around you.

Gear discounts, diner and gym at work, awesome concierge service, and great place to make friends with your coworkers. The "office hours" on the sales floor were often hands-on time with gear which was very beneficial. The facility was always super clean and friendly. The company *genuinely* treats customers right 99% of the right time, and in a customer-facing role, you have the ability to help customers in every single way without having to go through management. The best part about working at Sweetwater are the people you work with. Especially if you go through Sweetwater University - your classmates become your friends.

Access to insane gear discounts and a wealth of intelligent, kind, and talented colleagues; genuinely edifying "office hours" with manufacturers and reps; and the beautiful wide world of musicians I got to use my knowledge and talent to help. Friends were made, and good times were had. Even when no one ever quite knows what management's got up their sleeves. Frequently, that's what we bonded over. Not great...
Pay was decent, lots of good people in the company and Ft Wayne area, Diner food was great.
Great people on the sales floor but unfortunately the company as a whole does not value these individuals.
allCons: really none I can think of.

The music industry is historically male dominated. I think Sweetwater is taking the appropriate steps to contribute to the evolution of diversity in this industry by providing leadership development opportunities and actively pursuing diverse applicants.

Every company is made up of humans, so there are always going to be things that fall through the cracks, or situations that arise because of decisions made in the past. I've heard that there used to be a culture of fear in the tech side of Sweetwater, but this has not been my experience thus far.

Old school management style that at some point will NEED to be adjusted. In addition, there was a massive commission structure change, which resulted in most people either losing money (or at the very least having to work much harder for the money they were making) during a time where inflation was at its highest in years. Lack of work from home opportunities even the the tech is in place to do so. Way to many meetings that could be condensed into a video to watch on our own time, or just aren't necessary altogether.

First and foremost, you work in a "cubicle graveyard" and even though you can design your space how you like, nothing is more uninspiring to a bunch of musicians and creative minds than being in a cubicle all day without access to windows. Really tough in the winter when you quite literally do not see the sunlight at all in a single day. There's a massive issue with distrust between management and salespeople due to CONSTANT changes in policy, which seemed to have started RIGHT when the CEO changed over and the Providence buyout, although management insists it has nothing to do with that. Within just months of working there, the commission model changed entirely and changed how you can earn money, and it was not working consistently for weeks. it was very hard to understand if what you were earning was accurate and mistakes were often found. Since then, multiple other changes have happened that change what you can be paid on - most of all of which are ones that TAKE MONEY AWAY from salespeople - including a disastrous harmful change in shipping costs and how the CRM worked that was rolled out during Black Friday week which showed us how disconnected management was from the sales floor. Not just with commission either - tons of new "standards" rolled out that were extremely "corporate" in nature that suddenly punished EVERYONE when really it's just a few people who were taking advantage of the lax system. Suddenly there are write-ups left and right for hardworking folks, there's having to report numbers to your managers every day, there are performance plans, etc. all for a company that represents the sales roles as "running your own business". It's ok to have these standards, but how they're implemented created distrust, anxiety, and stress between what USED to be "sales coaches" and salespeople. Sales coaches used to be a resource for a very stressful job that requires tons of extra hours and often a massive emotional toll, but now they just play the role of "managers" who have to write people up left and right. To sum this all up, the president of sales wrote an email immediately before a massive winter storm when the county went into a state of emergency one evening due to not being able to keep up with the roads (no, sweetwater did not close early that evening) saying "weather doesn't make you late, you make you late", and giving 101 level advice on how to get your car unstuck - forgetting that people live in apartment complexes and have no control over plowing or getting their cars out. The Head of People wrote emails during every disastrous storm BRAGGING that Sweetwater has only closed twice, EVER, for weather - as if that's something to be proud of. The company will defend this, but their policies BLATANTLY put their bottom line ahead of employees' lives and well-being. From having to drive to work (and for a required and often useless 7:30AM meeting) in disastrous weather rather than letting us work from home for a day, from not having sick time (and saying that they can't give us sick time because it would take from vacation time... no, it really doesn't have to) and encouraging employees to come in and spread disease around because they don't want to use their vacation time or they can't work from home for 2 days, there's a massive lack of understanding and empathy in management. Unless you make the company a massive amount of profit. The people who are top salespeople can work from home on a day's notice sometimes, so the rules are not consistent among all employees. Just like most sales jobs, be prepared to take massive hits in commission when it's not your fault. Fedex errors? UPS errors? Broken items? Mispacking? Customer decided they wanted a car instead? You will pay for it. Overall - don't take a job in sales here if you are used to working for a modern company with a more understanding and empathetic culture. If you aren't prepared to not get paid for meetings and not get paid (and sometimes even lose money) on days you work, don't do it. You will work for free (basically serving as a customer service person) on weekends for years and years because of no hourly pay, and you will have to attend 3 (4 your first year) hours of unpaid meetings each week early in the AM. You will have little control over your schedule, and it will be chaotic - my schedule was a different starting time every day. It's very hard to work here if you care about work culture, mental health, (their mental health initiatives are an inside joke laughing stock among employees) consistent pay, and work/life balance. If you are easily affected by how other people treat you, phone sales positions are not for you. Lastly, Fort Wayne is FINE. It's just fine. It's nice. It's not bad, it's not great. It's Indiana. It's a nice small city. But you HAVE to move here. Rent is cheaper than other cities obviously, but it's not cheap proportional to pay. There are less than 15 women as sales engineers out of almost 600 and hardly any folks who are not white, so don't expect a diverse workplace. Don't forget Sweetwater was sold to Providence, which is a private equity firm... whose sole purpose is to generate a fast profit and then sell the business off. As much as Chuck is still involved, it doesn't feel like Chuck's ethics anymore.

They used to respect and support their salespeople, but no longer. When I signed on, we were treated with respect—we really were! And I don't want to directly blame the buyout by Providence, but over the course of '22-23 after it happened, the company went from a supportive, honest, open place where managers and colleagues had my back to a constant source of anxiety and stress; honest mistakes became grounds for termination when the same mistakes used to just be a matter of "sorry boss won't do it again." Again, it's not really the managers' fault themselves, but as a collective, the leadership of the company made it extremely clear that they didn't trust us or have our backs. By the time I left, managers had been actively gaslighting everyone in the department for a year or more in a pathetic attempt to make us think nothing was wrong. We began getting paid less for the same work (they'll argue that point because it was a lot more complicated than that, but some of us did the math and it's pretty damning), morale plummeted, downright insulting attendance and phone-stat standards were implemented (hence the newly fertile grounds for termination), and tenured SEs began leaving right and left. They're knowingly replacing us with people of lower caliber, maybe hoping to increase the chances they'll be satisfied to be treated like just any other retail worker. "We have a slide!!!" isn't enough. Sweetwater, you made me risk my safety at least once a year to drive there during horrific storms while bragging that you've only had to close twice in 40 years. Yeah. That number is nothing to be proud of. Shame on you. And you, prospective employee, can forget about trying to change any of this. When I was hired, there was a decent amount of productive dialog between management and salespeople. Now, if SEs try to talk to their coaches about anything of the sort, absolutely nothing gets done. I, like most of us, got writeups that any decent person would agree should've been expunged, but I was summarily shut down every single time I tried to have that conversation. "Rules are rules" - even when they make no sense, didn't exist when I was hired, and directly contradict the company's "do the right thing" policy. Interdepartmental communication also broke WAY down during this growing-pains stage, making simple tasks take hours multiple times a day, in addition to the fact that the company is still clinging to software from the early 90s to drive the entire business (seriously - entire). I'd be able to deal with things like this... if management had still been on my team. But as of early '22, they weren't. It's particularly upsetting that things have gone this way because there's no way all of the sales managers like it. Indeed, there are managers who never would've made it through the year while they were SEs, had the new standards been in place. Even I would've been fired when I was new because of the specific standards they set for new rollouts, and I was doing quite well by the time my book of business matured. I'm deeply disappointed. I really believed in what this company was doing when I joined. I wanted to retire there. But when the only policy was "do the right thing" and I no longer felt that I had the same definition of "the right thing" as management, I had no choice but to leave. Within a few years, at this rate, the best sales floor in the industry will be little more than a normal call center.

allPros: The team is young and the company is growing fast. It's a good place to get experience. There are lots of fun and creative people to learn from and collaborate with. Promotions come from within the company, and management isn't afraid to let employees grow into new roles. Their initial pandemic response was good, everyone possible was sent to work from home immediately. Management is flexible and accommodating with things like school schedules, drs appointments, and family needs. There are lots of fun activities and team building experiences, and it was cool to get involved with organizations like Utah Pride. The office is pet friendly. I made lifelong friends while working there, and a lot of really good memories. There are some absolutely stellar humans working at Oz Marketing.
allCons: There are issues that you might find in any company. For instance, you have to memorize the main clients mission statement and be able to recite it in front of a large group without warning. It's a stressful place to be introverted or have anxiety. I was pressed into prioritizing personal projects for management and other Young family members over my job on multiple occasions. I had my medical accomodations weaponized against me when I cancelled a meeting for a doctor's appointment I was on a waiting list for. A department head knowingly came to work and went to meetings maskless with COVID-19 and got multiple employees sick. Many of the problems stem from a fuzzy line between Oz Marketing and the Young Automotive Group, their main client. Oz Marketing's owner is employed by Young and is a member of the family. This led to multiple issues in my time there, one of the most frustrating being how much we were forced to undercharge them for our products. This made it hard to hire anyone with experience, as we could not offer competitive salaries. We were told to work harder and keep wearing multiple hats and that growth takes time, all while fighting to charge market rates for our products. Another large issue for me was how comfortable leadership is making insensitive comments. For example, I was speaking with the owner once and he talking about how male leadership is scared to promote women to positions where they would work closely with them, as they're worried about false sexual assault allegations. I am a woman. Whether or not he meant it, the message was "women are the reason there are no women at the top of this company". Another time he made a racist joke in a meeting, and upon seeing the look on my face, told me that I was supposed to keep him in line or something similar. I felt unable to work out these issues and others with management, as they are related. It's hard to go to your manager about their sibling for conflict resolution. In a similar vein, there are multiple Young Dealership GMs that female ad reps and team members knew to be cautious around, as they would make inappropriate or suggestive comments. Complaints were brushed off as far as I could tell, as the issue persisted the entire time I worked at Oz. I enjoyed much of my time at Oz Marketing, but these and other serious issues make it a workplace that I can't recommend. I wish it wasn't such a trade off.

As an HR professional, that really makes a difference in our line of work! As a person of color, Intuit has made genuine and meaningful strides in diversity and inclusion. I became a parent during my time at Intuit, and the support and work/life balance has been great. Internal mobility is also a big focus area, and that keeps me interested in working here in the long-term.

Tons of benefits but probably my favorite one is the Spotlight recognition, where any employee can give a cash bonus to any other employee as a way of saying thank you for going above and beyond. The senior leaders at the company seem to actually care about the employees. During COVID the message we continually received was take care of yourself and families first. They also gave us plenty of extra time off and sick days to help support our families or even our own mental health. The company is committed to creating a diverse and inclusive workforce. Tons of employee resource groups you can join to build community.

I have worked for Intuit for about 8 months now and I still love coming to work every day. I love my job, I love the people I work with, and I love this company! Woo!

Human Resources, especially recruiting, is viewed (and treated) as a strategic function. As such, we have better resources provided to do great work here. The bar for talent is very high at Intuit, and I enjoy working with some of the most brilliant minds in the tech world. That being said, culturally there is no room for big egos, and "stronger together" is a value I see modeled every day.

I've been on a number of amazing teams. People are collaborative, friendly, helpful and enjoy the work. I love working with so many cross functional teams - it's a real team effort between Engineering, Design, Research, etc... Everyone is very customer focused.

Great work-life balance High base pay Best 401K match - 125%, even better than Google Best WFH setup - widescreen monitors, ergonomic chairs, standing desks, HD webcams, and amazing headsets Transit and parking allowance (tax-free) for select locations Additional incentive - FTEs get to buy Intuit stock at a discount every quarter Amazing internal tools, the tax deductions on RSUs account for your state & federal rates Generous vacation policy with additional leaves for COVID & family support Free Udemy business account for upskilling
allCons: Not much problems or issues

I work 100% virtually/remotely, and I have had that arrangement since before Covid. Most employees (I'd say about 90%) are based at Intuit office locations. Intuit is still finding our rhythm with the hybrid model, and finding ways to encourage employees to come to the office more frequently. In the meantime, they are discouraging remote hires, and making it harder for employees to request to work 100% remotely. I understand the strategy, but as a remote worker, sometimes I feel like the company treats us like 2nd class citizens.

Intuit is a 40 year old company. With that comes a lot of legacy technology and systems that need to be maintained. On the plus side, we are undergoing a massive modernization effort to update to the latest technologies. There is a ton of work to do here across the company and our different products and we are well on our way in this journey. Rebuilding systems at scale and securely is not for the faint of heart.

- Some teams are still developing on medieval tech stack that were written in the early 90s. - The environment on some teams can be cutthroat and competitive. - Not much for upward mobility unless you really stand out or good at browning your nose. - The dynamics between certain teams can be hostile and uncollaborative. - Expect to work with a lot of Indian engineers and managers. They prefer to promote their own so upward mobility can be challenge. - Some code bases can be extremely convoluted due to lack of architectural planning and good housekeeping practices. - Occasional unexpected layoffs especially after the tax seasons. - The company is not yet ready to accept fully remote work even after the pandemic.

There really are not many cons at all. It is a bigger company, but as far as large companies go I would honestly say that Intuit is one of the best to work for. I don't currently have any cons for working for this company honestly - first time I've ever said that about a job!

Only people who have been there forever or are favorites get mornings, everyone else gets mids and closings. Performance metrics that compete with each other. Also normal in retail. Focus whatever the key metric is at the time and try to be passable in others. The downsides of this job are countless. You will essentially be given lists of hundreds of contractors and be tasked with cold-calling (pestering) them non-stop (unreasonable expectation to make 100 dials a day all whilst being monitored on webcam) to sign them up for a platform that is rife with flaws. While ethical practices are mentioned in training and you go in thinking you will be helping these contractors find new business, in reality this is not the case post-training. For one, the platform cost for contractors is exorbitant for the amount of value they get from it. While you will be coached by managers to tell contractors they will see estimates of 10-20 job leads per month, many contractors upon signing often see very little, despite proper attention to their profiles and collection of reviews. They also essentially get abandoned by HomeStars following sign-up and initial profile building with customer-service being practically non-existent for them (well documented in contractor online reviews). In the chance they do get leads they will be for small jobs of little value that would not be enough to generate a worthwhile return of investment into the platform. Data on the ROI for contractors on this platform is kept very secret (even a built in ROI calculator on profiles is not functional) but only a very small percent of businesses likely actually see value and a positive ROI (larger construction companies with a big marketing spend). You will be tasked with calling many small- scale companies, sole proprietors, and even contractors whose business is a side hustle and promise the world to them, encouraged to lie about metrics and the amount of jobs they will get from HomeStars. I was even told to encourage contractors who ran their business part-time to quit their full-time jobs to join HomeStars and take their business full-time, something that would have been financially ruinous had they joined. There will be many such situations like this and you will only be successful if you have the ability to lie, pressure, and have zero respect for hard-working small business owners ( elitism is rife in this company and many look down on blue-collar entrepreneurs, ridiculing their intelligence.) Technology and organization is also a mess. The lists of businesses you are expected to call are not properly sorted and often times you will be calling defunct businesses or those not even relevant to the construction world, wasting your time throughout the day. You will be expected to call "hot leads" and get notifications for them sent to your email, with expectations to call them at all hours of the day. Oftentimes these "hot" leads are anything but (for newer employees at least) and most often are individuals that clicked on HomeStars Facebook ads looking to find employment. In terms of your chances of success in this company the odds are heavily stacked against you. Out of an estimated 60 -70 sales reps around maybe 15 actually hit target monthly ( securing about the equivalent of a $65,000 salary) with perhaps 5-7 reps doing consistently well (six-figure take home.) HomeStars lies in their job postings and during the interview process regarding compensation here. These are terrible metrics considering what you can make in other legitimate tech companies. Base salary is also exceptionally low and not worth it for the amount of calls they expect from you. They will also bribe you to hit target with silly prizes like gift-cards and "spiff" that seems very juvenile. The commission structure often changes monthly as well making predicting how much you'll actually make a difficult task. Employee turn-over here is insane, both from people quitting once they realize how bogus the product is or from being fired for not hitting target, so HomeStars just runs job ads for account executives all year round. Contractor opinions of the platform are well-documented online. All of the positive Google reviews for HomeStars are homeowners reviewing the quality work performed by contractors, so HomeStars' online reputation benefits from the work actually performed by contractors, not the platform itself. The platform can in fact be beneficial for the homeowner (non-paying users). However, for contractors, the actual customers and paying users of HomeStars, negative opinions of the platform abound. You will be tasked with calling previous paying users to sign them up again as a "win-back" and you will often hear an earful of negative sentiment about the product. There are negative contractor reviews all over the internet (on Google reviews, trust pilot, site jabber and even documented on the company's Wikipedia page!) It's head U.S company ANGI also has a similar reputation with contractors. There are even class-action lawsuits ruling in favor of contractors due to deceptive business practices by ANGI leading to charges by the FTC. HomeStars similarly engages in these practices and it wouldn't surprise me if similar lawsuits emerge in Canada.

The most important Con: Uber has a difference in job ladders between S ladder and L ladder. If you are L ladder, you get stock, unlimited PTO, yearly perf review, bigger bonuses, etc. For S ladder, you do not get stock, you accumulate PTO, your perf review is either every quarter or 2 quarters. This role generally starts at S3 or S4, while the next major step is L3. The issue is that you would want to get to the L ladder as fast as possible, however the issue is, is that if you want to get to L ladder, you have to apply to the role against other people inside and outside of Uber. You're essentially stuck at S ladder, unless you want to leave Uber. TLDR : If you are S ladder, growth is extremely difficult, however of course, success stories do exist.

companies.name: Lacework
allPros: It's really exciting to be at a company with so much passion for the product and what we can do for the cloud security industry. Our mission is clear and there are so many talented, committed and FUN people that work here. I count myself as one of the lucky ones.

Incredible story to tell about a problem we are solving for. Company culture and team dynamics have improved tremendously. The ability to have your impact felt and a big investment in employee skill-building and success are just a couple reasons to wake up eager to tackle each work day.

I generally wait a year before I write a review to get a full picture. Coming into Lacework, I was uncertain. We went through a lot of change in a very short amount of time and that can be difficult to go through. However, the employees here are some of the most incredible people I've had the pleasure to work with, many have become friends. We've had some changes on the leadership (which were needed as we scale to our next phase) and we continually hire people who are experts in their field. I've learned a lot and been exposed to way more projects and learning opportunities than any other company. I'm definitely much more optimistic of our future with how the executive team has set up 2023 goals. Also the compensation packages are beyond the best I've seen in my 10+ year career.

The opportunity at hand is arguably the best in technology right now. We are competing for a TAM that is massive and still exploding. The leadership team that has been assembled is laughably talented (and proven). The IP we already have is for the part of the sec industry that no competitor has been able to figure out and tech is innovating at an industry leading pace. The company is growing rapidly which has led to an average of 4+ GTM promotions each month. The historic round of funding is being used on product improvements, professional development, marketing, and funding a compensation package that allows for some massive w2s. The sales culture has shifted away from the stressful days of the past into one where people are now energized by carrots instead of sticks and people are proud to work here because of it. First of all, I want to commend Newton's graduate marketing team. Credit where credit is due, you had me fooled. If you're considering working at Newton, it's important to be aware of the realities of the company beyond its polished marketing. The company perpetuates vacuous, vapid virtue-signalling and self-congratulatory lies from top to bottom. Their inclusivity policy is limited to those without their own opinions and diversity of thought is lacking. The company promotes a self-righteous and self-congratulatory attitude that can become overbearing. The idea that the company has a "secret sauce" approach is a clever marketing tactic used to convince employees they're part of something special and should be perpetually elated about the opportunity to work evenings keeping up with an unreasonable workload. The expectation that employees must pretend that Newton is the best thing since sliced bread coupled with the company's demanding culture, can be suffocating. Participation in company politics and unquestioning adherence to the company's culture is expected. There's a false belief among employees that the work is endlessly exciting and worth massive sacrifices. Newton rewards people who take themselves too seriously. In my experience, management at Newton proved to be conceited and misleading; happy to tell you one thing whilst believing another. They will not tolerate questions or challenges. Reminders of deontological principles are unwelcome. In short, I feel it is my duty to give those interested in joining Newton a better-informed view of their prospective employer. There is plenty of good feedback for this company, which I myself was sold upon. Many people who have worked at Newton advance their careers and move on, keeping their heads down in the process; but it's important to be aware of the damage that the company's culture can do to your spirit. I had a great impression of Newton when I joined, and I was ready to give everything to impress. My naivety in my genuine and open approach was a mistake. If you recognise yourself in my words, it may be wise to learn from my lesson. Despite the marketing, Newton is as cold and ruthless as any other corporation, if not more so. Their accomplished marketing makes them a wolf in sheep's clothing. I hope that in the future, the company's leadership may pause and reflect for long enough to realise the path they're going down.
