Acknowledgment: AEP is a large company. This is based on my experience within a single business unit. - Leadership is almost entirely based on networking and relationships; there are no established standards for any level of management, so promotions normally fall to those who are well connected. A quick glance at the prominent 'leader development' programs shows an overwhelming - almost exclusive - emphasis on networking and relationship building. I acknowledge that networking is an important tool, but it is the most essential skill for a member of management at AEP (instead of true leadership skills like generating trust, setting direction and goals, developing subordinates, etc.). Networking with leaders 3, 4, 5+ levels up is common and often encouraged. Networking at the local level with the intent of enhancing one's team is a good thing; networking 3, 4, 5+ levels up does little for one's team but helps with self advancement - which is toxic. This culture also prevents many people from speaking up or even reporting significant issues (i.e., discrimination) because it only takes one 'political' mistake to end your career aspirations. - Effective leadership training is largely non-existent. Leaders simply do not know how to lead, only manage (if that). For example, despite being here almost a decade, I have never received an articulated set of individual goals/expectations, nor have I received a professional development plan that would advise me on how to progress to the next level. The modus operandi is more 'management' than 'leadership' (i.e. the focus is primarily on just 'getting the job done'). I received leadership training from another organization and it was a night & day difference. We were taught things like subordinate development, setting direction, building plans, providing constructive feedback, accountability, recognition, motivating team members, engaging the workforce, training, etc. In addition, the leadership training I received previously was tiered, meaning the things I was taught as a manager were slightly different than what I was taught as a director (more emphasis was placed on strategy development, operations, and leading teams vs individuals); nothing significant like this tiered approach exists at AEP. - The lack of articulated individual goals/expectations means that evaluations are extremely biased and heavily influenced by relationships. In my 2022 evaluation, my boss gave me 14 areas in which I excelled and 0 areas for improvement - then rated my performance as "Standard". When pressed for an area of improvement, she responded that she could not come up with a single item. In addition, leaders are only required to perform one mid-year review, which in and of itself is inadequate (we performed monthly sessions at my previous employer). Despite only being required once per year, leaders generally treat it as a 'check the box' exercise that offers no real benefit to the subordinate (my last two mid-year reviews lasted less than 7 minutes combined). I compare this to how I do the reviews and there is a stark difference. I do them bi-monthly, am always well prepared, I provide constructive feedback on how to get the subordinate to the next level, and we review progress on their professional development plans. As a result, there are no surprises regarding their evaluations, they know their progress throughout the year, and evaluations are predicated entirely on established goals and expectations (that I set on my own initiative). My last mid-year review was not atypical by lasting just 3 minutes and simply being told to "keep up the great work you and your team are doing". - Planning is deplorable and amateurish. Even more problematic is that many leaders are convinced that they plan effectively, which strongly suggests that they have never experienced an effective planning process. Their plans usually consist of a spreadsheet of team or business unit goals. Also, it has become standard practice that no senior leader in our business unit thinks about annual goals and plans until Q2 of the year for which the plan/goals would be set (far too late). There is no established planning cycle or planning standards/requirements (even at the corporate level). Recent efforts have been made to generate something at the corporate level, but those are still nebulous. - Leaders use grass roots approaches frequently as a way to distance themselves from responsibility (i.e., 'well that is what the group recommended we do'). It is easy for leaders to find a viable scapegoat when they let others do all the work. When someone realizes in Q2 that annual goals haven't been set, an email is hastily sent to all managers requiring them to submit their team goals by a certain deadline. So, the entire set of business unit goals is created from the bottom up (i.e., backwards). This means corporate goals and priorities do not drive operations, and any link between corporate and small team goals is usually coincidental and/or made after the fact. - DEI is taken to extremes by some members of management. Our VP once said in a staff meeting that he would be fine with 50% or more diversity in the leadership team because executives put a premium on that metric (the unofficial, unwritten goal was 20%). When I asked my previous director about a particular job posting, he told me directly that despite being well qualified, I was "the wrong color and gender" for that job (actual quote because I wrote it down at the time). This is an indictment of the culture and not of him (my former boss). - In summary, leadership in general is primarily focused on their own preservation and advancement, and have not been trained to be effective leaders. Placing a premium on networking generates toxicity, suppresses the aspirations of people with true leadership abilities/potential, and ultimately limits team and group performance due to ineffective leadership. The company is generally stable, but this leadership framework and culture create substantial internal turbulence that can adversely impact jobs. The lack of a leader-driven vision, direction and goals facilitates autonomy amongst various groups (i.e. silos), making them highly resistant to any significant effort to centralize authority and/or unify efforts in the name of organizational alignment (such as a cohesive corporate strategy/plan). This autonomy also creates small fiefdoms within the company where the local senior leader, usually a VP, often grows their empire in whatever direction they desire, which almost always benefits their own aspirations instead of being focused on optimizing the company's effectiveness. Fred, or at least the current actions of Fred. In the past 40 years Fred Meyers did what so few can actually do; he started a company from nothing but an idea and decades of hard work to see it become a success. He's kept the company alive for all that time despite various crashes, recessions and dozens of other company killing events that so many succumbed to. He has been absolutely committed to the success of the company and works tirelessly to push it forward. He talks a lot about "Greatness" and becoming a "Great Company" and I believe it's genuine. So, where's the Con? Like so many other founders at this stage, Fred won't let go. Fred has not mentally moved into the "CEO" role and instead operates as if we're a one man show in the basement office of a factory in Astoria. He says he want to hire the best and greatest employees but then does not trust them to really do their job, micromanaging them to resignation. Should they speak up, they are promptly let go. The fact that this company is still alive is merely luck and good pricing. We desperately need a real marketing team that has actual experience, and they need to be allowed to make the changes this company so desperately needs. Too many decisions are being made by talentless-yes-men who do nothing but exacerbate the issue and allow Fred to operate in an echo-chamber.

This company looks nice and professional from the outside, a place you would be happy and comfortable to work. And it very well might be, in any other dept. However, the customs dept is in shambles. It is chronically understaffed and you are continually overworked. When I started, the dept was split into two sections, the admins and the entry writers. (Since then it has evolved after the merger and the structure is constantly changing while they try to figure out one that works) The head of the dept ( up until recently- Now Sal from Gori is above her), Lydia does not seem to make any of her own decisions and instead defers to the team lead of the admins, Carmen. Lydia has even sent out an email to the admins in error instructing Carmen to make certain decisions regarding the admins and just inform her what she decides. You will hear things being discussed and decisions being made and all of a sudden when Carmen yells and complains that she doesn’t like it, now it all only matters what she wants. Carmen is no higher up than any of the other team leads yet she is somehow in charge of almost every decision that is made. She will bully, lie to, lie about and gaslight every single employee as it serves her. All new team members are quietly warned or find out the hard way that Carmen will call you instead of emailing so that she doesn’t leave a paper trail. She will lie and say they what happened in the phone call is completely different than how it happened. Always follow up a convo with her with an email to document it, because it will always be her word against yours and yours means nothing. If you have any issue that you bring directly to Lydia or HR be prepared for a hissy fit by Carmen and retaliation. When I started there I was an admin under Carmen. You quickly learn the ‘training’ is completely inadequate and you learn nothing except how to do data entry. Which is fine, if that’s all the job was. There is a lot of procedural and regulation information that is needed to prepare customs entries. You will spend most of your days asking questions and trying to figure out things no one has told you yet Carmen expects that you should magically know. You also quickly learn that your team lead can not even accurately answer any of your questions, which is probably why she does not train anyone. The training is done by whatever admin she forces to do it, even the newest ones who know the least. You are forced to ask the other admins constantly for help no matter how long you’re there because you all have different knowledge and do things completely different because you were all trained by various people. It’s very hard to figure out a ‘right’ answer because most of the time it doesn’t seem like there is one. When the pandemic forced companies to WFH the company sent everyone home with their laptops to work from home. To provide context we worked with paper files in office with our laptops and 2 monitors due to the nature and volume of work. Then overnight we were left with just our small laptops to work on and had to transition to completely paperless work. Understandable under the conditions but we worked on solely a laptop for SIX MONTHS. And then it was ‘oh my god, we didn’t realize you guys only had laptops this whole time’ then we slowly got monitors to bring home. Which was not even the biggest issue. The issue is that we were told that overtime was NOT available, yet we were expected to finish all of our files and produce the same amount of work by the deadlines as if we had the same amount of resources available and could work just as fast. Almost every single employee was working 12-16 days regularly to keep up with the workload, for the same 8 hours of pay….we did not get to see our families or spend time with our children for the majority of the time even though we were all home together in quarantine. There was never any relief because there was no one to give the work to, we could all shift it around a bit but there was still far more work than we had employees and time. There was also multiple attempts to develop wfh strategies for the teams to work together to streamline this process for everyone. However, Carmen practices favoritism and if certain admin team members flat out refused to follow any new procedures the attitude was ‘oh well, that’s ____ for you. She doesn’t do what she doesn’t want to.’ It did not matter how hard it made anyone else’s job, she was given a complete pass. Once it was time for the end of the year 2020 bonuses we were rewarded for killing ourselves all year with a few hundred dollars and were told by Carmen that in a time when everyone was losing their jobs we were lucky to even have ours. The number of wildly inappropriate comments made by Carmen was never ending. She told a colleague she reminded her of an autistic kid. She makes racist jokes regularly. She has stormed through the office yelling about not trusting someone as far as they can throw them when they dared to raise an issue with the quality of the work produced by a favorite member of her team. She will make comments about colleagues’ sex lives, religion and political views. When a coworker had to put down her dog and was grieving she commented how ‘it was just a dog’. She will tell people who are overworked or have something to say that they are ‘having a breakdown’ and ‘just can’t handle it’ to completely dismiss the very real issue they and everyone else are having with the workload and quality of work. Most of these are said right in the office in ear shot of everyone around but sometimes they’re said in the GLASS office with gaps in the doors where she really somehow thinks we can’t all hear her making these comments or talking down to people. There was one time right after the merger where an admin was hired but because Carmen was not the one who made that decision she refused to speak to her or have her trained properly out of spite and then had her fired. While she was there the poor woman was iced out and made to feel unwanted and uncomfortable. I moved over to become an entry writer solely to have the chance to work under someone else. However, that was met with a whole host of other issues anyway. Not to mention that the admins giving us entry writers the entry packets were under Carmen and you weren’t allowed to complain if Carmen’s people gave you incomplete or incorrect packets, making your already hard job harder. The entry writer training was more informative and helpful. But that depended on who they got to train you and when. At one point, the only person they had training all the new entry writers was one particular team lead, on top of a full load of entry writer work AND being a team lead. I have no idea how she managed to do that as long as she did. I cannot speak for her or what the whole arrangement was. But I know she left because of it. We all witnessed her being absolutely overworked to the point of exhaustion. It was hard to watch. She tried to get everything done and help as many people as she could and worked all day and night. She was not able to give her full attention to train everyone and the training surely suffered and was incomplete and rushed or delayed. Through absolutely no fault of her own though. She asked for help and tried to refuse training new entry writers but was denied. It was yet another case of ‘just get it all done’. They have no problem piling far too much work on one person’s shoulders and then throwing their hands up and pretending they didn’t know they did that. They chronically let problems get so bad and for so long and wait until it blows up in everyone’s faces and then pretend they didn’t know about the issues….despite multiple complaints, examples, emails, warnings, and requests for help or changes. As entry writers we were also very overworked with far too many entries for one person to accurately get done. There was complete and total emphasis put on KPIs and not costing the dept money in demurrage, yet no where near enough support to get entries done on time and with accuracy. BUT they will constantly berate you with reminder emails about every single thing someone might be forgetting. Will they offer to help or retrain you or offer support??? No. But they will threaten to write you up at least once a week. It was clear they needed to keep getting more and more customers and more work but we didn’t get more entry writers to cover the work. Which also just means that if you did decide to actually use your vacation time you would come back to a HUGE mess because there was no one to fully cover your desk load while you were gone and you would come back to doing entries coming in THE SAME DAY you got back from vacation. It wasn’t even worth the headache to take time off. Everything was a rush. Everything was a mess. When you asked for real help or stated you literally could not complete as much work as they piled on you it fell on deaf ears. We heard regularly that ‘We know you’re overwhelmed, all of us are’. That obviously super inspiring pep talk doesn’t help much when you’re so overwhelmed that you miss one email for a delivery order and it goes down as a ‘strike’ on your record because you now cost the company money. At one point there was such a problem raised about the admins work being wrong and incomplete and the need to retrain them to get all the admins on the same page….they actually ended up having one on one meetings with all the entry writers to discuss. And do you know how that ended up? The one admin who provided the most complete and accurate work but was slower than the rest had her job threatened. The admins weren’t responsible for their work, the team leads weren’t responsible for making sure everyone was trained correctly…..the only responsibility for everything fell to the entry writers. The constant stress from working there was not worth the money. I feel like I gave up a few extra years of my life with the constant level of fear and stress we all felt. The pay was well below industry standard and as such they could not find anyone with experience to fill entry writer positions because of it. They are keen to hire within (moving admins to entry writers) because they can now pay an entry writer the absolute bare minimum because they are inexperienced. The long story short is that they are outdated and resistant to any helpful changes (thank you Carmen), they underpay, knowingly overwork you, exhibit clear favoritism, ignore your cries for help, berate you, and then punish you for being overworked. The environment is that all the worker bees need to be quiet and not talk too much meanwhile Lydia and Carmen will be yelling about anything and everything all the time….sometimes at our teammates, in front of everyone. But, they will wrap it all up a pretty bow with monthly thirsty Thursdays and a trip to a winery for team building. I would never in a million years subject myself to working there ever again or refer a friend to do so. Since the beginning of January they have lost an average of 1 person every two weeks. If that’s not a testament to how poorly the dept is run, idk what is. At one point they started to panic and brought in HR to find out what the problem with the dept was. However, nobody was listened to, everything that was said was dismissed and shut down and anything that was promised as change has not happened yet.

Growth within the company is actually possible and is an open conversation that can be had with managers and development plans are in place to support your goals. -Senior leadership are people centric and know that improving our culture is always work in progress, there is no stopping point. -Building a community -Changing lives through better hearing is at the forefront of what every person does on a daily basis. -New leadership and restructures within the past year have made a positive impact towards not only common goals but moral in the company. -Meetings, trainings, and town halls are fruitful. -Cultivating a community of diversity. -Our values really are the core of what we do and are represented well by leadership.

Knowing my company is helping make it simpler for more people to access hearing care, and as a result, better communicate with family and friends makes the work worthwhile. - There is transparent and consistent direction from the top leadership. - Performance objectives are clearly linked to the company priorities, taking any guesswork out of where to focus or how to be successful. - There is open and welcome communication with senior executives, who truly care about the client experience in our centers and the hearing care professionals providing the care. - There is an advisory board of HCPs setup because the leadership truly wants to understand and have the audiologist and hearing instrument specialist point-of-view, before making key decisions that impact the centers. - I appreciate the focus on diversity, equity and inclusion, backed by a specific DEI leadership role and a committee of employees empowered to bring change. - Employees are encouraged to share their professional development plans and take advantage of various development and training programs with others across the broader WS Audiology organization.

I really appreciate the "open ears" at the company. Ideas and insights are taken seriously. We have a generally positive and interested group of people at HearUSA that makes working here so much nicer. Management takes all feedback seriously, there are regular discussions about the feedback and what can be improved. The President is constantly traveling and visiting all areas of the company personally. He is very active in the operations, but not in the way. There are all of the general things that many good companies are now also offering: monthly pot lucks, exercise groups, snacks in the office... but much of these things are organized by employees and supported by the company. Very refreshing as it doesn't feel forced. A good mix of office and remote, where many prefer remote only. The offices are new and super nice to work from, with great and friendly IT support people, huge kitchen / break area, and something always going on. Regular training, very transparent and open updates from management, lots of communication, successes are celebrated and issues / problems are openly communicated and worked on together.

Leadership has provided great structure to help us stay focused on our mission. Very thoughtful and knowledgeable leaders and employees here that care about each other as people, not just employees. There are tons of contests for our in-center employees that create extra engagement and excitement - as well as some contests that are focused on the wellbeing of the individual. Unlike other employers in this space, you can see many examples where this is a collective effort of all focused on our company mission. Between the HCP ad board, CES ad board, and the other instances where we call on HCPs and CES to help be leaders on certain initiatives - HearUSA does a phenomenal job at giving employees the opportunity to be leaders and help shape the mission of the company. These are just some of the things that are creating a great culture at HearUSA.

A great company that can balance short and long term goals. Employee focused, trustworthy and service driven. Excellent leadership team that listens and values employee feedback but most of all takes the necessary steps when improvement is needed. Positive company culture exists due to their business strong values and ethics. I am going into my 6th year with the company and as much positivity as I feel about our leadership team, I have been truly blessed to have such an amazing direct manager who has mentored, guided and encouraged me in my 6 years of employment. She is irreplaceable. The best company I have worked for throughout my career.

The company values employee feedback and has established multiple forums to ensure employees have the opportunity to shape the future of HearUSA such as the HCP Advisory Board. The vision and priorities for the company are clear and transparent throughout the organization. Major investments have been made over the last year to grow and develop employees and the future for HearUSA is bright!

Comparing my work life experience to other companies I've worked for in the past, HearUSA stands out among the best I have experienced. A consistent 8:30-5:00 schedule, with all major holidays & weekends off. They have increased their starting pay in recent years to be more aligned with changing times, they offer great health benefits, and my personal favorite is the PTO structure. We use a PTO time accrual system, and this works much better for me personally than the set amount of days most companies offer. The company has great values, and I enjoy being in a line of work that really makes a positive impact on the lives of others. HearUSA also offers great career paths for employees who wish to grow with the same company. From personal experience, to watching other co-workers around me grow into new roles, HearUSA really does like to promote from within. Since starting with HearUSA, I have recommended three friends for positions, all of which were added to their respective teams. When telling them about the company and overall experience, I told them "I can honestly say in all the time I've been here, I can count on one hand how many times I've gone home for the day "upset". You'll go home feeling fulfilled more than anything". All three of my friends who joined our company all came back to me a few months later and said "you were so right". They're all still with the company more than a year, and they're all growing into different career paths within the company as well.

HearUSA offers attractive benefits to its employees: PTO, Health insurance, commission. Our manager is constantly looking for ways to work more efficiently and always make sure the task we are assigned it benefits the team (which is GREAT). I love this department and the manager I have to report too!!
allCons: -There have been many changes over the years, with those changes there have been some difficult times for many. Thankfully, HearUSA is on the upswing, the atmosphere feels refreshing, and it shows in our productivity and results! -Communication is a work in progress.

HearUSA in recent years has gone through many changes internally. With those changes we've tried things that have worked, and things that haven't. It can be a lot to take in when things change, but I think the current management teams we have in place are doing a fantastic job navigating all the new updates and changes. The only two things I would really like to see further improve are communications across all departments, and mutual respect amongst different departments. Part of the changes we have been through are to be a more united company, rather than the separate teams we had been more exclusively working with. I would say progress overall has been made, but I look forward to watching it further progress towards the goal of being a full united front.

The management also has favoritism, which creates a type of competition ambiance within employees to see who’s the best seller, preferred more by others and the managers. If you aren’t liked by other coworkers, they won’t really work fairly with you in distributing the customers evenly within all on the sales floor. Hence, you might be lower in sales compared to them, earn less commission, and be sent to work in the stock room to make way for the “best” sellers to work on the storefront and makes the daily goal. They will work with each other fairly within their cliques, but with newcomers or people they don’t like, they will have an unfair “first come, first serve” mentality-making them first most of the time. The best sellers will try to hog and hunt for potentially rich customers or those coming in making big purchases that have 3-4 digit receipt totals, instead of helping every incoming customer equally regardless of their background. Those with better sales will be given better work schedules, aka evenings when there’s an influx of customers compared to early shifts. The pay is also very low, making commission on sales the only way to advance in your financial situation, adding another pressure to make sales. I recall employees worried about living check to check and not getting enough work hours or getting hours that didn’t work with their school and life schedules. Eventually all of the best seller employees quit one by one, shortening a staff of 9 to 5 in the span of 2-3 weeks, making it tricky for managers to keep up with lack of staff.

Where to begin! This company used to be one that was completely member focused, employee led, and treated people as humans. Now? Well, there has been a fall of priorities. Ask any member who has been with the company for more than ten years, and they’ll tell you the differences—the increase in fee structure, the lack of leeway given to members who have fallen on hard times, and the overall sales nature the company has incorporated. Senior management is a closed door in terms of willingness to hear new ideas and desire to be better. Most of them have been in their roles for 10+ years and they have zero desire to change. They gaslight their manager into becoming bullies in order to be promoted and show more loyalty to themselves and their image than they do to any of the employees. (With the exception of Nora who was recently promoted. I haven’t worked with her since she became a senior exec, but the experience I did have with her is phenomenal. My only hope is that she can lead the way for some of the other execs) Branch operations is a disaster. They are consistently having panics about being out of compliance and then make the employees pay for it when in reality the branch staff are overworked and for the most part under paid. Now, I say for the most part because if you’re a lifer who has been there for more than 5-10 years, more than likely the co-worker that was hired a week ago makes much more than you do. Now as for specialty areas in the back office—all of them are severely underpaid. When I left back in 2019, I received a 40% pay bump and was at an entry level position within my specialty. It doesn’t matter if you show them what the market standard is for compensation. They say they have plans for you, but in reality that’s only a gimmick to get you to comply and not ask questions. As far as they’re concerned, you’re disposable and as soon as you ask questions or try to hold them accountable, they railroad you until you quit or fire you. During covid they advertised that they didn’t lay anyone off, but what they failed to mention is that they had a mass firing for anyone who was “not a high performer”! So many people lost their jobs in the middle of a pandemic and didn’t receive any severance because they were fired. So I’m not sure exactly what they’re proud of. All of this is to say, this company has some of the best people I have ever met, but if they don’t get it together and start taking care of their employees, it won’t last. Listen to what your employees are telling you. INVEST IN TECHNOLOGY THAT WORKS and stop paying the minimum amount and cheating out routine maintenance. If you value your mental health, steer clear of this place. The benefits are decent, but the pay and the unrealistic expectations they have will drive you into the ground. It makes me sad because I used to genuinely love working there, but as time went on I saw what they did to people and the cavalier attitude they had about kicking anyone out that didn’t fit their “culture”. Like other reviews mention, the rapid changes have left me personally feeling a lot of distrust for those in charge. Any concerns that are brought up by employees in company meetings, all hand calls, etc, feel glossed over and barely answered or addressed. The fact that negative Glassdoor reviews are posted every single day is a testament to the current tone and overall feel of the employees. I feel like I am working for a completely different employer than I did when I started. Forrester used to pride itself on authenticity and transparency, but now just tries to sweep it's employee's thoughts, opinions and concerns under the rug without addressing them.

Massive disconnect between frontline sales, Product & pricing teams, and Management and Executive leadership. “Customer-obsessed” was no more once the economy started to take a downturn and buyers cut their AR budgets. “We’re increasing entry-level pricing by 50%” was Forrester’s response. This made it impossible for reps to hit their quarterly and annual numbers much less come CLOSE to hitting Winner’s Circle. I used to be proud of the culture yet the layoffs showed that Forrester actually views employees as numbers.

A lot of us have lost confidence in leadership during the pandemic. An obsession with stock price and CV growth has meant that non-CV teams aren’t getting support and creates a “second-class citizen” dynamic and lack of trust across teams. Communication during latest layoffs was very poorly handled (get George some PR coaching!) and promotions/raises have been suspended for the second time in three years. Also, we had been told consistently that the reason salaries aren’t being adjusted for inflation was that inflation was thought to be temporary. It’s been more than a year now, so we’ve effectively been given large pay cuts with the earliest possible raises still six months away. There are also rumors that the company is going to be forcing employees back to the office, which is suspicious given the CEO’s personal investments in office real estate.

The executive team flipped a switch, going against the empathetic image they spent years building up for the company. I guess it was fake at its core because the empathy is gone. Employees are now just inputs. Executives have closed their ears and eyes and no longer listen to employees. That's not going well because morale is bad (layoffs and then a fast, unexplained return to office hybrid mandate, plus financial targets being hard to hit). There's an obsession with "contract value" (CV) that doesn't make a lot of sense because CV is a financial metric that means nothing to customers or employees. I have lost faith in the vision, if there is one.

People are the best and worst part of this company. Lots of tenured people who were very happy working here when things were good and money was flowing freely for unlimited travel, bonuses, employee swag, etc. Since the business conditions in the market have forced many of those perks to slow or stop, there are now a lot of those same people acting like a two-year-old who isn't getting what they want. Is it a perfectly run organization? No. But is it a horrible company to work for? Not from my perspective when compared to a lot of others out there. I can count on one hand the number of colleagues in my previous industry that saw no increase in their benefits costs year over year and who have any bonus structure left in place.

Huge premiums are offered for picking up extra shifts d/t absurd staffing deficit. allPros: Very communicative and puts the employee first

- You will do well at RTI if you have an entrepreneurial spirit. There are lots of opportunities to pursue your own professional development, but you have to be proactive in pursuing them. - RTI really cares about the well being of employees over profits when compared to industry competitors (e.g., pay is competitive and I've never seen layoffs, despite the fluctuating nature of federal contract work). - It's the most flexible company I've ever worked at, making it easy to have a good work/life balance (e.g., remote work, flexible hours, part-time, etc.)

Your experience at RTI is hugely dependent on your manager and the team you roll up under. RTI has several different business units which each have their own cultures. I worked in the administrative/corporate BU, specifically in Corporate Communications. We worked with people in most of the BUs on their various communication needs, so I also got a good sense of how the different spaces operated. In terms of Marketing/Comms teams, I would say SSES was the best BU to work in and with and IDG was the worst. Corp Comms fell somewhere in the middle. Overall, RTI is an EXCELLENT place to work. Great benefits, great company culture, extremely flexible/reasonable WFH policy, strong organizational focus on EDIB and opportunities for self-starters to get involved in things like Employee Resource Groups and form meaningful relationships across the institute outside their departments. I really enjoyed the CEO. He seems like a kind, thoughtful man who genuinely cares and wants to leverage his position to make a positive impact. He’s very reasonable and even-tempered and has provided a lot of support for RTI’s EDIB staff to grow and shape the company culture. He also makes an effort to remember the names of lower level employees too, which sounds minor but I think is a big deal for someone is a position of power at such a huge company. He did a good job acknowledging and honoring the disappointment that many employees felt when he, another straight, white male, was first appointed as CEO. He didn’t shy away from the hard questions or seek to downplay them, which gave me a lot of respect for him. There are more amazing people working at RTI than I can count, and the work RTI is doing across its many practice areas is incredibly impactful and important in so many ways. I loved so many things about working there. Get a solid manager on a solid team, and you’ll have a great experience.
The RTP campus is in a good location.

Like so many large organizations, RTI struggles to be nimble. The many channels you have to go through to get anything done by the book can be exhausting, slowing down productivity and reducing efficiency. That’s probably why they also have such a problem with departments “going rogue” and doing things outside of the approved channels or methods in order to do them faster. That being said though, it was always odd to me how siloed the various BUs and departments were at RTI. Many departments just sort of did their own things without any pushback from leadership. Department leads would even hire their own staff to complete work that was supposed to be done by existing staff in other departments, and no one would stop them. IDG in particular was known for this. This led to the right hand often not knowing what the left hand was doing within the same organization, resulting in haphazard, inefficient processes.

Employees are overworked and underpaid. Zero work-life balance. Morale is at an all time low. There's not enough work to go around which leads to competition and backstabbing. allPros: CSIS is one of the most prestigious think tanks in the world, and on a day-to-day basis you see both U.S. and foreign officials and thinkers coming to CSIS to add their perspectives to the intellectual mix. There are no predetermined right answers in this bipartisan environment, and there's a lot of great discussion. Everyone I've worked with is passionate about making a positive difference in their field. There's a great DEI program (5-star effort), and the Center is making progress on hiring more senior women, although progress on hiring senior-level researchers of color is slower.

As an intern or senior-level employee, you are likely to have a positive experience at CSIS, but this company can be an absolute nightmare for junior-level employees. Your experience as a junior staffer, however, is largely dependent on the director of the team you will be joining. However, CSIS is notorious for hiring toxic, depraved, egotistical directors. There is room for professional growth and upward movement, but really pointless when employees aren't being treated with basic dignity/respect. DLIA is taking "steps" to address the lack of diversity, but it's all at face value. No institutional changes are being made under the current director, Nicole Aandahl, who is known throughout the. center for her unprofessionalism.

There is little to no communication from top leaders on the struggles within the market, the changes the organization is going through and how leadership is working to protect its employees’ livelihoods. I believe there has been one solitary email from the executive level in the last two months. Meanwhile, turnover is escalating with top talent disappearing in droves. Layoffs do not appear to be widespread, but it is devastating to morale to watch some of the most enduring talent lose their positions with no explanation from leadership. Perhaps the most egregious decision Berlin has made recently is the postponement of annual salary reviews. These are normally expected in Q1, but they have been delayed by three months. Leadership has offered no substantive explanation (if I recall, the official explanation is that it would allow the presumptive leaders to focus on “growth”). To do this to your employees amid today’s inflation is simply cruel. Almost every individual at Berlin is juggling the workload of two or more people, and Berlin continues to expect this level of performance without appropriately compensating their employees. I have no idea if the company has a bright future as leadership does not provide any level of transparency. There is a pervasive fear throughout the company that seems to grow by the week. allPros: NWDLS is a fast pace, rapidly growing environmental laboratory. I have been working at NWDLS for almost 10 years now, some of the employees have been here for nearly 30 years. That to me speaks volumes of the company's culture. It is great working environment, team and management. It’s a faster paced environment because our clients must report to the TCEQ and there are State deadlines to meet. At NWDLS, there is lots of training and opportunity to grow and move laterally or up. Like any workplace, you are expected to do your work correctly and in a timely manner. There are clear expectations and SOPs to follow because we are in the environmental and public safety business. At the same time, we are still encouraged to have fun and be creative. NWDLS provides job security, as we were not affected by COVID or more recently, drops within the economy. I report to my manager, but she does not micromanage me, as my manager trusts me to do my job that I have been trained for. When I have questions, there is always someone I can ask. Even when my supervisor is not in, she is always checking her emails and answering them. The owners of NWDLS are down to earth and they are empathetic if you have a home situation, they will go out of their way to help you. I have worked many places before and I have been working for a long time, but I have never seen kindness and generosity that NWDLS has shown me. Derek, who is one of the owners, even goes collects samples when needed. NWDLS empowers their employees, encourages personal growth, independence, confidence, and they want to see their employees to step up and take charge. Fun company webinars often showcased the musical talents of the many creative individuals who worked at Roland. For many, the work was Remote since 2020 which was great to not have to commute. However, I think there are many positives that come from in-person collaboration and maybe a hybrid model could benefit people. I have to say some positive things about the Director of Human Resources of Roland Americas. She loves her job and is naturally gifted for the role. She has the ability to see potential in people and is passionate about their possibilities. She is optimistic. She is tuned into the needs of others. where do I even begin? the 5% staff discount is an absolute joke; even with it, i can't afford to buy the products i help produce. the abysmal pay. the current living wage is $27 per hour, and steadily rising due to inflation, and yet our wages remain stagnant. let it be known that employees were expecting a pay rise in 2020, and didn't receive said pay rise until 2022 due to 'unprecedented times', even though business profits skyrocketed during this time (& this was an 85c/15% pay rise that they delayed). the company culture. fear is used as a weapon, striking down from the upper management all the way down to your casual employee. bullying and harassment are rampant problems, as is favouritism, but we're expected to be too stupid to notice this. the faux 'mindfulness' crap upper management try to constantly shove down our throats. depressed?? write down three things you're grateful for today, and you'll feel better!!! definitely couldn't be depressed due to the subpar working conditions, so let's trivialise our workers mental and physical health problems!! we're severely understaffed, I cannot remember the last time I didn't work with a skeleton crew, and yet the pressure to do more in less time is always increasing (and when bringing up these issues, you get told "everyone else is coping, what's your problem"). we're all exhausted constantly.

Somethings I curse myself for working at Amazon is that you're within the Amazon programming ecosystem. It is true you deal with Amazon specific tooling, and thus is harder to have that knowledge transfer to different systems used by different companies. I'd say the tooling is based *off* of those existing tools, but specialized for mass consumption within Amazon. - Amazon specific tooling hides away all the nitty gritty and sterilizes the development environment to the point that it takes extra learning to adapt to more stock industry offerings.

Lack of growth. Amazon has a lot of people at one level reporting to individuals at the same level. This creates a huge hurdle for advancement in that most managers aren't going to push someone under them for promotion before they themselves are promoted. Some of Amazon's culture also gets a thumbs-down, IMO. Since joining the company, I've attended numerous meetings where we would debate trivial concepts and ideas ad nauseum for hours only to arrive at what was the most obvious way forward from the onset. Amazon has created an environment where everyone has a voice, but it comes at the expense of slowing down the decision-making process.

The work is hard. You will be sore the first few days. You have to watch your attendance, you earn time every shift, 30 mins, an hour, etc. Anna you can use the time to come in late or leave early, but if you get into negative time you get terminated. I've heard that if that happens you should just resign so you'll be eligible to work other Amazon jobs. I work at a logistics center instead of a fulfillment center and it gets HOT while you're working, f hot. During the COVID-19 pandemic Amazon employees were considered essential workers.

They promise much and deliver very little. There approach to safety is without logic, threat assessment and they are ready to full the exact letter of the rules - with no understanding of them. If you wear an Orange vest, you are nothing... Infact the if you look at most photos from warehouses, you mainly see happy smiling yellow vest wearing people. This is because they are all friends and you are promoted based on friendship rather than knowledge and experience. HR seems to not understand standard working practices within ISO 9001 in the slightest. They say it's a zero threat or bullying environment and then spend weeks threatening you with write-ups or firing. Training is absolutely the worst and most ineffective I have ever witnessed in my life. People do not last long here.

You'll probably feel that here everybody is working for themselves foremost. It's because promotion's pretty hard -- you won't get promoted so easily. Takes luck, hard work, and time. Since you need to prove it. Also you might not be able to convince everybody that you're right. They might not respond to you. Lots of people are also overworked. Poor work life balance if you're not careful. Also it take a while to get ramped up to Amazon and a few years you might feel you didn't achieve much. The training in amazon is really nice and you'll find they make a lot of sense but not all managers are able to practice it to heart. Though it's hard to master in the first place. Compared to other companies this place is going to have less weird and poor managers.

-Expect to work 50-60 hours a week if you want to succeed -Poor work/life balance -High turnover rate, don't be surprised if you have 5 different managers you report to in the span of a calendar year -Due to high turnover and the high likelihood of management not backfilling, expect to take on other people's roles & responsibilities along with your own -Amazon expects you to be a self-starter and self-sufficient, if you are not then you will be viewed as a low performer -Expect projects/initiatives that your team has worked on for months/years to abruptly be stopped and thrown in the trash in favor of another project/initiative that leadership would like to work on, so don't get emotionally attached to your work -Employee feedback is usually never addressed with actionable steps

Overall, ServiceNow is an outstanding place to work, offering a challenging, fulfilling career, and a supportive work environment. ABCD pays case managers with Bachelor’s degree a despicable wage (30k). At the time I worked there, had I either been married or had a kid, I would have qualified to receive their services myself. You sadly cannot afford to work there, not even as a young college grad (hello student loans!) -the work environment is highly stressful because you are often doing the work of 2+ people (running the front desk, attending food pantry, seeing clients, maintaining files/keeping up with paperwork, etc.) -as is typical in the caring professions, it is easy to get disheartened by the daily work. Providing transactional services while knowing that the families/individuals needed so much more was very difficult to come to terms with. For instance, we knew that the allotted food we were allowed to give out would realistically last 3-4 days, and families were only allowed to come ONCE A MONTH. I also had diapers to donate but could only give out 2-3 per family. Infants go through ~10 a day!!! -because of the above cited reasons, the sites have incredibly high turnover rates and are constantly hiring/training new people -the operations managers have a weird obsession with the way that employees dress. I once wore jeans with a nice blouse and I was given a speech about how unprofessional that was. I was also explicitly told I was encouraged to wear heels. I was young and naive, but now wish I could tell those folks (male supervisors) to try wearing heels and go back and forth to the food pantry all day.

Lower-level staff members are often overworked and underpaid. Tenure and age are often valued over work effectiveness and/or lessons learned from outside of the organization. Decisions are often slow going and not backed up by real strategy, but also often carried out by those not making the decisions. Work-from-home policies are not set or uniform -leaders often work from home but their staff members are advised they cannot. Communication is siloed and often times important information, scheduling, or deadlines are not communicated until the very last minute -causing undo stress.

I was part of the North America layoffs for SAP. I don't feel all too bad, because I thought SAP was rather courteous about it - given the recent news of other companies' layoffs, I got a message ahead of time, a month of sort-of not-really "employment" (to look for another role in the company, if possible), and general help with my sort-of not-really "unemployment". I mention all this because SAP, and I, prided the company's "family" values. It did seem the company cared about the employees. During the pandemic and after there wasn't a point where my arm was twisted and I was forced to do so-and-so. My team and I worked at our own pace and took the breaks we needed for our mental health - and we worked better for it. While I considered other opportunities in the past, this culture really stuck out to me and I felt this would have been rare in other companies. All the compensation in the word really doesn't touch upon this.
allCons: need to wait for the promotion(very long time).

Teams are also now left with too few resources to accomplish essential tasks which will put increased strain and stress on those who remain.

- like any company, some leaders exhibit bad behavior but are not held accountable. That being said, I was bitter over not being bitter. I had been re-assigned to a different project last year and it was intolerably difficult to affect any change. There is a prevalent sense the company should be Agile, but no one, with any influence, was willing to criticize very slow, essentially Waterfall practices. My team and other teams were re-assigned but we had little training and were given few tasks to do; it would take several months to actually get features - fairly small in anyone's definition - shipped. New projects would be planned and talent would not be assigned. It was a huge waste of resources. Meanwhile, our competitors were soldiering ahead. In this environment, one inevitably thinks about their own career. This hurt because I like the company. I understand Rome wasn't built in a day. And, with Scrum, it's not about blaming anyone. But that's my honest opinion. My hope is that other domains in SAP take the actions to be and remain competitive.

Now we have to choose between losing vacation or failing to meet sponsor expectations/deadlines if we use weeks of vacation with zero notice. Modernization of financial tools was rushed and poorly planned by management. The financial worker bees busted their butts but were shoveling against the tide. The contractors were scared at how fast they were pushed to get their software working for MITRE. And the recent RIF of FAA supporting employees was done with one day notice by auto-gen email when those same skills are needed on the defense side which is hiring! No opportunity for them to find a new position on the defense side. Leadership at the top is making decisions that have made me lose confidence in their ability to lead.

Said initiative's poor execution has resulted in end-of-year funding shortfalls, an abortive five-day November furlough, reduced holidays/vacation time, and a handful of quiet under-the-radar micro layoffs, all presented under the guise of "We're in good shape, we're a very successful company, check us out on Google and Glassdoor, you'll see how competitive we are." Hundreds of staff are currently scrabbling to find billable work, due to a mixture of paperwork logjams and billable-cost overruns. Another staff reduction is clearly imminent, despite management's demurrals and evasions.

The CEO always wants his decisions implemented quickly, which means care is not exercised in implementation. A reorganization in 2020 led to a reduction in the number of women and POC in positions in management and senior managers appointing their friends to positions because time could not be taken to do a thorough vetting process. Senior leadership impulsively added Juneteenth and Election Day as paid holidays and are now in the process of reducing the number of holidays, presumably to bring costs down. The guidance on remote work has been all over the map despite a large number of workers pre-pandemic being remote already. The CEO said in an all-hands that (paraphrased) collaboration is hard when people won't leave their basements, which was obnoxious and shows a clear disconnect between how people work and how senior management thinks people work. I've been considering leaving for a while. Most recent action by the company may tip the scales completely.

Current leadership is seriously out of touch or is intentionally trying to drive away people with more than 5 years invested in the company. Communication is terrible. As I mentioned, this place started changing around 2020 following a major reorganization. Senior leadership decisions, direction, and communication are reactionary, confusing, inconsistent, and at times detrimental to employee morale. All signs indicate that the company is going through financial challenges. They cut our PTO and holidays and are suddenly doing random webinars on what makes up our overhead and fringe rates. We have grown in number of bodies but I don’t see that we are growing in skills and knowledge. And with all this growth, a lot of staff are short on project work. There are just so many things off right now and all together they make for a negative experience as an employee.

Would not recommend for new grads or people moving from fast paced companies who enjoy making impact.

First off, the job description was incredibly misleading and did not give any proper insight to the actual unsafe and underpaid duties of this job. There was little to no training, guidance, or support from management before being thrown into a caseload of 30+ clients with mental illness diagnoses and substance abuse struggles. As a woman straight out college, I felt underprepared and unsafe on numerous occasions- basically every day. You will drive by yourself to some of those most crime-ridden parts of St. Louis with no preparation or safe-guard measures. They reimburse you for gas, but the thousands of miles and wear and tear you will put on your vehicle driving all over St. Louis (most days anywhere from South County, to downtown, to North County driving clients around) is not worth it. In addition, you were expected to see 3-5 clients in-person a day, yet management was not expected to see clients. Management DID expect for you to see them in-person, ONLY work 8-4:30 pm (no earlier or later so they didn't have to pay you more), find time to chart every interaction, phone call (with clients, doctors, therapists, pharmacists, etc.) , and so much more while you're spending at least 3 hours everyday just driving. There was genuinely just not enough time in the day to get everything done that was unrealistically expected of you, but my manager always had time to remind me I was not doing "everything" I was supposed to do in a day. Not even to mention that while you're with one client, you have 10 other clients calling and texting you and screaming and cussing at you for not providing immediate service to them (and you have to chart EVERY phone call with them, even if it's them just cussing you out, which takes up just more of your time.) Most days you will basically just feel like a taxi service to them. The verbal abuse and unsafe conditions you will face in this job is absolutely, under no circumstances, worth the laughable $17.32/ hr they pay you. I couldn't afford one-bedroom rent in St. Louis and had to move back in with my parents. The only reason I left my previous, livable wage job for this one was honestly to just get further experience in the social services/psychology field before applying to PhD programs. I endured this job for 2 months before I mentally and physically could not function anymore and I quit. I now do nothing in the social services or the psychology field because this job was that detrimental to my well-being. Save yourself the mental and physical anguish. You will be stressed, unsafe, unappreciated, and underpaid in this role.

This lack of proper workforce planning negatively impacts productivity and contributes to a stressful work environment. Lack of Ethical Standards: Cvent demonstrates a concerning lack of ethical standards in its business practices. The company prioritizes short-term gains over ethical considerations, resulting in questionable decisions that compromises integrity and customer trust. However, the suits decided one day that they were going to change the pay structure to base trainer leveling on the number of clients a trainer maintains. As of the date of this review, trainers need to keep 55 sessions every two weeks in order to maintain level 3, and your sessions are counted in order to reassess your pay rate every 3 months. Ultimately, if any of your clients leave or go on vacation, there goes your pay , your pay rate, and your insurance if you had it in the first place. companies.name: Altum Health
allPros: If you miss the pre-pandemic days of being in a depressing, windowless office 80% of the time while toiling away in a grey cubicle then this is the job for you!
allCons: I'll start by saying this is the most toxic workplace I've ever encountered. Why? Well, as with many private sector health care jobs the CSR's are stressed out, overworked and underpaid. Altum Health cares so little about them that they were called back into the office 2 months into the pandemic, long before vaccines were available, and forced to work in close, enclosed quarters with only a thin mask to protect them. This is a job that could easily be done from home, but the company refuses to invest in software to route calls to worker's laptops or personal devices. Not surprisingly the workers were given no bonus pay or extra incentive for literally risking their lives. These kind of working conditions create an atmosphere of intense pressure, low level hostility and resentment among the workers there. Fun! Also keep in mind that despite the job title this is both a call center job and medical admin job at the same time. It's very difficult to get both jobs done in 8 hours so I frequently saw coworkers doing overtime, which though not required is necessary if you don't want to fall behind. Guess what? It's also unpaid. The management structure is ridiculous. There are 4-6 CSR's at any given time and most of them report to different managers. Since these managers often work down the hall or on other floors they have little clue what is going on with you and your work. While I was there I saw my manager in person about every 3-4 weeks. They farm out most supervisory duties to "Office Admins", who are also overworked and have to combine supervising with CSR and other duties due to the chronic understaffing. Many of them behave like obnoxious andpetty high school hall monitors, abusing the pathetically small amount of authority they have been given. If you (unwisely) decide to take this job have a look at the UHN website, where you can compare the pay and benefits YOU receive to those given to the Union employees at UHN. Then you'll know how exploited you are. Altum Health is of course non-union. In closing I'd say look at how long the CSR job ad has been up? I've seen it for at least the last 6 months. Don't you wonder why they have such a problem hiring and retaining people?

They have also listened to feedback and done what they could to narrow the salary gap. When I made a case that software engineering (the design of new software) was a different skill set from technical support work, they went to bat for me and created a software engineering position that paid a much better salary, and have included both raises and merit increases during my time here.

Those pros stated, there's not much *reason* to do well and succeed, because you won't be paid well. UK knows their benefits are great so they use them as an excuse to lag behind the rest of the market in pay. Outside hires will do best, because UK recognizes they kind of have to compete; if you're an internal hire moving from one area to another, your experience will be functionally cut in half, which for many employees means they get dropped into the entry levels of a salary grade even if they're mid-career. IT recently performed some salary adjustments, but those are largely a joke—in my case I received a ~12% bump, which put me right about where I should have been when I *started* in the role four years ago. Also worth noting, for anyone considering coming to UK Healthcare, future pay increases will "merit-based" but not in any meaningful sense. They are also using that new merit-based model as an excuse to eliminate the previous across the board increases all employees not on probation would receive. So now your performance matters, and you might get rewarded for it, but if you don't you'll be out of luck when cost-of-living goes up.

As a former employee of FTD, I feel compelled to share my experience with others who may be considering a career at this company. While FTD has a long-standing reputation in the floral industry, I cannot say the same for its executive leadership team. In my time at FTD, I witnessed many members of the executive leadership team making rash decisions without thoroughly considering the potential consequences. These decisions often resulted in negative outcomes for the company and its employees. Additionally, many members of the executive leadership team appeared to lack the necessary qualifications for their positions, which led to a lack of direction and focus at the company. One particular issue that stood out to me was the executive leadership team's tendency to embark on partnerships they couldn't uphold. This left FTD in precarious positions, and often it was up to subordinates to pick up the pieces and try to salvage the partnerships. Furthermore, I witnessed members of the executive leadership team frequently shifting blame onto their subordinates when things went wrong. This created a toxic work environment and a lack of trust between leadership and employees. Overall, while FTD may have a recognizable name in the floral industry, I would caution anyone considering a career with this company to thoroughly research the company's leadership and direction before making any commitments.

You get down and dirty, mix paint, and check out customers all day. After you do this long enough they place you at a store as an Assistant Manager. Then you get paid the same as you do as a MT, but you are bonus eligible, which you can make a grand or so a quarter typically, but all depending on your stores performance. You can get 0 bonus if you do not hit the budget set for you. Also this "yearly salary" is accounting for you to work 44 hours a week. You are an hourly employee as a MT and Assistant manager. The last 4 hours of your week are scheduled overtime and you are paid time and a half, which if done every week consistently adds up to the 49,000. If you take vacation you are losing out on your last hours which means you are missing out on your highest paid hours. Store managers are salary but expected to work 48 hours a week. Often they end up working more than that for no extra pay.

I took the position based on what the recruiter said to me, but after weeks of employment my supervisor told me that none of the recruiter's promises were valid. I expressed my displeasure at how poorly I had been treated, specifically about being lied to about the compensation. I was told that my contract is all that matters, and all of the promises made by the recruiter can and will be reneged. I was gobsmacked to hear this, but both my supervisor and his supervisor confirmed that whether or not I had been lied to was irrelevant. My supervisor ended our last meeting by telling me that I was not welcome at the company, though his supervisor immediately walked that back. My only recourse is to keep working, and warn others against joining an unscrupulous company such as this. I am shocked at how I've been treated, but you won't be after reading this!

The benefits are exceptionally good, for what is needed. Healthcare for me that would have cost well over $15,000 on many non-Tesla plans was achieved for well under $1,500 out of pocket, during my time of employment. Let us face it, in America, ultimately the good healthcare plan is what you need, the house with the Spanish style architecture and palm trees is what you want, yet the top-notch employee benefits are what you need that are there at organizations like Tesla who hire direct, and not with organizations that do the 12 month contracts or 15 month contracts through a 3rd party. Given the wages are not high due to the industry having tighter profit margins compared to other Silicon Valley businesses (SaaS, IT consulting, Internet companies), I hoped for some sort of tuition reimbursement, yet I cannot just expect that any company is going to foot the bill of my education loan debt; they did offer benefits for refinancing education debt, as well as other debt. Note: I can only speak to my role as being direct hire. In the 9-to-5 itself, I really loved the structure. You always know exactly what the expectations are.

Now, at the first sign of an inclimate economy, their first action is a reduction in forces. Now, many would say that this is expected, and to be fair, Assurant hasn't been laying off employees. In the last 30 days, I've seen them 1. Mark a position as redundant, forcing out someone who had spent 31 years with the company. 2. "Restructure" roles to force three others out who had been with the company for many years. 3. Shows zero compassion or appreciation for the work that these individuals, or others that have left, have done, or their contributions in a company wide communication. Your friends and former colleagues at other companies are getting promoted and growing their careers every few years because their employers believe in promoting and growing their employees. Meanwhile at Yamaha, employees are stuck in their same role until they quit, get fired, or die. You are SOL if you get laid-off because Yamaha did nothing to help you grow. The job title/role Yamaha restrained you with for years will be junior-level elsewhere when you leave Yamaha. Candidates much younger than you have now lapped you. You get older, but your career does not mature. There are many people at Yamaha in their 50s and 60s with entry-level job titles elsewhere. People Ops says it is up to the employee to determine their growth path, but this is not only ridiculous, but it is insulting and lazy. We do lots of family friendly events, so our kids all know each other as well. The training this company gives advisors is also wonderful- there are so many resources and experts to reach out to when an advisor has questions on something they might not have expertise in.

I've worked for First Command for almost 32 years now. I love our Mission of "coaching those who serve" and have seen firsthand the value our financial Advisors provide to clients, which include members of my family and me. As an employee, First Command has taught me the importance of "paying yourself first," and thanks to their generous profit-sharing plan, I can look forward to a very nice retirement when the time comes. Until then, I will continue working at a job I love for a company I'm so proud to be part of.

One's abilities and the accomplishments therein govern the path and success one achieves. As the sole business owner, the decisions and management style of others is not part the equation, as it relates to your day-to-day operations. Rather it is you the owner that charts your own course and manner in how you the owner pursues the goals inherent in that course. Owners have access to the best mentors, educational programs, principals. With that support, establishing a business model best suited for me, pursuing that which I deem worthy, and achieving success on my terms, based upon my merit is why I have chosen as a life long career, First Command.

companies.name: Meta
allPros: pay is really good and plenty

As part of the onboarding process we are given a robust 4-6 week training schedule alongside new talent acquisition hires to understand the intricacies of recruiting. I cannot recommend enough how informative and useful these trainings were to understand Meta's unique applicant tracking system and the various tools in use to facilitate the search and candidate management process. In addition to the onboarding process there is also a period of ~6 months where all new hires have an onboarding buddy, either on the team or who works adjacent to, in helping new hires ask questions as unique circumstances arise. The are resource galore at Meta, and they have their own unique Wiki page to find any information you may need. It's broken down for general employee usage as well as function specific - in short, what one role function can see, is not the same information someone out of that role can see. Unlike other large corporations that have a more strict policy & procedure in place, Meta allows you to cross-collaborate across regions, teams and functions to see a task or project to completion. There is much more visibility and agency into owning your work.

* salary/perks/401k contributions * A lot of really smart people to learn from and grow your skills. Well-seasoned "engineers at heart". * Access to incredible scale (of systems) not present outside of FAANG * If you get lucky, you'll get a good manager who has your back and maintains integrity and helps you grow. If you're even luckier, you'll get into a functional team with reasonable expectations.

If you are an engineer who loves autonomy and is self-driven, this is the place for you. This company is entirely run by engineers and managers play a supporting role. I've never had so much freedom to work on things I loved, try out new experimental approach without worrying about failure. My team members provide honest and direct feedback and help me be as successful as I can. Only results are rewards, failure is definitely not punished. This is definitely not one of those places where you can coast by not taking any risks. I have had several different managers and they have been extremely invested in my growth and constantly work on my promotions without me asking for it. The company takes fairness to a whole new level and ensures pay increases and stock refreshers are all formulaic. I have worked at several companies and Meta has been the fairest and also the place I have grown the most as an engineer.

- Very solid pay and benefits; - Coworkers are generally smart and nice people; - I have decent direct manager who address IC's needs pretty well, but this is team-dependent; - Meta experience is still valued by industry (based on my very limited job hunting experience)

* lots of toxic senior people and management that will use any excuse to cut you down and lie to your face repeatedly without consequences * Lots of insufferable politics that leave services in a terrible state and the team ends up with really high turnover rate because no one wants to stay * Extreme, constant, and unnecessary pressure to "perform" that may leave you with poor mental and physical health. * If there's no metrics to back anything you've invested effort into in order to do it right/better for the long term, it didn't happen and it doesn't matter. * Be prepared to constantly defend your entire existence and worth, especially if you're an early-career engineer. There's no trust in engineers, only engineers who become at least part-time politicians. Be prepared to become a blogger so you can advertise everything you're doing to people who don't care by posting to internal groups so that it looks good in front of management and is easier to "sell" during performance evaluations. An introvert's nightmare. * There's no "bottom-up" culture anymore, you do what you're told, or else.

companies.name: Family Health Centers of San Diego
allPros: I came to Family Health Centers hoping to learn more about integrated mental health and primary care. I definitely got that and so much more. It is thrilling to work in a place that values whole person care particularly for underserved communities. While I knew that I would learn more about integrated care, what I didn’t anticipate was all the new opportunities for me to be inspired by our department leaders, executive management, and also my fellow colleagues. I have grown so much in terms of my clinical, managerial, and organizational skills. The other thing I didn’t expect was the new and innovative ways that I have been involved in diversity equity and inclusion efforts, either through membership on a DEI council or workgroup, or through culturally-based trainings and related community engagement activities. I especially enjoy the monthly diversity trainings that are available for the mental health staff. My schedule is jam-packed, but there are many times during a week when I will take time to reflect on how I’m happy to be here at FHCSD. I am so glad that I took the plunge to switch gears in my professional path to come work at FHCSD. The work is challenging, but also very rewarding because of the clients, the colleagues, and support from leadership.

I have worked in different non-profits and the county system throughout my 14 years of service in Social Work. I took a risk when I moved to San Diego from a different county. I read the mission statement for FHCSD and wanted to a part of the team. The risk of moving has payed off! We have a very diverse population across all levels. There are different committees to become involved in, like our weekly diversity discussions. This is the first time I have felt absolutely supported by my immediate Clinic Manager, the Associate Directors and the Director of Mental Health. I have been able to see my direct feedback implemented on services to specific locations and populations while serving on our Mobile Counseling Unit. I have worked at two other stand alone clinics and have felt that my coworkers have been very supportive, especially thru the lockdown. It's also the little things that are important, like the type of programs and tools we are provided to make our daily work efficient. I have worked here for 3 and a half years so far, it has been the best agency I have worked for my 9 years of service as an LCSW.

Everyone in the organization really cares about the mission and are there for all the reasons. Leadership strives to make a difference in the lives of vulnerable and disadvantaged members of the community and continues to find way to reach and help those that need the most help. One aspect that is particularly rewarding is the emphasis on improving mental health care access for these groups. The organization recognizes the complex social determinants that can impact and health and well-being and focuses on serving from that perspective.
