Terribly run company that relies on overworking employees throughout the year. In my opinion, bdo operates like it's stuck in the past. The company uses outdated software and processes for work that is already being automated by companies both in and outside of public accounting. For them to claim that one of their core values is "embrace change" is laughable. The company operates on a churn and burn model for its hiring- overworking new hires in the first couple busy seasons to extract the most billable hours, only for those employees to burn out and leave. It wouldn't surprise me to find out if they have the highest attrition rate in the business. There is no real direction from the top on where the firm is headed or how they differentiate themselves. This shows in the ambiguous "culture" the company claims to have. Those in leadership can't clearly articulate what this "culture" actually is beyond the usual buzzwords. During busy season, certain offices hoard work leading to extreme and unnecessary burnout for employees. To make things worse, the admin task of having to constantly confirm and coordinate what clients you're working on (even if there are no changes) creates an unnecessary burden for client-facing professionals. I get that it's public accounting and it comes with the territory to expect long hours, but the inefficiencies and the lack of forward-thinking leadership at bdo make for a terrible working environment.

You were given 6 hours to learn about different parts of the company's service offerings and then just assigned to your manager. At that point, your manager gave you videos to watch, minor tasks to complete, and you were assigned to shadow your colleagues. There really needs to be a better onboarding and training program. Lucky for me, I am a go getter. So I jumped right into my new role, asked a ton of questions, found the resources I needed in order to get the learning and training I needed. It was just a ton of extra work to have to try to find my own way instead of it being provided upfront. I will admit that there is NO ONE in this company that won't stop and help you if you need it. Like I said, I asked a TON of questions and there was always someone that was able to help me or point me in the right direction. The team comradery at Arcoro is great and gives a sense of "No Man Left Behind" feel. I was provided with different colleagues names, people who were subject matter experts, to help me when needed. There were different team chats started for all new hires so that you can get the help you needed just by posting questions into a chat and it was well monitored. Though the training and new hire onboarding program wasn't the best, I was still able to quickly and easily find my way through the things I needed to. I have a clear understanding of what my role is, what my responsibilities are, and company goals that I can help contribute to. Prepare to fight for work life balance. Since Covid, the remote work battle has been raging here. Leadership expects staff to be in the office at least four days per week even though it’s not job required. The more frustrating aspect is that leadership refuses to admit the reason they want staff in the office: they do not trust their employees and have an intense culture of learned helplessness. Leadership, and many agents, treat support staffers like personal assistants, not people. I’ve seen a manager ask his admin to walk into his office, pick-up a document off his personal printer, and hand it to him. Many admins spend at least some of their time booking personal flights, assisting with exec’s other businesses ventures, dealing with wives, etc. These tasks are not part of their job, and they are not compensated enough to do them. Staff is underpaid. Period. It almost benefits you not to show your value. If you show that you’re good at your job, you get rewarded by getting to do someone else’s job too. Without a pay increase. Many people have quit without their positions being backfilled. Everything is focused on closing deals and supporting the 1099 contractors, which is understandable at a real estate firm. However, leadership should note this is often at the expense of the staff. If you are a TSCG employee, do not expect fair salary increases, continuing education, or even the ability to use your PTO guilt free. They will call you on your vacation and ask you how to covert a pdf to a docx. At the recent “university” 100% of employees were required to sit through 9 hours of training. That training had no merit for, or even anything to do with, the staff or property managers. It was 100% about the brokers, per usual. POC prepare to be tokenized. In a post-BLM world, clients noted how White TSCG was, and they began to lose business over it. Since then there have been surface level attempts at diversity, including a DEI committee, which is trying. Yet some leadership still gives big “I stormed the capital” energy. There are very few women or POC in leadership. I heard more racist and sexist comments than I can possibly count. The property management department is revolving door and leadership pretends like they have no idea how or why. It’s because everyone in that team is underpaid. They would rather grab people fresh out of college and throw them into a fire with zero training than pay seasoned people what they deserve. Sorry not sorry.

This company has terrible leadership. They take advantage of new people in the industry by overloading them with work and high expectations. There is an “always on” attitude about work and everything is “urgent” which creates a lot of stress. It’s impossible to take a vacation because everyone is so overwhelmed there is no one to cover for you. It’s difficult to get things done because most people are new and haven’t had enough training. There is freedom to make your own work schedule and you don’t have to be in the office every day, which is nice…but you must always be available. Property managers can leave the office whenever they want for a property inspection or meeting, but that comes with a price - 24/7 work ! Also, work is not distributed evenly amongst all staff. The more experienced employees have to do more work which isn’t fair. The turn over is extremely high, there are many people in accounting and property management that don’t even understand basic concepts and it’s very hard to get things done correctly. TSCG has lost a lot of business due to their messy accounting which effects property management as well. Upper management has no empathy and they will load up managers with other people’s work if someone quits, instead of just hiring someone. They expect everyone to work 24/7 and we don’t get paid enough. Property managers are seriously underpaid for all the work we have to do without any administrative support or assistant property managers.. don’t believe the false reviews. Yes the people are fun and they will reel you in with the ping pong table and free coffee but trust me, it’s just too much.

I am writing this review as a warning to anyone considering working at IBS of Annapolis. With over 10 years of work experience there, I have never encountered such a toxic work environment. I was subjected to micromanagement, verbal threats, and even physical intimidation. The owner, who initially seemed to have good intentions, eventually became a menace who constantly scrutinized our work and never acknowledged our achievements. The warehouse was not only micromanaged but also hazardous, with piles of pallets stacked in an unstable manner that posed a significant risk to workers. We were criticized for using necessary safety equipment, and on multiple occasions, I was threatened with physical violence by a former supervisor. Despite the owner being aware of these incidents, they were ignored and swept under the rug. Additionally, half of the company was engaging in illegal activities such as driving company trucks while under the influence and wasting company time and resources. The conditions at the warehouse were deplorable, and I suffered physical consequences as a result. The owner expected us to charge batteries at a dangerous level, and there were regular explosions that resulted in me developing tinnitus from the lack of proper ear protection. We were also instructed to clean old batteries with paint thinner in a poorly ventilated area, and sometimes without gloves. The winter months were also a struggle, as we were either exposed to the cold or inhaling diesel fumes from an outdated heater that ran on kerosene, which was deemed too expensive to purchase. Working at IBS of Annapolis caused me immense psychological and physical stress. The job itself was manageable, but the constant fear of dealing with the toxic work environment was unbearable. I developed anxiety and stomach issues from the constant stress and uncertainty of what each day would bring. I strongly advise against considering IBS of Annapolis as a place of employment.

Parental leave policies are fairly outdated. For a company that has so many women in leadership, I would expect to see this change in a few ways. First, equality across the board with parental leave - rather than "maternity" and "paternity" leave, which greatly vary in length as it is, and can inadvertently ostracize individuals who may not fall into one of those categories. Parental leave benefits should be standardized across the board, for all employees, entering their journey into parenthood. Secondly, the length in which parental leave is given, should ideally be extended. As it stands, new moms gets 12 weeks and new dads get 2 weeks (yikes). Would love to see a more progressive approach that is equal and only referred to as "parental leave," and also offers new parents a bit more time to bond with their new additions - 4-5 months would be a huge win.

companies.name: Glassdoor
allPros: I've been at Glassdoor as an Enterprise Account Executive for just over a year now, and I have to say I don't think that I could ever work anywhere else. I've never seen such a genuine focus on transparency and accountability, and I feel empowered to be true to myself. When I first joined my manager told me that "Not everyone will be your type of person, but everyone is a really good person.", and I've come to find that to be true every single day. Anywhere you go there are always miscommunications and frustrations working across different departments and teams, but at the end of the day everyone is seen as a person rather than an obstacle or just a worker. I've never had a situation that I went into assuming best intent and with a genuine attitude where I ever felt that wasn't reciprocated and I wasn't treated with respect. I've made some really close friends working here, and they're some of the most incredible people I've met in my entire life. I'm pretty happy with the pay and benefits, and I'm always finding competitions or incentives that let you bring in some extra $$ outside of just your standard commission check. They approach this in a pretty fair way, and with how much pretty much every member of the sales org continues to succeed, there's very few cases where any rep doesn't make more than their OTE. Paternity leave, fully paid healthcare premiums with a large HSA contribution that's almost as much as my deductible, and a really generous disability leave make me feel incredibly supported and valued. I feel a strong culture of innovation and striving to be better, while at the same time realizing that work is just one part of life. I've had some pretty serious health issues that have been challenging over the past few years, and for the first time I feel incredibly supported and enabled to grow and overachieve despite this. I've also found an incredible focus on career development as well as working on yourself personally and professionally. There's a huge focus on internal promotion and growth, and I'm excited for where things will be at 5 years from now. The last piece that I'll touch on is our amazing senior management. Whether it's the VP of sales being genuinely excited to see you and congratulating you on your last quarter, or someone on the C-suite sharing where we're headed over the next 5 years and carefully considering your questions, I feel incredibly inspired and honored to be a part of the team. Glassdoor is on a mission to do good in the world, and I truly feel like what I'm doing is making a difference.

At Glassdoor you feel like your helping and working towards a common goal of helping employees and would-be employees know whats happening behind the curtain at potential careers, again unfortunately Glassdoor has its own internal problems, bad managers, and integrity issues.
The people there are amazing and the office culture is really good as well. Management is also really good and actually care about you outside of work.

Glassdoor is the best company I've ever been employed with and I hope to have a long career here. Some of my favorite pros are as follows: 1. Benefits: * This is inclusive of PTO, Maternity Leave, Transparency, Remote Work flexibility, etc. I honestly feel like we have some of the best benefits in the market right now and I am extremely happy to have them. 2. People: * They people who work at Glassdoor are quite literally some of the best people out there. I enjoy everyone I come in contact with and love what we each bring to the table. Management is also some of the best. My managers have helped my elevate my career, are very people oriented, and words can describe how happy I am to work with each of the leaders I've come in contact with. 3. Culture: * Glassdoor puts in the effort each and every day to make sure that every one feels that they belong. The effort is what truly makes a difference in having one of the best company cultures.

- the GTM co-workers are some of the best around - amazing remote-first culture, very inclusive and no micro-managing - You get to work with clients to instill real change at a company and industry level. it goes a long way in providing purpose to our jobs - very heavy focus on supporting DEI internally, which is AWESOME! - lots of opportunity to give feedback

- Culture is like nothing I've experienced before. Co-workers truly assume good intentions, I haven't encountered any snarky or pretentious people. If you make a mistake nobody belittles you for it. - The mission is really important. Hiring seems broken everywhere, and Glassdoor is genuinely trying to fix it. -Benefits are quite good, with great health insurance family plans and wellness options like Classpass - Work life balance actually means something. I generally start and end my day at reasonable times and rarely need to work beyond that. Unlimited PTO and ability to actually use it is also great -Transparent leadership
Great environment to work in. The people were helpful and supportive. Everyone I worked with in leadership was motivated and pulling the same rope. It was the best job I've ever had.
My co-workers were great and very dedicated to their jobs. People are passionate about what they do at Glassdoor.
allCons: You'll find in nearly any sales organization that there are some administrative restrictions and niche ways that sales/quotas are set up, and Glassdoor is no exception. There are more than a few things that you have to get used to, but the grace and support of everyone that you're working with doesn't make it seem like a big deal.

Leadership has never handled layoffs well, you are constantly fearing for your job and those of your fellow co-workers. Sad because there was so much potential all those years ago I worked there, I’m so happy to be on the other-side, working for a company that truly makes a difference in this world. The same cannot and will not ever be said about Glassdoor.

Glassdoor has done layoffs twice in the last 3 years. I saw lots of amazing, hard working people leave that I thought would have never gotten laid off. I felt like my job was never secure there and I know a lot of others were feeling the same way. From the minute I joined I heard talks of layoffs for the 2nd time in 3 years. The partnership with Indeed is very frustrating and unorganized as well. It seems like Indeed is getting the better half of the partnership and Glassdoor is losing out on a lot of business. Glassdoor also doesn't pay nearly as much as other tech companies out there. This is across all tiers.

While Glassdoor is one of the best company's in my opinion, there are areas of improvement. 1. Career Track: *We do have a fantastic structure to help you understand what tools/skills are needed to get to the next level in your individual contributor role - which is fantastic. However, there isn't a clear track to move from IC to Management. For those of us that want to move into a leadership position it would be helpful to have something is place to guide us in that direction. Otherwise, how are we supposed to gain the skills needed for the position? 2. Pay: * While we do have a decent pay range, and a transparency chart to help us understand what to expect in each role, the compa-ratio structure is confusing and honestly a way I believe to keep you from earning more. I'd like to understand this better, to know how I can elevate my pay within my pay range. Other companies do have a higher pay in tech as well, so understanding this will help with retention in the future. 3. Transparency: * Our leadership does a great job and trying to keep all employees up to date with what is going on with the company. However, we were all aware of the economic state for some time now, and while measures were taken to prevent a layoff, it still felt as if that came out of no where. We were constantly given the news "it's the last resort", but can you let us know when we are about to reach that last resort? Otherwise you keep saying it for months and months and months and nothing happens, we feel as though it's still in "talks" but not happening. If we're going to be transparent, let's be fully transparent. 4. Indeed/GTM Partnerships * Working in GTM we work closely with Indeed, however, it feels like they have ALL of the control. While it's difficult enough as a CSM working with Sales Reps and getting them to understand we are NOT their assistants, now we have to fight harder to do our job because Indeed thinks we're their assistants as well. It tiring, and frustrating, and we feel like we get stepped on and looked over all the time so that Indeed and Sales can hit their numbers and our metrics don't matter. I'd like to have the space to have the relationship with my clients and really provide them with ROI, but it's a constant power struggle. We need to see BOTH Glassdoor and Indeed leadership come together on the same page.

- like most companies effected in the last 3 years, Glassdoor is grasping for a way to stay relevant in the market. Evolution and change is hard and the path forward hasn't been clear. - Pay is average at best. There has been a lot of changes to the compensation model in the last year with inadequate transparency around it. - Lots of turnover in mid to senior level management resulting in slow or halted progress internally - The partnership with Indeed is VERY messy and it often times feels as though Indeed is in the drivers seat for Glassdoor's future.

Job matches in particular have been wonky for a long time and frustrating to use, especially compared to LinkedIn. - Strategic direction could be more clear - Smaller company so fewer lateral growth opportunities, although you can definitely get promoted

Gem laid off 30% of the company which felt out of left field as it was described to us as "a last resort" only a few weeks before. It was done on a day we typically have a company all hands scheduled and our CEO decided to send a generic email to the entire company instead of announce the news in person over zoom. As a company that prides itself on transparency, support, and being a family; this felt like an easy out that was not in line with the values we had. I understand that wasn't an easy decision either way but it would have meant more to the team to not wake up to an email and calendar invite with access cut so early no one could download any of their work for their portfolios. There was definitely an ego that Gem was an amazing company that I think did give some employees a different level of entitlement. I think the layoffs was a good level set on this because it showed that even Gem isn't immune to the market and we aren't as invincible as everyone made it out to be. Additionally, a lot of leadership is too junior to be in their roles but had been in the right place at the right time when Gem was founded thus putting them in very powerful places when the company scaled. This can cause some friction when they are making decisions and doing things they have never experienced before. This is a common growing startup pain at any company but still worth noting.

companies.name: Boa Technology
allPros: BOA has hands down the best company culture anyone could ask for. Its very much a work hard, play hard atmosphere. Everyone is very passionate about the product and what they do, and truly believe that the company treats the employees well. There is constant innovation and new stuff being released, which personally keeps me very excited about what we are doing here. In addition, the benefits package is unbeatable and there are constant opportunities to not only connecting with co-workers, but to get involved with volunteering in the community. I think many people would agree working at BOA heightens your sense of feeling purposeful, both inside and outside of the workplace. Overall, this place is the best and I cannot say enough great things about working here!!!

Having worked at BOA for nearly four years, I can safely say that the company attracts some awesome, talented people. These folks make going to work a pleasure - it's been a great environment to learn and grow professionally. Our benefits are competitive and I always feel that the Sr. Leadership Team has my best interest when it comes to career growth and taking on new roles or challenges. Given the nature of the company, we get to work with so many different brands and athletes in different industries, which makes marketing at BOA fresh and exciting.

The company culture is something that really stands out about BOA. The company is packed with very driven individuals who take a lot of pride in the work they do. On the product development team, you won't find many people just looking to punch the timecard. Work tends to ebb and flow and it's not uncommon to have periods of high work, but you are surrounded by teammates who are supportive and working just as hard with you. It's been my personal experience that hard work above and beyond is recognized and rewarded. By no means do you have to be the super driven overachiever type to be successful here either, people have no problem balancing their work life with their personal lives and families. If advancing your career is your first priority and you are personally active in making that happen, I've seen many people make large strides in their career at BOA. The other very important thing about BOA is that it's not all work and no fun. It may be cliché, but people play just as hard if not harder than they work here. Most people have an array of activities they engage in outside of work. That may be typical of any outdoor focused company, but the company culture very much supports and encourages activity. Organically operated interest groups such as biking or climbing are abundant and easy to join for newcomers, the company brings in a personal trainer to teach fitness classes twice a week, and a yoga instructor that leads a meditation session as well as virtual and in person yoga classes. For those looking to engage socially with others the company hosts an impressive number of events every year. It seems like just about every other month there is a social event where the focus is simply having fun and getting to know people outside of your own department. There are other smaller and individually run social activities to engage with as well. Really, it's what you want to make of it, BOA provides seemingly endless opportunities for their employees to engage in actively and socially, it's completely up to you how much you want to take advantage of. It should also be noted that the company is very committed to giving back and being involved in the community. There are at least a half dozen volunteer event opportunities each year for employees to engage with. Those events range from hiking trail maintenance to building bikes for kids. The senior staff is personally involved in various community programs and the company will assist employees looking to make donations to charities. Again, the employee can participate in whatever way they want or works best for them. The benefits at BOA are competitive. The work structure is a hybrid of work from home and a couple of in office connection days.

When someone asks me where I work, I am proud to say that I work at BOA. BOA has shown me over the years that they truly care about their employees. For example, career development opportunities, competitive benefit plans, and mental health workshops. The positive list continues on, so if you are looking to be part of the BOA community I recommend you research more about the company.

I must acknowledge that the company did have some positive aspects that were worth mentioning. Despite my negative experience with the company's logistics department, there were several pros that I appreciated during my time at Ecolab. Firstly, the company did provide a decent work-life balance. They offered a flexible schedule, which allowed employees to adjust their work hours to fit their personal needs. This was especially useful for employees who had families or other commitments outside of work. Additionally, while the raises were not significant, Ecolab did offer small raises on an annual basis, which was better than nothing. It was a small gesture that showed that the company valued its employees and their contributions. The on-site gym was another perk that I appreciated. It allowed employees to stay fit and healthy without having to leave the office, which saved time and money. The gym was dated but had the basic equipment. Furthermore, Ecolab also offered a hybrid schedule, which allowed employees to work from home part-time. This was a significant benefit, especially during the pandemic, as it allowed employees to stay safe while still being productive. However, one downside to working at Ecolab was the favoritism that existed within the company. It was evident that some employees were given preferential treatment, which created a sense of inequality and mistrust among other employees. The also keep a fast track list of personal who all seem to get opportunity every two years. Overall, while my experience at Ecolab was not entirely positive, the company did offer several benefits that were worth acknowledging. The decent work-life balance, small raises, on-site gym, and hybrid schedule were all perks that made my time at Ecolab
Good pay, nice work environment
allCons: Personally, I’ve only worked here for less than a year, so I don’t know what there isn’t to like yet; however, isn’t it awesome to know that you will, at the very least, love your introductory to Ecolab??? I’ve worked for companies where I can’t even vouch for the team in the beginning stages! So far, the earnings are fair, the benefits are plentiful, and the folks are down-to-Earth — I have no reason to lie! I will say that it may be stressful here for someone who isn’t at least 30-years-old because y’all haven’t learned yet what to take seriously in life and what to absolutely roll your eyes at (INCLUDING YOURSELVES)! Many members of senior management, particularly in supply chain, have zero leadership ability. Extremely siloed departments mean that no part of the business works effectively. Company is extremely outdated and does not care to invest in updating - software, management philosophy, manufacturing practices are reminiscent of 1985 which can be extremely frustrating. Workload and expectations are absolutely unreasonable - expect to work 80 hours a week unendingly without getting everything done. TPM is aspirationally used without a basic understanding of the principles, so it just becomes a blame game exercise. Ad hoc reporting is created ad nauseam with the worst systems I’ve seen in my 20 year career. Feedback is a one way street and goes down the ladder only. Benefits were great at one time but are now pretty poor compared to competitors, with the exception of the pension plan if you can stick it out without working yourself to death. I truly worried about my direct reports having heart attacks and strokes from overwork so take that for what it’s worth.

The new "One Institutional" ruined this division. We used to be heavily commissioned sales professionals that did some service work here and there. Then we turned into hourly service techs that got incentivized on how much we sold. And the targets to hit swung wildly depending on what the company thought was going on at the field level. Also, we used to be compensated for helping cover vacant territories in the form of receiving the commissions that the territory generated and the customers that you took care of (Paid-Caretaking). With One Institutional, the new way forward is to suck it up and help the team. Sure, we got more hours, but what does it matter? We could work the same hours in our own backyards and actually generate sales. But every moment spent with someone else's customer for zero incentive was time and money lost. We told you that this was not right, but you said it was legal....good for you.

Beginning of 2021 was told we are separating service and sales. Here in 2023 that is slowly being eroded and have constant sales pressure as someone that took a service role as I’m sure numbers are down. On call 24/7 is pretty much a cause of constant turnover and leveling veteran reps being constantly asked to run 2 territories which leads to more burnout. Upper management capped earnings for the field which has led to everybody in the field not really caring or putting for much effort or not my job attitudes. When I was hired I was told this was a career, which I believed when I started. One institutional has turned it into a a job…A terrible one.

High turnover. Spread thin wearing lots of hats and covering for open territories. They dont pay the best for the hours of work required. Top down business approach leaves little room in the hands of the account managers to make good business decisions.

There are no bonuses if you don't have a manager title! They hide this from all employees. I must say that my experience with the company's logistics department was nothing short of frustrating and disappointing. The poor management, antiquated tools, and being cheap with the company's money were evident from day one. The company's lack of investment in its employees was glaring, and it was evident that we were nothing more than a number on a spreadsheet to them. The logistics department was plagued with outdated technologies that made our job more complicated and time-consuming than it should have been. Despite several requests for upgrades, the management continued to overlook our concerns, showing no interest in improving our working conditions. It was evident that the management was more interested in saving a few pennies than investing in the department's future. Despite being a profitable company, they refused to spend money on tools and technologies that would have helped us do our job better and more efficiently. To add insult to injury, a new VP was hired who, instead of addressing the issues, decided to hire 15+ new people right into the job. These new hires were given little to no training and were expected to learn on the job. After a year or so, the same VP laid off several employees, citing budget cuts (they all were over 50). It was a shocking and distressing experience, and I couldn't help but wonder how someone in such a high position could be so callous and unprofessional. Overall, my experience with Ecolab was nothing short of disappointing, and I wouldn't recommend anyone to work for this company, especially in the logistics department. The lack of investment in modern tools and technologies, combined with poor management, made it a challenging and frustrating workplace, ultimately leading to my layoff.

I have worked at Purple Communications for a year, and unfortunately, I have found the company's commitment to accessibility and inclusion to be lacking. While Purple Communications aims to provide communication services for individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have speech disabilities, there are several areas where they fall short. One of the main issues I encountered was the limited availability of reasonable accommodations. Despite my repeated requests for specific accommodations, they were not consistently provided, resulting in significant challenges in carrying out my job effectively. This lack of support made it difficult for me to fully contribute and excel in my role. Furthermore, the company's culture does not consistently foster inclusivity. I witnessed instances where individuals with disabilities were not given equal opportunities for advancement or were overlooked in decision-making processes. This created an environment that was not truly welcoming or supportive of diverse perspectives. Communication from management was also a concern. There were instances where important information was not effectively communicated, leading to confusion and frustration among employees. This lack of transparency and clarity negatively impacted morale and productivity. While Purple Communications has the potential to be a leader in accessibility and inclusion, there are significant areas for improvement. It is crucial for the company to prioritize providing comprehensive and consistent accommodations, fostering an inclusive culture, and improving communication channels to ensure a positive and supportive work environment for all employees.

I was lucky to have auto deposit through an app on my phone, so I could take a photo of the physical check (there was no direct deposit at the time, even though it was 2019) as soon as I got it and deposit it that way. Many other employees were not so lucky, and would have checks bounce. He does a lot of work at Texas Live; but not real work. Little side jobs like wrapping game tables. Expect to be assigned these tasks, but don't expect measurements or to be able to go there yourself to be able to make sure the job is designed to proper specs. You'd think that a sign place would have more to do at a place with so many signs, but I think that's left to the real professionals. I was asked pretty regularly to fudge paperwork and dimensions, in order to slip things past city regulations. All signage work is done on Illustrator, instead of the proper drafting software, so the computers are bogged way down all the time. Files are kept on paper, and are a mess due to high turnover. The owner tries to pit employees against each other; but it's pretty transparent, so it rarely works. I'm embarrassed to ever have been associated with this business, and leave this place off my resume. Fun fact - When Tiger King first came out, I thought it was funny because Joe Exotic reminded me of the owner 3Di, and the toxic work environment. However, the owner of 3Di is actually in Tiger King 2, as one of the "Free Joe Exotic" people. You might remember that even the insurrectionists at the capital on January 6th (because he was there - it's on camera) wanted nothing to do with these guys. So this is probably a good place to work if you're the type of person who wants to associate with that type of person. I'm not sure how else to put it. If you want to wrap Ted Cruz's bus and a bus that says "FREE JOE EXOTIC" and also be berated the entire time while receiving no guidance, you're set.

Capital Group use to be the place everyone wanted to work at due to its culture, long-term approach and history of taking care of it's associates. With the change in leadership and structure the sales Career has become linear in progression and can be capped if you do not desire or get the chance to go into an external sales position. There are other roles in the organization that you can take but it could lead to a cap in your professional growth. An alternative route is being a site sales manager, but this role is more of an order taker and order distributor role than a decision maker role. There are currently some incompetent and out of touch managers in place who are only there to collect a paycheck and weren't previously actually excelling in the roles of the associates they manage. They recently demoted managers who had the lowest tenure and were out of touch with the business, and even promoted some outward to flush out the fluff and incompetency, but it is still to be seen how this will affect the organization, and there is still more trimming that can be done. DE&I has become a check the box exercise where managers are explicitly told behind closed doors that their next hire has to be a diverse candidate, even if they are not truly qualified. The company goes for the two immediate visual characteristics that can be seen as Diverse - Sex and Color. This has led to poor hiring of under qualified associates, and excluding talented individuals who have earned the right to be promoted into roles that they would excel in. Lack of location Flexibility - the firm is globally requiring associates to go into the office 3 days a week due to the value they see in "team collaboration" but it's really a way of holding accountable underperforming associates, who do not work well from home. As a result of management not holding individual under performers accountable, the rest of the associates are punished. Finally, much of our new talent in decision making roles are coming from competitors like Vanguard and BlackRock and the culture that once made Capital Group different is vanishing. We are becoming BlackRock/Vanguard 2.0

companies.name: Sploot Veterinary Care
allPros: Wonderful place to work at!

Friendly people to work with for the most part, so I actually enjoy going to work in this industry! I'm used to more toxic environments and it seems like the gossip/cattiness is kept to a minimum here (only one unkind instance I've experienced so far for being different). Very nice that there are snacks provided and Doordash credit given on weekends. Direct RVT manager is very accommodating in helping you change your schedule when you unexpectedly need a day or few off!

1. Benefits are nice (401K, PTO, Health insurance). 2. Pet benefits are okay if you schedule an appointment ahead of time. 3. Snacks are always available which is great for the 10 hours shifts. Company pays for dashpass and gives $15 towards weekend lunches on doordash. Management also buys company-wide meals every so often. 4. Holiday parties! Team-bonding outtings. Very little drama within the staff. 5. Lots of opportunities for growth. Schedule is fairly nice, they try to give 2 straight days off. Overtime is typically approved when needed. Very good support-staff scheduled (~3techs per doctor).

Love working here so far! The atmosphere is welcoming and warm, and they take the time to listen and talk about any and all questions or concerns you may have. The pay is extremely fair and truly competitive, and the company is always openly appreciative of their vets, techs all the way down to their pet parent experience associates. It's genuinely a breath of fresh air to be in a work environment that works hard to keep everyone on board and happy.

Competitive pay, stocked break room with snacks and drinks, door dash pass covered for the entire year, door dash credit when you work on weekends. What more could you ask for?! Sploot is definitely a breath of fresh air in what can be a toxic field to work in. With so many locations opening, the opportunities are endless!

Sploot provides some of the highest pay rate for veterinary assistants in the Denver-area with amazing benefits. The community inside the clinics is outstanding and has provided friendships for me that expand outside the workplace. Everyone is willing to help a hand throughout the day. Sploot also prides itself on providing a work-life balance and management is very transparent and open to feedback.

I have been in Veterinary Medicine for the last ~6 years and what makes Sploot different is.. The team of Dr's and Technicians are phenomenal Gold Standard Medicine Work life balance They treat the team like family
Great work culture. Great work-life balance. Can have fun while also using my skills to care for animals and do what I love.
allCons: None that I can think of

Would be nice to have paid sick days and a 401K company match! Staff only get 25% off personal pet surgeries and dental cleanings...would be nice to have at least 50% off...please consider revising Sploot management! At cost medications for all meds please! Currently there is a very small at-cost medication list for staff. Also same day exam fee is not discounted for staff, which is not good when one of our own get sick unexpectedly. I personally would enjoy more scheduled surgeries/dental cleaning procedures per day...often only two or none. No Good Sam fund for pets in need or ability to discount services for struggling pet parents. Healthier snacks would be a plus!

1. No real "sick" PTO. It comes out of your accrued PTO. 2. you pay the "same day" exam fee if your pet is sick unexpectedly which is unfortunate. 3. No true "break". There's 1 hour scheduled as "lunch" but you are required to stay on premises and/or help out others. While this is to maintain the "urgent care" need, it does make for exhausting days when you are unable to have true down-time. 4. Lots of meetings.. you could have 2-3 meetings a week sometimes (team meetings, nurse-specific meetings, trainings...) 5. Management sometimes does not communicate well, whether that be changing policies, adding policies, switching doctor schedules unexpectedly, etc. Also, hiring process is not entirely streamlined.
No identifiable cons so far, but Sploot is new so it's certainly best to come in with a bit of piror experience!

However, that all changed in June 2022 when we got a brand new head of the department and after that, things started to dwindle quite rapidly. What then ensued was, a constant changing of processes that served no purpose or benefit towards the department or the team. But, were implemented so the new head could implement an autocratic, tyrannical and domineering management style. A mere and futile excuse to exhibit power, when the occasion never warranted it in the first place. These never-ending changes meant that we had to come into the office every day with no means of notice even though, the fraud department had been operating on a hybrid working policy for two years. Despite the team's personal circumstances: Childcare, travel costs and caring responsibilities we were still forced to come into the office on a daily basis. Furthermore, internal system changes to the department deliberately prevented staff members from establishing a positive career trajectory along with, development and promotional opportunities. Despite so many staff members rightfully leaving to protect their peace of mind and well-being, nothing was done to accommodate them nor was there a compromise to better the situation. This is because you were regarded as nothing more than a subservient, indebted, duty-bound wage slave expected to bow down and obey the master at all times regardless, of the impact this had on an individual's well-being. The idea that you are a human being with a personal life was not only unfathomable but, far too big of a concept to comprehend. I have never witnessed such a neglectful attitude towards employee welfare then I have in the CMT and fraud department. I lack the requisite words to describe, just how awful the treatment is towards colleagues in this department and how much I want others to avoid this entirely. I appreciate we are currently dealing with a poor job market and the cost of living crisis which makes finding a job that much harder. Therefore, I highly encourage people to exhaust every available option first before considering a job within N Brown.

When I worked at Sonicwall I enjoyed the comradery with my co-workers. While the work was never intellectually stimulating or satisfying in any real way, the social aspect of the company pre-pandemic was the main attraction. Unfortunately, when private equity (Francisco Partners) acquired Sonicall from Dell they brought in, along with a new management team, a toxic culture which included a two-tier employment structure.

Over the last almost 13 years, I have been able to do many different things throughout the organization. I have had the pleasure of watching SonicWall ebb and flow. The magic of team work exists throughout SonicWall no matter which department or division you work within. The culture is great, leadership is supportive and genuinely cares about the wellbeing of the employee and the employee experience. When something doesn't work out, leadership is there to help find a solution. They don't allow you to just throw in the towel and walk away. Sometimes they see things in you, that you wouldn't necessarily see in yourself. That is an important quality in leadership, and this is the first company that I have ever worked for where that quality exists. You get out of this company what you put in. Like with most companies, the chances to advance or learn something new doesn’t just appear at your feet. You have to be a part of the team, you have to put in the work, and ditch the “that is not my job” mentality. When you do, the return is pretty awesome!

I'm 67 years old, and I'm incredibly proud to be working for SonicWall, a major player in the high tech industry. This is a huge honor for me, and I feel like it speaks volumes about the company's commitment to diversity and inclusion. But I want to be clear: SonicWall is not a company that's behind the times. In fact, I've been consistently impressed by their willingness to embrace new technologies and innovative solutions. The company is always looking for ways to stay ahead of the curve, and I think that's a big part of why they've been so successful. Overall, I can't recommend SonicWall enough. They're a company that truly values their employees and is always looking for ways to push the envelope. If you're looking for a company that's going places, I think SonicWall is a great choice.

Francisco Partners has a deserved reputation for having sketchy ethics in their laser focus on profits. Non-management employees at Sonicwall are often treated as second class citizens. While those in management are given fancy job titles and multiple promotions, along with extra PTO and larger bonuses, non-management staff are held in low regard. This shows up in the paltry pay raises and rare promotions. In fact, it is obvious that Sonicwall's management (at the behest of their private equity overlords) doesn't give a hoot about the non-management employees because they intend to either send their jobs to India or automate the jobs away completely. Beyond this behavior, Sonicwall management also finds all kinds of excuses for denying employees bonuses, using fine print in some obscure "bonus policy" that is not widely disseminated among the company employees. While Sonciwall has pretensions of being a Big Boy company, its management tactics are those of a Bush League player. My advice to anyone considering working at Sonicwall is to Stay Away!! You won't regret it.

It seems like SonicWall has returned to many of its old ways. Over the past several years, there's been multiple reorgs within management that has pushed everyone else down the latter a few rungs, adding layers of management, and destroying the once communicative and fairly open-door culture that existed. There used to be plenty of transparency but that has evaporated to the point that no one other than perhaps the top execs will give you a clear answer on where the company is headed and its goals other than what's written in a presentation somewhere. That's if you are even given an answer at all. Often times, they'll provide just enough vague sentences to pacify you while changing or providing nothing at all. Furthermore, much of leadership is quite simply, not interested in addressing any problems that come up that they didn't identify themselves allowing things to snowball unsustainably. As vertically as SonicWall has grown, there is barely any initiative from leadership at all yet plenty of them want to show their worth by adding their own spin on everything that comes from the top to the point that it looks like pure disorganization and chaos from the bottom. When SonicWall left Dell after being purchased by Francisco Partners, the new owners cleaned house and then started hiring plenty of sales folks to help grow the company and take it to a new direction. However, sometime, not-long down the line, they stopped midway and failed to refill positions as they opened up naturally due to folks quitting or dismissal. While much of sales stays a slimmed-down skeleton crew, short of the total number of employees the company really needs to meet it growth targets on a consistent, long-term basis, SonicWall continues to invest evermore in the ever-growing leadership apparatus. If you're a leader at SonicWall, you'll probably get promoted every year and will never be short of opportunities. If you are anyone else in the company, you're likely to never do anything else at SonicWall than the position leadership hired you for.

The culture at amfam is to provide no growth opportunities, flood you with work, provide no training, and under compensate you. AFICS is not customer OR employee focused. It is a very stressful position that results in many people going on “stress leave”, taking anti anxiety medications, bursting into tears during their shift, or simply quitting. I stuck around longer than I should have because I cared about my coworkers from my initial op co. I hope they all find a great replacement job as I have done. If you’re considering amfam/AFICS run the other way!

AmFam/AFICS has been in a constant state of reorg for seemingly years. I entered shortly after one occurred, and was let go in the last one. For context, leadership dragged on the reorg for nearly six months, kicking it off by going back on remote work promises (attempting to make us come back in office, likely to kick start attrition to avoid paying severance), and then tortured staff by providing little to no details over a span of months. Keep in mind, when I was hired I was promised that my role would always be remote and that there wasn't even an office for me to go to near me (turned out to be a lie, there is indeed an office near me). Towards the end of the reorg, I couldn't go a week without being in a meeting with someone in tears or venting about how stressful this whole situation was. Internally the company is a mess as well, no one knows what anyone else should be doing. During my entire tenure with the company I had constant discussions with other teams what exactly knowledge management was, and no one seemed to grasp it. In fact the woman who eventually took over the group that included the KM team had been on record saying thinking the KM team was useless. This should have been something they cleared up on day one of the team being established. Processes are messy at best, with teams using multiple platforms, processes and methods to work that conflict with each other in bad ways. As a result, communication between teams can become broken and it will result in frustrating situations and missed deadlines. I would frequently have to suddenly turn around large projects over night because no one involved with a project actually understood what processes and procedure needed to be followed. So we would wait until it was an emergency. Additionally, AFICS brought in Mckinsey as a consultant group that assisted with the reorg. Historically they're known for being the grim reaper of staffing, and sure enough it resulted in me being let go. While it's a relief to be away from AmFam, they also did this in such a way that ensure they paid me the least amount possible on the way out. I have always been a top performer at previous roles, and yet somehow was constantly floundering in this chaotic environment according to them. They used this as an excuse to tank my annual performance review and cut my annual bonus to nothing before sending me off. Likely at the recommendation of Mckinsey, as the word from others noted that this years performance review cycle was particularly brutal and harsh for seemingly no reason. But if you know you are letting someone go, why pay them their full bonus? Finally, progress is frowned upon. A lot of the leadership is much older, and has been with the company for quite some time, which seems to result in being terrified of change. When I was hired in, I was told my job was supposed to be SharePoint development and had an extensive background in process improvement. However about 2 weeks into my new role I discovered that they actually meant to hire a copywriter, and really my skillset was useless. Any suggestion I made to streamline processes or assist with automation was shot down very early on, I was told that there was too much change and their employees couldn't handle more. I was snapped at quite a few times for trying to push process improvement out. Eventually I gave up trying to assist with this, because leadership pushed back so hard it just wasn't worth the fight. For reference when I was let go, I was given the option to apply for roles and retain employment with the organization. I declined to do so, and even though I didn't have anything else lined up the idea of no longer working for AmFam was more appealing than their paycheck. My mental health and happiness has been significantly better since I've left that dumpster fire of company, and I feel horrible for the amazing coworkers I met during my time there having to deal with the fallout of this botched reorg. Regardless of where I landed in this reorg, laid off or not, I have had these thoughts about the company from virtually the beginning.

I have now been Truv for 5 weeks and this has been my emotional Journey at Truv. Day 1: "Hope and Optimism", Day 5: Panic and confusion - Did I join the worst culture on this planet?, Day 35: EXCITED TO BE HERE! As a startup, it is imperative that the management clearly articulates and manages that culture. When there are conflicting messages, whether it is in form of unclear guidelines on PTO policies, or unclear feedback, it can lead to lot of frustration. This was the reason for the roller-coaster of emotions I felt in the first few days. Over the following few days, as I engaged with the leadership team, I got their thoughts and expectations and culture, team norms and behaviors, and very importantly context about some of the ongoing situations that had made me question my decision to join Truv. Truv's culture is that of a sports team working hard to win a championship. If we do not win, no one will remember that Truv existed. As such, at this moment in the company's journey, there is a singular focus to win the championship. We will win as a team and lose as a team. There is a high level of accountability that comes with a high level of autonomy. Each team member has a lot of flexibility on their hours as the focus is on quality output and even more importantly outcomes. Leadership has strong opinions, but in my limited time here so far, they are open to doing a full 180 on their opinions. There is no dog-eat-dog behavior, there is no expectation to work 60,70,80, 100 hours a week. Everyone works hard but there is respect for personal time and needs. Is one startup culture better than the other? In my opinion, it depends on what a person joining the team is looking for. If the expectations of the company culture and the team are not aligned, that is a recipe for disaster. I do believe that some of the recent departures were due to this misalignment. If hard work scares you, this is not the place for you. However, if you are ready roll up your sleeves, and just focus on the end goal, you will be pleasantly surprised.

companies.name: Cram Crew
allPros: -Your coworkers. Ranging from consultants to office workers, you will meet extremely intelligent and caring people. Everyone who works here is a team player and sincerely wants to help others succeed. You will encounter people of many different backgrounds with impressive educations who are great to talk to, to bounce ideas off of, and who may even become your close friend. The people are what make the job tolerable. -Looks good on your resume. The sheer volume of things you can learn at this company can surely pad your resume. If you stay long enough, you just might be able to make some (lateral) moves across the company, in which you can pick up a lot of transferable skills along the way that can make your resume and LinkedIn look a little more appealing.

Your coworkers are life-long learners who care about each other. I cannot say enough good things about consultants and coworkers. In the office, there's extreme opportunity for internal work and additional work. The culture has the feel of a start-up which is exciting for individuals who enjoy fast-paced and intense environments.
allCons: -Upper management. When it comes to direct supervisors and facility managers, the company has it made. The people in these positions are wonderful and helpful and do a really great job at trying to take care of their people. Upper management is where we crash and burn. Don’t expect anything from upper management besides superficial shoutouts in front of the crowd–and don’t be surprised when you’re spoken ill of by upper management behind the scenes. -Turnover. Whether you’re applying as a consultant or for an office position, expect turnover to be absolutely insane. Office turnover is unusually high and should concern you–the offices can’t usually keep anyone for even a year. As of my departure, the most tenured office employee (not including family..) had just passed two years–far below the national average of office tenure, which is 4 years. -Pay. Do not come into this company thinking you’re going to be paid fairly for your workload (which I’ll discuss later). The pay is abysmal at best, although you’ll be made to feel extremely guilty if you try to advocate for yourself and your need for a livable wage. If you live alone as I do, don’t expect to have a large margin of money left over after bills. In fact, bet on having to work doing something else on the side to keep yourself afloat. You may even consider waiting tables at a midrange restaurant to provide you with better pay and less stress. The level of intellectual work expected of you versus payout is laughable. Employees are expected to be gods of their trade while earning a salary that may have been okay at best a decade ago. If going after a raise, expect a lot of pushback, guilt-tripping, and manipulation. -Being valued. You will not be valued here. You might get a shoutout here and there, but anything beyond that is incomprehensible in this company. Whether you’re a consultant or an office employee, upper management will see you as 100% disposable, no matter how much you bring to the table or how much you have sacrificed. One slip-up and you are forever on their bad side. In my experience, I had to drop my classes to be able to work two jobs within the company (office during the day, consulting at night), all the while I was promised that my insane workload would be ending “soon”. I am well aware that the owner knows that I did this, and one year later I have never heard a peep about it, which I find ironic as an education company. Along the same lines, I was sexually assaulted by a student (“client”), and absolutely nothing was done about it, besides having a big meeting where I had to detail the assault to a group of three people that I didn’t know. I declined counseling for personal reasons, but I at least expected the student to no longer be serviced by the company. However, I later found out that the student was simply reassigned to a male tutor, and went on their merry way. Even if you get entirely sexually assaulted on the job, upper management could not care less about you or your experience–it’s all about making more money. Similarly, do not expect to be appreciated for your hard work. If the owner is in a bad mood (which can be often), you will be endlessly questioned and critiqued about anything and everything. You will be relentlessly picked apart via email and teams about trivial things that, in the grand scheme of things, mean basically nothing to the end goal of your job or projects. If you do not perform perfectly, you will receive a barrage of professionally-worded insults, and if you fight back or call it quits, you’ll just be labeled as someone who “can’t hack it”. -Workload. Chances are, you will be given way more than you can reasonably manage due to the comically small office staff (thanks to the high rate of turnover). Your team might be a team of one, where you’re doing work that could be sparsed between 2, 3, maybe even 4 people. Expect random and vague projects to be thrown your way–and don’t ask questions, because if you do, you’ll be talked to like you’re either the biggest idiot on the planet or like you apparently don’t know how to do your job. -Money/the budget. You will likely never see the fabled budget. You’ll be told you have one, but you won’t ever be able to see the lifecycle of the dollar made at Cram Crew. The only people who ever see actual dollar amounts are the family of the owner. Although these people are wonderful and do a great job in their positions, it’s very curious that the budget, which is brought up in every meeting or used as a weapon to deny raises or reasonable spending for the good of the company, can only be seen by the owner himself, or those in his own family. Five salaries might be freed up within a month due to mass exoduses of employees, but the idea that the budget is in apparent shambles will still ring through the hallways–however, the budget never affects the owner's ability to go on multiple trips a year around the country and globe, it will only affect you, your paycheck, your hours, and your department: you will absorb the blow, never the owner. Even in the company’s “worst financial state” (as is echoed in the form of many different phrases), the owner’s ability to spend extravagantly on himself while his staff and company suffer will not wane. -The owner. It seems as though everyone’s experience with the owner is the same. At first blush, he seems to be a reasonable and charismatic person. When you meet him, you’ll receive his “crazy entrepreneur” spiel for an hour and walk out of the room thinking you’ve landed yourself a job with the right person in the driver’s seat. Wrong. The owner allows his feelings and paranoia to dictate his behavior and business decisions. After a few months at the job, you can expect a few nasty emails to come your way that will be sure to kickstart your anxiety to carry you throughout your day. As a consultant, you can be punished for basically nothing if a client or their parent says one thing (even if it’s a lie) that looks slightly bad on you, even if you weren’t in the wrong. As an office employee, you will be attacked for things that you didn’t do or say, and even if you are proven to be innocent, you won’t receive an apology for your poor treatment. Prepare yourself for meetings in which the owner says illegal and immoral things (like threatening to fire any employee who speaks about pay, which is illegal), where you are yelled at or humiliated in a group setting, and where you are made to feel so uncomfortable you might just put in your two weeks the second you walk out of the conference room. If not in person, you might get really lucky and be called out by name in a company-wide email. Prepare yourself for emotional manipulation, where the owner might make you out as greedy for advocating for better pay for yourself, or where he might lie to you and use things in your personal life to manipulate you. The owner is well aware of his behavior and every few months will attempt to repent in front of the entire company in an uncomfortable meeting where he airs out his feelings. Although I hoped to believe he legitimately wanted to change his toxic behavior, I have learned that it’s just a cyclical ruse to keep people baited to the idea that it might get better. Don’t be fooled, it won’t.

A big challenge encountered has been management and work life balance. These two directly correlate to one another as the owner demonstrates an interesting lack of boundaries when it comes to employees. Experience of high turnover in office and in the field. An example of poor work life balance that I've experienced is the company forcing hourly employees to use personal PTO when they contracted COVID. I’ve never seen a company TAKE from their employees while they’re sick until working here. Taking unpaid sick time as an hourly employee would have been sufficient, but the company gives 40 hours of "credit" PTO at the beginning of the year that is deducted from your last pay check if you leave before the calendar year is up. In addition to work life balance concerns, employee handbook policies would change at the drop of a hat with no update from HR nor the owner, except in cases where immediate action needed to be taken on part of the employee. To give you an example of policy seemingly changing overnight, one of the few "perks" used as a feature to recruit employees was the ability to take your birthday off as a paid holiday. This perk mysteriously disappeared without notification, employees only discovering it was gone upon requesting time off as the handbook had not been updated to reflect that this perk for employees had been taken away. This example is a metaphor for pretty much every situation encountered with the overly hands-on CEO and a prime example of how business is ran and employees are treated.

The situation at the company has gone downhill since the takeover of Clarke Capital Partners. They have poor communication, no transparency, and make a lot of grandiose statements and promises they don't keep. The CEO is behind the times and out of touch with employees' needs. The past year has been very chaotic with a mass exodus of employees, layoffs, and now an extreme and poorly-executed shift in policy surrounding work-from-home and remote hiring. Leadership failed to anticipate the effect that a nationwide recession would have on its business, and instead of taking responsibility for its poor planning and bad investments (i.e., a giant new office building that nobody asked for), it's trying to blame employees and punish us by taking away benefits and perks.

- No additional compensation outside salary and $50/mo gift cards - Company culture on the decline with returning CEO forcing everyone within 50 miles to come into the office even though remote work was promised upon hiring.

I had to rewrite an old review that was titled "More good than bad". In the last year+, our CEO James Clarke has shown us that he, in fact, does not have our best interest at heart. In a sweeping attempt to..I'm not sure what.., he mandated a 4 day/8 hour in-office return and removal of half-day Fridays, effectively implementing a company-wide pay cut while giving employees two weeks to figure out the logistics of finding child/pet care, extra cars, how to afford time and gas for long commutes, etc., etc. Like many others, I had taken James at his word and when he promised no layoffs and no mandatory returns to office, I believed him. Like most others currently at the company, I was hired during the pandemic when Clearlink was selling their "permanent" remote-first perk. Waiting until the job market was tight to require such a life-changing policy is borderline horrific. I've never experienced this level of demoralization and I can say first-hand that the productivity that James said would occur has definitely swung in the opposite direction. I don't know who is advising this man or if the level of narcissism he exhibits prevents any advice from being taken. Either way, this was such a bad move, I have to wonder how James earned his level of success. Truth? The reason we're in a bad position as a company is that all the seasoned people left. More truth? It's going to happen all over again. Whether people quit immediately or wait until they find a new opportunity, the level of attrition is going to be insane. You can't treat people like this without serious backlash.

I’ve been grappling with whether it was time to leave Clearlink for some time now. There’s zero growth potential, poor communication and very little vision. Many senior leaders seem to lack a basic understanding of the digital media landscape. There’s no willingness to make the investments that are needed to be competitive in the long term. The benefits have also become terrible. Many people have had routine claims for healthcare denied or can no longer afford their prescriptions. But it became clear that the time to leave is now on Monday, 04/03, when employees were told they would need to return to the office by 04/17 if we live within 50 miles of an office. This comes after years of being told we’re a culture that embraces remote work. There’s no reason for this mandate, but we were told in an email that “we will all benefit from the relationships, mentoring, and elevated mental health that only in-person can work can provide.” Many people will be left scrambling to find child care and will now be commuting 2 hours a day. So please don’t pretend you give a damn about anyone’s mental health. A lot of employees moved further out because they were promised remote work would continue. Senior managers were blindsided by this announcement. Yet they were then forced to have meetings with their teams despite being shell shocked as well.

Everything was perfect until James Clarke took over. Everyone started quitting or being laid off. He’s slowly been taking away all of the perks of working here. They replaced our fantastic insurance with literally the worst garbage insurance I’ve ever even heard of. Now he’s forcing us to go back into a new office for anyone who lives within 50 miles of it, all day 4 days a week. Even though he promised he wouldn’t do that. You can’t believe a single word out of his mouth. And he does not address our concerns. He didn’t even consult anyone before he made this announcement, a mere two weeks before we had to do it. And after the announcement, they ignored 95% of our questions or concerns, and said they would answer our questions in a town hall meeting a week and a half later (three days before we’d have to be back in the office). Before this, all employees were remote, so you can imagine the insane level of inconsideration and disrespect for our lives and time here. I’d quit right now if I could. I probably will soon after I find a new job.

As many recent reviews have stated, we have recently been hit with a return-to-office mandate that has only provided us with 2-weeks turnaround. It had been disclosed to us on many occasions by all levels of executive leadership, that it would NEVER be a requirement to return/work in the office. Many people built their lives around those promises over the past three years and although I understand that sometimes changes are necessary, this situation has been handled awfully by our executive leadership. Not only was this EXTREME poor change management but also highly insensitive for many minority groups. As a single parent, WOC, I can't help but feel highly targeted in this change and as if they are trying to push more females out the door (as they are normally seen as primary caretakers in their households). I have felt undervalued and have lost all trust in our leadership team. Our executive leadership are the majority (white, caucasian, men), not only does this decision feel as though it is based on privilege, it disproportionately impacts various minority groups greatly (parents, neurodivergent). Unfortunately, this group is underrepresented, not only in leadership but in the company.

Utterly toxic work environment. No support from immediate supervisors, despite constant micromanaging, lots of smiling assassins. If you don’t plan on living and breathing Pepperells-including bombarding your nearest & dearest with social media advertising, don’t go. If you have children, they can never be ill, despite company policy being 5 day absence with covid, you can’t take the 5 days without hassle.

First and foremost, it is disappointing to note, Pepperells do not believe in bad reviews and therefore take it upon themselves to ask current staff members to place positive reviews on here, to outnumber the negatives. The same with their Facebook, you will hardly ever see a negative review as they are removed and the persons account blocked before you even realise. Secondly, the micromanagement is exhausting. The nasty and underhand emails which circulate on a day to day basis are nothing short of bullying tactics. Which leads on to the training upon your arrival and during your time at the firm, there is none. From day one you are expected to pick up your own work load and provide advice and assistance, when you yourself are not even sure of it yet. I have known junior members of the staff provide advice in appointments, which when has been repeated has been incorrect and ultimately negligent. Whilst it can be accepted, a lot of legal training is obtained through the work itself, this should be taken in steps and not to a point whereby within a two month time frame you are completely overwhelmed and thereafter spending your time on administration and being chased recklessly for things via snotty email, rather than focusing on the parts that really matter and never knowing if what you are doing is exactly correct. If you approach the board about your struggles, you are told the issue lies with you and you should "manage your time better" or learn to "prioritise tasks". No consideration is given to the fact you are running complex cases, some of which can take up an entire days work. There is no administration help and as well as running your files, attending court and client appointments, you are then left with the task of opening files, and all other administration tasks that follow. Not to mention being chased to generate bills on files for work which hasn't even yet been completed. The firms do well for advertising but do not be fooled as the positive affirmations and work which is completed within the community is not reflected in the work place. The staff turn over is ridiculous to the point you see people walking around the office and do not even know if they are a colleague. You can expect each Monday morning to see a flurry of new comers excited to start their career at Pepperells, to learn only months later they have left. Everyone in the firm is overworked and exhausted. There is little to no praise however because you get a free lunch and an award ceremony you best believe you should be grateful. I wouldn't mind but most of the time, leading up to the awards most people were heard saying they don't want to attend because they don't wish to celebrate such an awful firm and simply do it as it is an afternoon off work. If you look at the majority of solicitors to paralegals/interns you will see the firms works on a "cheap labour" module. Numerous uni leavers starting the firm in hopes of a bright future to then find they are working in an absolute hell hole and count down the days until they are able to qualify and leave some even have changed their career paths completely after being put off law. The firm itself does not have a good reputation to outsiders, most people you will meet will offer their sympathy that you ever worked there or will ask if the stories about how bad it is are true to which you will tell them, yes. There are very little to no repeat clients, and much like their staff after experiencing Pepperells once, leave to go elsewhere. Th only people who are genuinely happy to work at that firm are those whose pockets are being lined or those whom generate excellent fees for the firm. I have seen a number of talented people leave that firm and move on, and have flourished. If Pepperells had the time and drive to put as much effort into their staff's wellbeing as they do keeping their very chaotic social media active, they may have better outcomes in being able to retain staff. I think I could name no less than 50 people who have left in the last two years alone and 50 people is being nice! Your mental health WILL be compromised. No one wants to offer you help and no one is there to genuinely listen to you. Attending counselling in order to be able to get yourself to work will become the norm. You won't sleep and most nights, you will cry yourself to sleep after you've stopped working about 1am to the get up and do it all over again. In a nutshell you can never explain to people how bad things really are until you have experienced it yourself and even then i would not want people to go through it. Other law firms ARE NOT like this! Please, if you are looking for a career in law, do not approach this firm. This is not how law firms work and you should not put your career at risk for the sake of the poor management structure at this firm!

Firstly, the positive reviews they have are all from their current staff being forced to try out weight the real negative truth about the firm. Everything about that place is a con. Poor management, micromanaging, poor communication and unprofessional. It's very much like mean girls (and boys) The "managers/head of departments" are egotistical. They don't care about their staff at all. It's very toxic; this is highlighted by their quick turn around of staff. They don't know how to keep good employees or listen to their employees.
