If you take a job at pepperells and later down the line find something MUCH better (which wouldn't take a lot), and hand in your notice, be prepared to be walked out of the office. Their ego's cannot take the fact people don't want to continue working in their horrible company and departments. The hours aren't so flexible. It's pick and choose. You have to beg for this. It's a shame because the amount of people who are currently working at pepperells hate the company and management but still stay due to the false hope and promises of some head of departments. Stay far away from Pepperells. They do not have their staffs best interest. They think a pen, jelly beans and water bottle makes them the best firm to ever exist. What a joke.

This is, hands down, the worst legal workplace I have worked at. Pepperells is, chronically, a medium sized business caught somewhere between their small business management style, and trying desperately to be seen as a big business. Things are incestuous and spiteful, and genuine concerns and queries are either ignored or fall between the numerous cracks. When you start, you will be invited to their head office in Hull. This so called induction has two purposes; to give you your IT equipment, often a laptop with no bag or case, and to tell you how amazing it is to work for Pepperells. Do not be fooled, you will recieve no training on this day. You might not even be told about needing to be in Hull for your first day until the Friday before - this has happened to multiple people. After you have been given the merch (this varies depending on the state of the company at the time, but often a water bottle and a sticker, men sometimes get cufflinks and everyone used to get a pin), your laptop, and preassured (some may say forced) to invite all of your Facebook friends to follow Pepperells, you might think, like I did, that this was a good firm to work for, that cares for it's staff. Then you arrive at your working office on your second official day. If you are lucky, you will have a person in that office that suffered the first time around when they were hired, someone who has organised for you to spend the day with them to learn how to use the case management system, and the protocols (or lack thereof) of Pepperells. Most of the time, this person will not have been told the day that you are starting, or even that there will be a new starter. Pepperells air of secrecy is a well known issue within the firm. You will not be told when someone is starting, but more importantly you will not be told when someone has left. you could spend weeks waiting for a response to an email, sending follow ups, and come to find out down the line that the person you needed help from has left. This is because, when you hand in your notice, you are sworn to secrecy. No leaver is ever celebrated in Pepperells. Officially there are no leaving drinks. Once your notice is handed in, you are a traitor, and once you have left, it is expected that nobody talks to you again. It's very much like you have died. I watched an enourmous amount of staff leave this way. One day I called the second most experienced member of the accounts team, only for her to tell me she would have to handle it that day, as she would no longer be with the firm the next. The only exceptions I have seen to this are Maternity and Travelling, both examples where a person might choose to return to the Pepperells fold. Otherwise, you are likely to be marched out the same day, and forbidden from returning to the building to give back your work from home kit. You will be expected to meet someone on the corner to hand it over. Back to the subject of training. You get none. There is no official Pepperells training, it's on the job, in at the deep end, figure it out yourself, which while fairly common in law, is not generally to this extent. It is VERY easy for a new member of Pepperells to make a mistake when they have no guidance (and are being actively ignored), and later be discussed behind their back for it by more senior staff. I have seen emails, saved to a client file, discussing just that. The emails were later deleted from the file, and no action was taken about them. Gaslighting is very common in Pepperells. Quiet Hiring is even more so. I and other members of staff (staff who were qulaified, experienced and dedicated) were strung along for so long, all you can do is give up. Yes, you can have a yearly review with upper management and talk about your career progression, and yes, you can take on more work, but you will not be paid more for it and you certainly will not have a change of job title. It's a not very cunning plan to make it harder for you to get a better job. Do Not be fooled by Pepperells having a Head of People. Although their intentions may seem good, and they may appear as frustrated and tired as everyone else, it is their sole job to report back to the very top what you are complaining about, whether they mean to drop you in it or not. This has not ended well for anyone yet. The Peps Perks you will be sold, apply for the most part to Hull staff, such as the Thyme cafe, where Head Office staff can have a free lunch every day. On visiting the satelite office, and seeing that staff had filled the fridge with their packed lunches, one member of the Hull team commented on how it 'looked like a food bank'. Multiple, repeated begging attempts for more merchandise for events yeilded foam coasters, and four mugs. It was an embarrasment. Further embarrasment comes from being preassured to share nonsensical and depressing social media posts, while the firm pays nothing to actually advertise it's teams. There seems to be no understanding of touchpoints, or specific media targetting, from the decision makers. Pleas to advertise different areas of law in appropriate formats were ignored in favour of sharing the facebook posts. Pepperells takes wonderful, ambitious people of all ages and grinds them down and spits them out. I am eternally unsurprised their trainees leave as soon as they are qualified. I have never worked somewhere with such a high staff turnover, I have never worked somewhere with such disheartened staff, and I have never worked somewhere so stingy. Run, don't walk, away.

Furthermore, they hindered communication between our team and other counterparts, resulting in tasks taking longer to complete with inferior quality. Instead of providing feedback directly, my manager spoke negatively about team members behind their backs, creating an unpleasant and toxic work environment. Their actions and words were inconsistent and confusing, making it difficult to understand their intentions. When they did give us "feedback" to our face, it was done through passive-aggressive comments. I received many unclear tasks that were unrelated to my job and was expected to complete them with no incentive or negotiation. After these unrelated tasks became a big part of my routine, I questioned the situation, and was reprimanded for not being a team player. I was expected to be available 24/7 - sick days, holidays, days off. When I wasn't available for these reasons I was given passive-aggressive comments about my personal life, hobbies, and wellbeing. Although I loved my job, and still care so much about the cause, I could only tolerate such behavior for a limited amount of time. Eventually, I made the difficult decision to leave the organization, despite the significance of the cause. It was a saddening realization, but I had to prioritize my well-being and mental health.

Individuals who go above and beyond in their work are typically those who genuinely find enjoyment in what they do.
allCons: From this passion, people often worked 60+ hour weeks without fail or hesitation just to get the most done for the company. For me personally, my manager was in the office a rigid 50 hours per week, with other interactions while out of office (emails, slack, etc) and I was asked to attend meetings spanning a range of 12 hours (not in a single day), which allowed for flexibility, but hard to develop consistency.

Senior leadership doesn’t seem to respect or understand how to set teams up for success. The push to return to office has made it clear that leadership thinks they need to monitor and control behavior (and just have butts in seats to assuage egos). The org is in a crisis, and instead of focusing on defining a clear business goal and trusting teams to do whatever they need to do to chase it, leadership is ignoring business problems and micromanaging how teams structure their work and physically where they do it. Conversations about return to office have also been explicitly disrespectful of the realities of people with disabilities and have ignored the reality that parents are not dealing with the same child care landscape they were navigating pre-Covid. There is also a dizzying level of complexity in org structures, which makes it a massively high friction political undertaking to push a small action through. Most alarmingly, the org has been extremely slow to act on abusive and dysfunctional people in senior leadership roles. This is hugely disappointing, since decency is actually pretty deep in LendingTree’s legacy leadership’s DNA—but that decency doesn’t count for much if you’re not prepared to address inappropriate behavior among your peers.

- Poor management decision led to several round of layoffs on top of economy - Big increase in "Office" politics - Forced Return to office pushing much talent else where - Low moral - No clear vision on how to turn things around - Investing in products that have little to no ROI

-Management is lost. Doug the CEO has been there forever. They are chasing projects and growth in areas that managers and teams can tell will not be a win. Everyone is looking over their back expecting another round after being told after each that they were the last -Has completely reversed course on work from home. Mandatory return to the office and the CEO during every townhall says if he had it his way everyone would be in 5 days a week -Once you get you salary, expect it to never change. Executive and upper management decisions are concerning and have led us to a point where 13% of the company were recently laid off in order to save money in this economy. The mandate back into the office is forcing more great people to leave. Strategic outlook is questionable and now is not a safe time to be employed here.

Mandating employees to return to the office will not solve the challenges faced by the global economy, nor will it address the issues stemming from senior leadership's inadequate decision-making, at times. Double-digit attempts of the same project is not a sign of sound decision making, no matter the sycophant running it. The data organization has been slow to evolve, reminiscent of the 2008 era. It has primarily fostered nepotism and complacency, with a significant dearth of experience, teamwork, and effective leadership. Individuals in the data org who position themselves as the ultimate authorities on all aspects of applications, and the senior leaders who endorse this notion, display a profound lack of understanding regarding the realm of software engineering. The data org's mere existence in its current form is determinantal to the company. Lastly, it is important to understand that starting from 2018, HR plays a significant role in running the company, but unfortunately, the outcomes have been unsatisfactory. Some HRBPs lack sufficient experience and readiness to effectively address the genuine challenges that emerge. Instead, they frequently form support cliques resembling those found in middle school, catering to individuals with weaker personalities and a tendency for passive-aggressiveness. This approach inadequately addresses the core concerns and burdens managers with unnecessary personnel-related tasks.. HR needs to be reminded that running a business is an operational endeavor, not a playground or a game.

The top three areas that made this experience far superior to others were 1) "high quality communication" meaning that the ability of the hiring team to communicate expectations, coach, provide answers to questions, and ask questions in a respectful and thoughtful manner were far above the benchmark 2) willingness to allow the process to unfold naturally, rather than fitting it into a "box" meaning that instead of running candidates through fixed steps like a factory, they were willing to tailor the hiring process to my interests, needs, and availability 3) clear vision setting for the initial role as well as long term growth, meaning that the hiring team made it clear that hiring for long term growth was part of the goal for Waters. I have worked at six other companies, and none have been as organized, as focused, or as courteous throughout the hiring process. Of course, that is the "show room" so to speak. I work right next to one store that starts at $17 an hour and within a walking distance of many businesses that pay the same or more for arguably less work. Many supervisors I have spoken to only stay because the benefits are better here or they are in a contract with the company. Sheetz claims to care about its employees but I disagree. They do not make it easy for people to give direct feedback or suggestions as employees. They donate to charities such as Autism Speaks as well which as someone with family members with autism puts a bad taste in my mouth. Their attendance policy I think is not great. It is a points based system and you will earn a certain amount of points depending on how early or late you call off, no show, or leave work early. Once you hit 33 they do a point review with HR. You can bring doctors notes but these will not automatically deduct points, those points will stay till the review and are not even guranteed to remove them at review. Managers are required to maintain 40 hours a week which means anytime they get sick, have car issues, etc they have to use PTO to cover this time which is a lot when the beginning balance for supervisors is only 120 hours. (Working 10 hour days). The treatment of nightshift workers is insane. Depending on your store the nightshift will likely be understaffed and overworked, often having the most tasks assigned to them while also making orders, again, usually understaffed. The other shifts often do not appreciate them and talk bad about overnight.

- 24hour business creates conflict between shifts due to the workload - Business is not always the cleanest/safest due to a regression in their quality standards (Columbus Market) - Corporate enforced attendance point system REQUIRES at least 4+ hours of overtime work in order to remain in good standing - Points are given to employees even in the event of very common life occurrences (ie., calling off sick for less than 3 days without a doctor's note, leaving work early (even with manager approval/requirement (in the event of vomiting or the like) at times), and calling off -- even with more than 24 hours notice -- just to name a few instances of strict adherence to schedule). - Shifts are commonly understaffed, as stores only get enough hours to schedule a few people per shift -- generating mounting stress after back to back shifts with too few people for the workload demands. - Most holidays are required to be worked - Stores can undergo cuts in hours with little notice (Columbus market) - The company will force stores to stay open and be staffed in severe weather (aside from evacuation level threats or the highest level road closures), or with as few as 3 people, which includes the manager on duty, in the store to run a full drink station, register, sales floor, and kitchen with as many as 100 customers in the building at the same time --to including online orders and drive-thru business (in select locations). - Working can feel dissatisfying and monotonous due to the store never closing, and regularly having inconsiderate customers, causing the same tasks to be done multiple times (even in the same hour). - Company turnover rate is high and growing - Store Managers have little power to assist anyone except sales people, leaving management members to defer to a very disorganized and slow-to-reply corporate office, with even the most pressing issues taking well over two weeks to even begin to be addressed (Columbus Market especially).

They’ve never been careful about covid or put the health of their employees above having bodies in the office. We were required to come back July 2020, long before vaccines were made. Even after vaccines when there were waves of covid going around in 2021/2022, covid would rip through everyone at the office and there were no options for flexibility for anyone with health concerns. I think this speaks to how employees are seen how inflexible the wfh policy is. There’s a constant rotating door of new employees coming and leaving after a few months of employment. There’s no structure within the company. Because of this workflow and processes are consistently chaotic. Because of this, the day you start you’ll already be 3 months behind. This is pretty much an inside joke at the company, and it’s very true. If you are or were with a company that and flexible WFH schedule and are not sure about the companies strict 4 days in the office policy, think very carefully about how much being required to be in the office, as well as daily commute, will impact and take away from your work life balance. Also, don’t take employee longevity for satisfaction within their role or the company. Some people have been at the company for years and years yet have felt unhappy, demotivated, taken advantage of, and undervalued for years. But they have their own personal reasons for staying and do what they need to to cope. Also, if you’re applying for a job for a specific department and you’re not seeing reviews from that department here, it’s not because everything within that department is fine. They likely have these complaints and more, and their department is too small for them to feel like they can safely leave a review with their honest insights and feelings. Actually, their team is likely as small as it is because they’re not being given the financial resources and support they need, aka hiring additional team members. I will say, that while having a good manager will never negate the reality of the way the company is run, it can make your experience a smoother. A bad manager will make the burn out and mental toll significantly worse. In terms of what others have mentioned about the CEO, he comes for about a week every month and yes he makes employees during meetings cry. During that time you’re not allowed to have jackets or anything hanging on your chair, he’ll say something to you if you do. You’re not allowed to eat at your desk, he’ll throw out your food if you are and he’s there to see it. Your desk has to be very clean and organized. When people have been out of the office the week before he comes into town, they will come in during the weekends to clean up and organize their offices or desk areas. It’s unacceptable for your work area to be cluttered or messy while he’s there. If you think this is an exaggeration, you’ll find out quickly that it’s not. Work life balance is very hard. This company operates very differently from others, and you’ll both feel and experience many of these things when you start, as well as hear it talked about within your first few weeks.
